items.title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
items.summary: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. When one Region runs short of capacity A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. How cross-Region inference routing works Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use. SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably. Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does. You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why. A few terms describe the pieces: Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes. Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model. A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others. Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only. Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy. Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why. The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region. Figure 1: Each request goes to a healthy destination, with the router preferring destinations in its own Region How routing decisions are made The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance launches or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests. The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery. Figure 2: How each destination health state changes the traffic the router sends to it SageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own. When traffic moves, and when it comes back The more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted. When a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors. For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request. Figure 3: The router retries a real-time request once on another destination, and only when the model didn’t run Figure 4 shows where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model. Figure 4: Where requests were served as the local endpoint was overloaded, a destination in another account lost and regained access, and the local endpoint recovered What you can route The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. Keep serving when one Region runs short of GPU capacity. When your G-series instance type runs short in US East (Ohio) during peak traffic and requests start to throttle, the router shifts new requests to the same model in US West (Oregon), where autoscaling absorbs the overflow, and moves traffic back gradually after US East (Ohio) recovers. Route across endpoints owned by separate AWS accounts. When a central platform account owns the router and other accounts own the endpoints, each endpoint owner grants access to one named router, and requests reach those endpoints only through that router. We cover the setup after this list. Serve many models from one router. Create one router with one routing target per model, each listing that model’s destinations, and pass the routing target name on each request. Each model fails over independently. Put the router behind your own gateway. If you operate an API or model gateway, you can point its SageMaker AI integration at the router, so SageMaker AI handles Region selection for SageMaker-hosted models while your gateway decides when to use a different provider. For example, see the Salesforce post. Route asynchronous requests. Asynchronous endpoints, in the router’s account or in other accounts, can be destinations. Your application calls InvokeInferenceRouterAsync with the routing target name and the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) input location, and gets back an InferenceId and the output and failure locations, as with InvokeEndpointAsync. Protect a receiving endpoint from other Regions’ overflow. On a real-time endpoint, you can set an optional cross-Region traffic cap so that requests from other Regions can use only part of its capacity. Your endpoint’s local callers keep the rest. We cover the details later in this section. When a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination shows its status as unknown. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowOneRouter", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root"}, "Action": ["sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint", "sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync"], "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:endpoint/my-endpoint", "Condition": {"ArnEquals": { "sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-2:444455556666:inference-router/my-router"}} }, { "Sid": "AllowStatusVisibility", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root"}, "Action": "sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint", "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:endpoint/my-endpoint" } ] } In the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations. Figure 5: Controls the endpoint owner keeps: an endpoint policy that allows one named router, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap When the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use. You set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig, which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload. MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint is the share of that capacity that other Regions might use. SageMaker AI multiplies the per-instance rate by the instances in service and applies the percentage, so the cap follows autoscaling. For example, with 50 invocations per second per instance, a 20 percent cap, and 4 instances in service, the endpoint accepts up to 40 requests per second from other Regions. When autoscaling adds 2 instances, the cap rises to 60 requests per second. sm = boto3.client("sagemaker", region_name="us-west-2") sm.create_endpoint_config( EndpointConfigName="my-model-config-us-west-2", ProductionVariants=[...], # your existing variants, unchanged CrossRegionTrafficConfig={ "MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance": 50, "MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint": 20, }, ) Only requests from other Regions count against the cap. Requests from the endpoint’s own Region, including direct InvokeEndpoint calls and calls from a router in the same Region, are never throttled by it. When cross-Region requests exceed the cap, the endpoint rejects the extra requests before your model runs, and the router retries each one once on a different destination. If no other destination can take the request, your application gets a throttling error. The cap applies to real-time endpoints, and all inference components on an endpoint share it. For an endpoint that hosts inference components, load test one instance with its usual mix of inference components and payloads to measure MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance, and run the test again when that mix or your payloads change. If you leave out CrossRegionTrafficConfig, the endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic. Get started: One model in two Regions In this example, we deploy Qwen3-4B with the vLLM container as an inference component in US East (Ohio) and US West (Oregon), in one account. Because the inference router doesn’t support response streaming, the application sends non-streaming requests, and each request must complete within about a minute, the same limit as InvokeEndpoint. We then create a router in US East (Ohio) with one routing target that lists both: sm = boto3.client("sagemaker", region_name="us-east-2") rt = boto3.client("sagemaker-inference-router-runtime", region_name="us-east-2") sm.create_inference_router( InferenceRouterName="my-router", RoutingTargets=[{ "Name": "my-model", "Destinations": [ {"ResourceArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-2:111122223333:inference-component/ic-us-east-2"}, {"ResourceArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:inference-component/ic-us-west-2"}, ], }], ) Run DescribeInferenceRouter and confirm that each destination’s RoutingStatus is Routable before you send traffic. The application invokes the router with the routing target name and the same payload it would send to InvokeEndpoint, and reads the serving destination and routing reason from the response: resp = rt.invoke_inference_router( InferenceRouterName="my-router", RoutingTargetName="my-model", ContentType="application/json", Body=json.dumps({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"}]}), ) print("Served by:", resp["InvokedRoutedResourceArn"]) print("Reason: ", resp["RoutingReason"]) What we observed Step RoutingStatus in DescribeInferenceRouter (us-east-2 / us-west-2) Served by Routing reason Both inference components running Routable / Routable us-east-2 local-preferred us-east-2 inference component removed Unroutable / Routable us-west-2 only-healthy us-east-2 inference component restored Routable / Routable us-west-2 only-healthy Traffic back in us-east-2 Routable / Routable us-east-2 local-preferred Traffic stayed in US East (Ohio) while its inference component ran, moved to US West (Oregon) with no change to the application when we removed it, and came back after we restored it. The complete notebook for this example is available on GitHub. Tip: Use instance pools and cross-Region inference routing together. With a capacity-aware instance pool, SageMaker AI can use another instance type in the same Region at creation and during scale-out. The router moves new requests to another Region when the local endpoint as a whole can’t serve. For details, see Capacity-aware inference: Automatic instance fallback for SageMaker AI endpoints. See where each request went The inference router gives you two views of routing: a record on every real-time response and metrics in CloudWatch. Per-request routing record Every real-time response includes the ARN of the destination that served the request in InvokedRoutedResourceArn, and the routing reason in RoutingReason. The routing reason is one of the following: local-preferred – Served by a healthy destination in the router’s Region. capacity-available – Served by a destination with available capacity. failover – Moved away from a destination that couldn’t serve reliably. only-healthy – Served by the only eligible destination that was healthy. We recommend logging both values with your application’s own request logs. Asynchronous responses don’t include the serving destination. Router metrics in CloudWatch show where asynchronous requests were placed. Router metrics in CloudWatch The router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, labeled with the router, routing target, and destination: aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations – Requests per destination, with an error.type label on failures (invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx, or invocation_model_error). aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration – Time at the destination, including your model. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration – The router’s own work plus network time to and from another Region. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status – Each destination as healthy, overloaded, or degraded. Alarm on destinations that aren’t healthy and on the error rate across all error types. See Monitor an inference routers with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail. Figure 6: Requests per destination from the router’s CloudWatch invocations metric during the test shown in Figure 4 Each destination endpoint keeps publishing its existing SageMaker AI metrics in its own account and Region. To view them in one place, use CloudWatch cross-account observability and cross-account cross-Region dashboards. AWS CloudTrail records the router’s API calls (create, update, delete, describe, and list) as management events and router invocations as data events. You enable data events on your trail as you do for other SageMaker AI data events. Plan your deployment Keep the following in mind when you design with the inference router: Put the router in the Region where most of your traffic originates. The router always prefers destinations in its own Region. Size each Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you want it to absorb. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so configure autoscaling with headroom for the overflow you expect. To protect an endpoint’s local callers, set a cross-Region traffic cap, as described in Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap. If every remote destination reaches its cap, requests beyond the combined caps return throttling errors. Keep a low-cost standby Region. You can register an inference component in another Region and keep its cost low, but plan for how it gets capacity. A remote inference component with zero copies receives only a small share of traffic during failover, and those requests fail until it has copies. Keep at least one copy running, or configure autoscaling on copies and confirm that it scales out before you rely on the standby Region. Plan for resilience at the entry point. A router is regional, so if its Region is impaired, calls to it fail. Create routers in two Regions and switch between them on the client side. Register only destinations where your data might be processed. A request can be processed in the router’s Region or in any Region where you’ve registered a destination. For data that must stay in one geography, use a separate router, for example one for US data and one for EU data. You are responsible for configuring your routers to align with your data residency and compliance obligations. Keep your own retries modest. A throttling error means every destination was busy, and a service-unavailable error means no destination could take the request. A service-unavailable error after about a minute means the request timed out and the model might have run, so don’t retry it automatically. Remove deleted destinations from the router. Traffic already avoids a deleted endpoint, but the router never removes a destination on its own. Call the router privately. Applications in a virtual private cloud (VPC) can call the router through an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink), which supports IPv4 (IPv6/dual-stack not supported). Also note the following limitations: Response streaming isn’t supported. A real-time request that the destination doesn’t respond to within about a minute fails with a service-unavailable error. Each router holds up to 20 routing targets, each routing target holds up to 10 destinations, and real-time payloads can be up to 6 MB. For default quotas, such as routers per account and request rates, and how to request an increase, see Service Quotas in the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation. Conclusion Cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in multiple AWS Regions and AWS accounts. The router prefers its own Region, shifts new requests when a destination can’t serve reliably, returns traffic gradually after recovery, and shows you where each request ran and why. Your endpoints, models, containers, and autoscaling policies don’t change. Cross-Region inference routing is generally available starting today in most commercial AWS Regions (except me-south-1 and me-central-1), for real-time and asynchronous inference. There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. You pay for the SageMaker AI endpoints and inference components that serve your requests at standard SageMaker AI pricing, whether a request reaches them directly or through an inference router. The inference router publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the router’s account, and you pay standard CloudWatch rates for those metrics and any queries you run on them. For details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing. To get started, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation on cross-Region inference routing and explore the sample notebook on GitHub. About the authors Dmitry Soldatkin Dmitry is a Worldwide Leader for Specialist Solutions Architecture, Amazon SageMaker AI Inference at AWS. He helps customers design, build, and optimize generative AI and machine learning solutions, with a focus on inference performance optimization, deep learning, and scaling ML across the enterprise. In previous roles, he led teams at financial services, insurance, and telecommunications companies. Apoorva Chandra Apoorva is a Product Manager on the Amazon SageMaker AI Inference team, where she focuses on the endpoint experience and hosting experience. She works with customers deploying generative AI models in production to make accelerated compute easier to obtain, more cost-efficient to run, and more predictable to operate. Outside of work, Apoorva enjoys hiking, exploring coffee shops, and spending time with friends. Deepti Ragha Deepti is a Senior Software Development Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker AI team, specializing in ML inference infrastructure and model hosting optimization. She builds features that improve deployment performance, availability and reduce inference costs, and make ML accessible to organizations of all sizes. Outside of work, she enjoys traveling, hiking, and gardening. Felipe Lopez Felipe is a Principal AI/ML Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS. Prior to joining AWS, Felipe worked with GE Digital and SLB, where he focused on modeling and optimization products for industrial applications. Barkha Saxena Barkha is a Software Development Engineer at Amazon SageMaker AI Inference team, specializing in ML inference infrastructure and model serving optimization. Her work spans efficient multi-adapter inference, which serves hundreds of fine-tuned LoRA adapters from a single endpoint, and bidirectional streaming for low-latency, real-time applications such as voice agents. Outside work, she enjoys table tennis, painting, and puzzles.

items.title: OpenViking 3D 理解模型 X 汽车行业 Benchmark 数据库
items.summary: 原创 OpenViking 2026-11-19 18:00 北京 OpenViking如何理解整车数据 OpenViking 10月20日发布原生3D内容理解模型，支持三维.STEP, .DWG文件的导入与解析，信息还原率做到 100%。以如下整车模型为例，包含174个零件定义，445个安装实例。 导入整车模型，OpenViking首先会围绕零部件、装配关系进行拆解，形成【整车概览-车身-底盘-动力总成-内饰-仪表盘与中控-外饰-座椅-电子电器-空调-流体】的结构目录。 原始模型 整车模型结构目录 再基于3D理解模型，将零件拆分归类，分别解析出其中的几何、尺寸、公差、工艺数据，并保留完整的装配关系。 解析目录 正交六视图 轴侧八视图 信息摘要（含PMI） 模型明细 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 以上内容，OpenViking 均会建立索引，并用于下游模型推理。接入 Agent 后，可以在以下场景感受到价值。 场景一｜一句话找到设计参考 一位底盘工程师要做前置后驱跑车的后悬架，想参考捷豹 E-Type。 以前，你要在库里逐层翻目录，从底盘一路找到动力总成，再打开 3D 模型区分前后零件，半天才能整理出一张表。 现在，只需要将模型库、项目资料、采购清单上传到OpenViking，连接到你使用的 Agent。 对它说：“参考捷豹 E-Type 的后悬架，列出零件、材料和重量，说说布置特点，再估一下总重和成本”。 Agent 会跨目录找齐零件，按装配位置排除前悬架，还能看出每侧两套弹簧减振器的经典设计，最后给出清单：后悬架约 73 kg，加入差速器和半轴后为95.71kg，共29个零件和49个安装实例。 OpenViking + Codex检索 检索到的库内模型 模型信息摘要（含PMI） 生成的BOM清单及成本估算 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 甚至，当你说不出名字，Agent也能通过特征，帮你找到那个零件。例如：“发动机舱里那个装液体的塑料罐子是什么材料”。 OpenViking + Codex检索 检索到的库内模型 模型信息摘要中的关键信息 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 以后，产品怎么设计、用什么材料、有多重，一句话就能拿到参考。 场景二｜设计完快速估算成本 一位动力总成工程师刚完成变速箱方案，但他并不知道设计的零件、系统，成本是多少。汽车行业卷成本，但最懂设计的人却无法进行成本估算。 现在，只需要将历史的BOM清单、采购记录上传到OpenViking，连接到你使用的Agent。 对它说：“统计这台车变速箱的零件，按材料汇总重量，结合库里的单价和费率估一下成本，列出最贵的 5 个零件”。 Agent 会自动按公司的计价口径逐件核算，并给到结论：共统计出 42 种零件、99 件，净重合计 48kg。总成本为 2,348.61 元/套，含 12% 管理及利润。零件已按单价直接成本排序。 以后，工程师不仅专注设计，也能兼顾成本，甚至做到初步的采购，交付速度更快、采购成本更低。 OpenViking + Codex检索 定位到的目录 所有相关零件 生成的BOM清单及成本估算 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 场景三｜标准件归并，降低成本 一位成本工程师在为新车型找降本空间。整车有几十种紧固件，同一个规格混用了好几套标准，零件号越积越多，采购和库存成本也跟着上涨。但要逐个比对规格、标准和使用位置，人工几乎做不完。 现在，只需要将公司的紧固件目录、归并原则、采购单价上传到 OpenViking，连接到你使用的 Agent。 对它说：“整车的标准紧固件用了多少种规格？找出规格相同、标准不同的螺栓，给出可以合并的建议”。 Agent 会读取每个紧固件的名称和 3D 几何，名称里没写规格的，也能从直径、六角对边和长度推断出来。再按公司规则逐条判断：同为 M8×40 的六角螺栓，澳标件可以直接改成 ISO 标准；细牙件要先确认使用位置；英制螺母需要连同配合件一起替换。最后给出结果：参与分析的 47 种紧固件，直接归并后剩 43 种，待确认项全部通过后可降到 38 种。 以后，标准件归并不用再靠人工逐项比对，一句话就能找到降本空间。 整车解析目录 定位到的零件之一 生成的归并示意图 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 最后 OpenViking 作为首个原生支持 3D 理解的 Agent 上下文数据库产品，能够帮忙汽车行业快速构建Benchmark数据库，连接 Agent，快速找到设计参考 -> 估算成本 -> 归并降本，大幅缩短交付周期，降本增效。现在接入，点击「阅读原文」，即刻使用。 🚀 上手试用，前 50 文档免费： volcengine.com/product/openviking-service 🌟 开源 OpenViking： 访问 GitHub 仓库（https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking），为我们点亮一颗 Star！ ❓三分钟测出你是哪种 Agent 饲养员选择属于你的 OpenViking https://blog.openviking.ai/post/should-you-use-openviking/ 💬 加入飞书交流群&微信群！ 阅读原文 跳转微信打开

items.title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
items.summary: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call. Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste. The six optimization levers The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact. Phase 1: Configuration only, no infrastructure change With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching). Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response. Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes. Phase 2: Architectural changes Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer. Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains. Phase 3: Infrastructure and training investment Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers. Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment. In production: Four client engagements Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever. The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition. The second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks. The third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment. Results Outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. These savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works. Production governance: Four operating tenets Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record. These four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers. Getting started You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization. About the authors Ilan Geller Ilan is a Managing Director at Accenture, focused on artificial intelligence, delivery, and client growth. Steven Cox Steven is an Associate Director in the Accenture AWS Business Group and a Principal Architect specializing in AWS. He leads token economics work across Accenture client engagements. Manoj Ravulapati Manoj is a Senior Customer Solutions Manager at AWS who leads strategic AI initiatives, helping enterprises scale agentic AI. Rajdeep Banerjee Rajdeep is a Senior Solutions Architect in the AWS Cloud Center of Excellence. He works with AWS partners to design and optimize generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock.

items.title: PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
items.summary: Dialog-RSN-1, a reasoning model built for real-time complex dialog, is available today on AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It powers frontier dialog: agents that hear a live call, reason about it, and act in real time. As an AWS customer, you can subscribe to Dialog-RSN-1 through AWS Marketplace and deploy it as a SageMaker endpoint inside your own AWS environment. You can also deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker Studio following the steps in Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. That means the model designed to handle your customer conversations can be deployed like other Amazon SageMaker models with an AWS Marketplace subscription. Deploying Dialog-RSN-1 inside AWS Dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace. It runs inside your own AWS environment on the same AWS cloud that powers PolyAI’s compute and model training and serving. All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time. On SageMaker, it deploys as an endpoint like other models you run there. It is reachable from your own architecture, billed through your AWS account, and covered by the same virtual private cloud (VPC), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and monitoring you already have in place. You keep ownership of orchestration, telephony integration, and business logic. Dialog-RSN-1 takes off your plate the hardest part to build yourself: understanding a live call and responding to it in real time. The endpoint speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol, so an existing Realtime client connects through PolyAI’s bridge by changing its base URL. Audio in is 16-bit PCM mono at 16 or 24 kHz (transcode G.711 or Opus first). Connections last up to 30 minutes, and the model is English-only today. To get started, find Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace, then deploy it straight into an Amazon SageMaker endpoint in your own account. Or you can deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. With Dialog-RSN-1 now onboarded to SageMaker JumpStart, deploying Dialog-RSN-1 takes one click. From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open the Model Hub, select Dialog-RSN-1 from the JumpStart catalog, and choose Deploy. SageMaker JumpStart then spins up a real-time inference endpoint on a serving stack it has already tuned for you. No containers to wrangle, no instance types to second-guess, and no manual benchmarking. For automated workflows, the same one-click deployment also runs in a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. The Dialog-RSN-1 endpoint runs entirely within your own AWS account. It is deployed in your VPC, accessed through your IAM roles, and monitored with the same Amazon CloudWatch logging and metrics you use for every other workload. Because inference happens inside your account, your callers’ audio and transcripts stay within a boundary you control. For a model handling live customer conversation, this helps support your data residency and auditability requirements. Built for speed and accuracy Models built for live calls may make you choose between speed and understanding. And models built for speed may miss the meaning, and ones built for reasoning may lead to wait time for callers. Dialog-RSN-1 avoids the tradeoff. With PolyAI, you can build dialog agents that hear and handle calls the way your human agents would. These agents catch hesitation, hear frustration before it escalates, and know when to speak. Real-time customer conversation is the job PolyAI’s Dialog-RSN-1 is built for, and it is already handling live calls in production today. Because the model reasons directly over the caller’s audio, it picks up tone, hesitation, and timing, the signals a plain transcript loses, and decides for itself the right moment to respond. A model that hears calls the way humans do Dialog-RSN-1 is a model focused on real-time conversations. There is no separate speech-to-text step and no reasoning model on the appropriate moment to talk, so thereby no multiple handoffs. In practice, that means the callers get responses faster: Barge-in keeps working even when call volume spikes, instead of getting switched off to protect performance. Responses keep pace, so the model is not lagging behind the conversation while it reasons through what to say. Transcription is produced from the audio itself, because Dialog-RSN-1 is reading the actual audio, not someone else’s best guess at it. Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is the machine learning hub inside Amazon SageMaker AI, and it exists to collapse the distance between choosing a model and running it in production. For Dialog-RSN-1, that means the frontier of real-time dialog is a few clicks away. You can discover it, prove it on your own data, and ship it to a secure endpoint, all in one place. Here is what you get. Figure 1: The Dialog-RSN-1 model card in SageMaker JumpStart The code path using the SageMaker Python SDK is explained in our GitHub repository: Deploy PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker AI. Discover and evaluate before you commit Dialog-RSN-1 shows up in the SageMaker JumpStart catalog with overview and sample notebooks in one place, so your team can understand the model before spending a dollar on infrastructure. To try the model on your own calls, deploy the endpoint and run PolyAI’s sample notebook, which streams recorded caller audio and prints the model’s turn decisions, replies, and transcripts. One-click deploy and optimizations for your workload From the same model card you choose Deploy, and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart stands up a real-time inference endpoint with a pre-configured serving stack. There is no manual container selection or instance guesswork. The real convenience is the named optimization profiles: instead of hand-tuning infrastructure, you pick the target that matches how you run Dialog-RSN-1. Latency optimized minimizes Time to First Token for interactive, real-time calls. Throughput optimized maximizes tokens per second for high call volumes. Cost optimized minimizes infrastructure cost per request. Balanced is an even tradeoff for general-purpose use. Because Dialog-RSN-1 is built to respond in real time, you can use the latency-optimized profile to carry that responsiveness straight to your own endpoint. Before you deploy, SageMaker JumpStart surfaces the key performance metrics: P50 latency, Time to First Token, and throughput. This lets you right-size the ml.* instance for your traffic instead of benchmarking dozens of combinations by hand. You can run the whole flow from the console, or script it through the SageMaker Python SDK to wire deployments into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD). Figure 2: The Deploy workflow for Dialog-RSN-1 in SageMaker JumpStart Figure 3: Choosing an optimization profile for Dialog-RSN-1 in SageMaker JumpStart Deployed in your account, governed by your controls The endpoint runs inside your own account boundary: in your VPC, under your IAM roles, with the CloudWatch logging and metrics you already have in place. For a model handling live customer conversations, that means your call audio and transcripts stay in an environment you control, which keeps data residency and auditability straightforward. The result is a frontier voice model that deploys like the other workloads your machine learning team already runs, using the same hub, the same discovery and evaluation tools, and the same security posture. The hard part is the conversation Dialog-RSN-1 handles, not the infrastructure behind it. For more detail on the architecture behind our frontier dialog model and the evaluation results behind our benchmarks, read our Dialog-RSN-1 launch post. Get started today with Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace or directly deploy from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Also explore SageMaker JumpStart pretrained models. About the authors Helen Greul Helen is Senior Vice President of Engineering at PolyAI, where she leads the team building the company’s Agentic Dialog platform. Before PolyAI, Helen led engineering at Multiverse, building AI-driven learning products at scale. At Spotify, she shaped developer tooling and played a key role in bringing the podcasts platform to life. Vamsi Goparaju Vamsi leads Go-to-Market (GTM) and Revenue Acceleration initiatives at AWS, enabling Inference and ModelOps workloads for our customers, and driving OSS Use Cases and Product features for Amazon SageMaker AI, JumpStart and Generative AI. With over 16 years of experience spanning AWS, Dell, and Infosys, he brings a unique blend of technical depth and business knowledge across cloud, high-performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and analytics. He holds an MBA from Texas A&M University’s Mays Business School. Naidile Murali Naidile is a Product Manager at AWS based in Bellevue, WA. She focuses on enhancing the AI/ML developer experience on Amazon SageMaker AI, including new customer onboarding to Studio, SageMaker JumpStart model hub, and GPU capacity management for IDEs. Prior to AWS, she worked as a software engineer at HSBC and holds an MBA from Georgetown University. Gula Nurmatova Gula is a Software Development Manager at AWS based in New York, USA. She leads the engineering teams behind Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, making foundation models from providers like NVIDIA, Meta, and Mistral easy to discover, evaluate, and deploy across SageMaker and Amazon Bedrock. Prior to AWS, she held engineering and engineering management roles at RTX and GE, and holds a Master’s degree in Computer Science Dan Ferguson Dan is a Solutions Architect at AWS, based in New York, USA. items.title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
items.summary: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor. The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents act through tools, and tools move data Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Sensitive data leaves through tool arguments. The model writes the arguments from everything in its context, including details the tool doesn’t need. Ask an agent about a customer, and the customer’s name, account number, or email goes straight into a query to a third-party server. That server sits outside your AWS account and your compliance scope. Sensitive data comes back in tool results. Scraped web pages, CRM records, and case notes land in the model’s context, memory, traces, and logs. This happens even when the task never needed them. Documents bypass text inspection. Document tools such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Box, and Google Drive return a signed URL, not text. A filter that inspects strings sees a link and lets it through, and the agent then opens the original file. Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code. Example: A dispute-resolution agent at a large European bank Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes. An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen: The model builds the search query from everything in context. The search provider receives ‘Mateo Jackson dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’. That’s the customer’s name, sent to a third party, for a search that only needed the merchant. Scraped merchant pages bring unrelated personal data into the model’s context. The agent reads the original case note, with the customer’s full name, email, phone number, and card details. With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently: The search provider receives ‘[NAME_AJbrIud] dispute AnyCompany Electronics London’, where [NAME_AJbrIud] is a reversible vault token. The merchant results come back the same, the provider never learns who the customer is, and the analyst still sees the real name in the agent’s answer. Web content reaches the model already de-identified. The agent only ever receives a link to a de-identified copy of the case note. Solution overview The Skyflow interceptor is a single AWS Lambda function attached to both of the AgentCore Gateway interception points: REQUEST runs before the gateway calls a tool. RESPONSE runs after the tool answers and before the agent sees the result. At each point, it calls Skyflow Detect to find sensitive entities such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, government IDs, card numbers, dates of birth, and locations. It replaces them with tokens, or restores the originals. Skyflow Vault stores the original values so authorized systems can reverse the tokens. The Skyflow gateway configuration decides, for each tool, which of three protection modes applies: Shield the tool, Shield the model, and Shield the document. Mode What happens Who sees real data How it works Typical use Shield the tool Sensitive values are stripped from arguments on the way out and restored in results on the way back The agent and user, not the tool Uses reversible vault tokens, so values the tool echoes back are restored before the agent reads them Web search, enrichment, and third-party APIs that don’t need customer identity to do their job Shield the model Prompts, history, files and tool results are de-identified before the model reads them. The answer is re-identified on the way back Agent and user, not the model Model calls go through the gateway’s inference endpoint. On the way back, only the tokens minted for that call are restored Customer conversations, scraped web content, cross-Region or third-party models Shield the document The file’s signed URL is swapped for one pointing to a de-identified copy No one on the agent side Skyflow Detect v2 (preview) fetches the file, cleans it and stores the copy in an approved Region. The file never passes through Lambda, so payload limits don’t cap file size Case notes, statements, contracts in Amazon S3, Box, Google Drive Four properties matter in production: No change to agents or tools. Agents discover the gateway and sign requests with their AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) role as before. To shield the model, the agent points its model client at the gateway’s inference endpoint. The interceptor is otherwise invisible to them. Configuration without redeploys. The policy sets the direction, entity types, and token type (reversible vault tokens or one-way tokens) per server and per tool. It lives in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, and changes take effect without redeploying. Fail closed. If de-identification can’t complete, the call is withheld rather than sent in the clear. The interceptor fetches files only from allowlisted locations, and it blocks traffic it can’t inspect rather than passing it silently. Operations built on AWS. The Skyflow API key lives in AWS Secrets Manager. Every decision is logged to Amazon CloudWatch, with metrics for alarms, and the interceptor never logs credentials or original values. Architecture The reference architecture shows where each component sits. The three walkthroughs after it follow a single tool call through the Shield the tool and Shield the document modes. The following diagram shows how the interceptor sits between AgentCore Gateway and your tools. Figure 1: Reference architecture. The numbered steps match the following flow. The flow: The agent calls a tool through AgentCore Gateway, signed with its IAM role. The REQUEST interceptor matches the tool against the policy and, where required, de-identifies the arguments with Skyflow Detect. The gateway calls the tool, which receives tokens instead of sensitive values. The RESPONSE interceptor re-identifies the result, de-identifies it, or swaps a document URL, as the policy requires. The agent receives the result. The agent runs on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Alongside that flow, the interceptor reads its policy from Parameter Store and its Skyflow API key from Secrets Manager, and it logs each decision to Amazon CloudWatch. It calls Skyflow Detect and Skyflow Vault in an approved Region to de-identify and re-identify data. The targets sit outside the gateway: a third-party web search MCP server, a case-note store in Amazon S3, and a model in Amazon Bedrock that the gateway reaches through an inference target. For model calls, the interceptor keeps a short-lived record in Amazon DynamoDB of which tokens each call minted, so it restores only those. The record holds no original values. For documents, Skyflow Detect fetches the file directly through a presigned URL, so the file bytes never pass through Lambda. Walkthrough: Shield the tool This is the web search from the dispute example, step by step. The customer’s name leaves as a token and comes back as the real value, so the search provider never sees it and the analyst still does. Figure 2: Shield the tool. The customer name is replaced with a vault token before the search provider sees the query, and restored before the agent reads the results. Walkthrough: Shield the model This is the analyst asking the agent to draft a reply to the customer. The customer’s name and email address reach the model as tokens, and the draft comes back with the real values in place. Figure 3: Shield the model. The interceptor de-identifies the prompt and the conversation history before the model reads them, and restores the tokens it minted for that call before the agent reads the answer. Walkthrough: Shield the document This is the case-note request. The interceptor never handles the file itself. It checks the presigned URL and hands it to Skyflow Detect, which returns a link to a clean copy. Figure 4: Shield the document. The interceptor checks the presigned URL against the allowlist and size limit, Skyflow Detect fetches and de-identifies the file, and the agent receives a link to the clean copy. Here is the case note as stored in Amazon S3, beside the copy the agent receives: Figure 5: The case note as stored (left) and the de-identified copy the agent receives (right). A token like [NAME_AJbrIud] is a vault token, which an authorized user can reverse through Skyflow. A token like [NAME_1] is a one-way counter that nothing can reverse. The following video shows Shield the document end to end. The agent asks for the dispute case note and receives a link to a de-identified copy instead of the original. Video 1: Shield the document in action. Without Skyflow, the agent reads the original case note. With Skyflow on the gateway, it reads a de-identified copy. How it fits with the rest of AgentCore The interceptor complements the controls AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock already provide: Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore authorizes what agents can do, using Cedar and Dogwood. It goes beyond deciding whether a principal can call a tool. It can base decisions on earlier actions in the agent’s trajectory, control access to agents and models, stop specific arguments from being sent to specific tools, and check the data passing through the gateway using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Skyflow works alongside Policy. When Policy allows a call, Skyflow swaps the sensitive values in it for reversible tokens, so the call goes through without exposing real data to the tool or model. Policy decides what an agent may do, and Skyflow controls how sensitive data is handled when it does. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails handle content safety and sensitive information redaction for model interactions. Skyflow adds vault-backed tokenization and document de-identification to the same gateway. Use them together for layered protection across every model and tool call. AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS IAM stay as they are. The interceptor adds no credentials for agents to manage. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch record interceptor decisions alongside gateway traces. Deploying the solution The Skyflow interceptor is open source in the agentcore-skyflow repository on GitHub under the MIT license. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace. To add the interceptor to a gateway you already run: Subscribe to Skyflow in AWS Marketplace, create a vault, and store its API key in AWS Secrets Manager. Deploy the interceptor stack from the repository with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). It creates the Lambda function, its policy parameter, a DynamoDB table for model-call records, and the Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms. Attach the interceptor to your gateway at both interception points. A script in the repository does this and grants the gateway role permission to invoke only that function. If you manage the gateway with AWS CloudFormation or the AWS CDK, declare the interceptor there instead, so later stack updates keep it. To shield the model, add an inference target to the gateway and point the agent’s model client at the gateway’s inference endpoint. The repository also contains the complete reference deployment from this post, including the agent, the gateway, and its targets, which you can deploy with the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There are five ways in: Existing gateways. Attach the interceptor to a gateway you already run. Agents and tools stay as they are. New agents. Put tools behind AgentCore Gateway from day one. MCP servers outside AWS. Front them as gateway MCP server targets so their traffic passes through the interceptor. Document stores. Tools that return signed URLs are covered by adding their location to the policy’s allowlist. Model calls. Add an inference target and send the agent’s model calls through the gateway. Skyflow offers several vault deployment models and Region choices to meet residency requirements. See Skyflow deployment models. Considerations Formats. Text and Office formats (TXT, JSON, CSV, XML, JSONL, DOCX, XLSX, and PPTX) keep reversible vault tokens. PDFs and images are fully de-identified but receive one-way tokens, so the original values can’t be restored from those files. Availability. String de-identification and re-identification are generally available. Document de-identification through signed URLs uses Skyflow Detect v2, which is in preview. AgentCore Gateway availability varies by AWS Region. Before you deploy, check Supported AWS Regions in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. Document size and latency. Document de-identification is bounded by design. The interceptor checks file size before submitting, so a file above your configured limit is refused immediately rather than timing out. Files within the limit complete within the connection window AgentCore Gateway allows. De-identification time scales with document size, so set the size limit to match your documents. Skyflow Detect v2 is in preview. Validate latency against your own workloads and Region during a pilot, before you widen the rollout. Conclusion Agents are only as trustworthy as the data they move. With AgentCore Gateway and the Skyflow interceptor, you can enforce a privacy control at the one place every tool call passes through. It works in both directions, covers documents and text, and needs no change to agent code. Where to start Pick one agent workflow that touches customer data and calls at least one tool outside your account. List the entity types that must never leave, and the tools allowed to see them. Deploy the interceptor from the GitHub repository and attach it to that workflow’s gateway. Start with Shield the tool. Then add Shield the document for your document store, and Shield the model once the agent’s model calls go through the gateway. Watch the interceptor’s CloudWatch metrics for a week before widening the rollout. If you have further questions, see the Skyflow SDK documentation. About the authors Joe McCarron Joe is Head of Developer Advocacy and Product Lead at Skyflow. Joe spent the last decade building API and developer platforms at Zendesk and Apollo GraphQL before joining Skyflow to lead platform product management and developer advocacy. Sindhu Jambunathan Sindhu is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS. Sindhu works with ISV customers to build scalable, secure, cost-effective data and generative AI solutions. Sunita Koppar Sunita is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect in Generative AI and Machine Learning at AWS, where she partners with customers across diverse industries to design solutions, build proof of concepts, and drive measurable business outcomes.

items.title: Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick
items.summary: Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it. AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace. At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use. Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer. 1. Why Quick is right for Amazon sellers Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust. Quick knows your business, not only your prompts Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it. Quick does not stop at your Amazon store A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone. It turns data into decisions you can act on Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it. Your data stays protected on the infrastructure you already sell on Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate. The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays. The Amazon Selling Partner plugin The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. The plugin is in beta for US stores. Figure 1: The Selling Partner plugin consent screen, where the seller grants None, View, or Edit access per data category The permission screen is worth a pause. The seller grants access per data category, choosing None, View, or Edit for each, and reviews an agreement before authorizing. Nothing is all-or-nothing, and access can be narrowed or revoked later. 2. How to redeem the Quick Plus offer Claim your free AWS Quick Plus subscription (12 months free plus 10 delegated users, by December 31, 2026). Connect the Selling Partner plugin with one sign-in to your Seller Central account. It installs like an app. Ask your first question, something you would normally build a spreadsheet for. Figure 2: Connecting the Selling Partner plugin from the AWS Quick sign-up flow 3. What the experience looks like After the plugin is connected, the work happens in a conversation. You ask in plain language, Quick pulls the relevant live data, and it comes back with an answer and a recommended next step. Instead of checking a dashboard, exporting a report, and reconciling it in a spreadsheet, you move from a question to an answer to an action in one place. You review what Quick proposes before anything is sent. Figure 3: Quick diagnosing whether a sales dip comes from traffic or conversion, using live selling data 4. Two use cases a seller can build At the Accelerate workshop we had sellers build real agents live, from a plain-language description, in a few minutes. Quick turns the description into a working agent, which the seller then refines in conversation. Use case A: Inventory Launch Prep The seller is staging a new product into Amazon and wants the lowest total landed cost. The agent reads supplier data and weighs the fulfillment options per SKU on inbound cost, storage, and speed to sellable. It walks through placement choices and returns the output the seller picks: a shipping plan, a cost comparison, or a combined packet. It explains its reasoning and confirms before it creates anything. Figure 4: The Inventory Launch Prep agent comparing FBA and AWD fulfillment per factor and recommending a hybrid approach Use case B: Post-Launch Product Health After the launch, the agent reads four signal families through the Selling Partner plugin: listing health, inventory, sales, and traffic. It connects them to find the cause rather than just reporting numbers. Flat sales with healthy traffic points to a conversion problem. Flat sales with falling traffic points to discoverability. Good conversion with falling units points to supply. It returns a health summary per ASIN, the diagnosis with evidence, and a ranked fix list, labeling any low-confidence call. Figure 5: The Post-Launch Product Health agent’s weekly summary, with week-over-week sales evidence One honest limit, handled honestly: the selling data does not include cost of goods, so the agent reports margin after Amazon fees and labels it that way. When the seller wants true gross margin, the agent asks them to bring their cost numbers into the conversation. It never presents after-fees margin as if it were gross margin. 5. Skills and connectors in action The Selling Partner plugin and Amazon Ads MCP bring the Amazon selling and advertising data into Quick. Other connectors in AWS Quick bring in the rest of how the business runs, organized by role. These include a second storefront (orders and products from another channel), email and calendar (draft a supplier note, track what is due), team messaging (share an update), and accounting and inventory systems (cost and stock context the selling data does not carry). Because the pieces sit together, the seller can ask one question that reaches across Amazon data and the tools around it. 6. A seller’s morning, start to finish At Accelerate, Richard Brown, who runs the sneaker care brand Proof Culture and sells across five stores including Amazon, showed what this looks like. He had built his own AI assistant over time, and the hard part was never the AI. It was getting his selling data connected in real time. “The hard part was never the AI. The hard part was getting my selling data into it, and that is the part that is now simple with the plugin. With Quick and the Selling Partner plugin, just connect your account and start asking questions.” — Richard Brown, Proof Culture, at Amazon Accelerate 2026 In his demo, Richard asked Quick about upcoming sneaker drops and checked whether he had enough FBA stock to cover a major release. He had Quick model how far his current inventory would carry him. Then he asked it to draft a reorder purchase order and a message to his team. A morning of research across different tools took a few minutes. 7. Getting started Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus (by December 31, 2026). Connect the Selling Partner plugin. Follow the setup instructions to connect the Ads MCP within AWS Quick so you can manage campaigns conversationally alongside your selling data. Connect the rest of your business by role: your other storefront, email and calendar, accounting and inventory systems, team messaging. Start with one real question you would normally handle in a spreadsheet. Next steps: Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus Learn more about AWS Quick Read the AWS Quick documentation Media captured from the Amazon Accelerate 2026 workshop ‘Build It Live: Automate New Product Launch in AWS Quick.’ Non-Amazon tools referred to by role, not brand. About the authors Josh Anderson Josh is a Senior Worldwide GenAI Solutions Architect for AWS Quick. Josh works with customers large and small to adopt AI solutions that accelerate their growth. Jessica Fung Jessica leads Product Marketing for Selling Partner Agentic Primitives & Interfaces at Amazon. Jessica works on go-to-market strategy and enablement for selling partners. Jessie Nishimiya Jessie is a Product Marketing Manager at Amazon owning GTM strategies for seller AI products. Jessie’s work focuses on bringing AI-powered tools to market that help sellers simplify and automate how they manage and grow their businesses. Weiling Gu Weiling is a Senior Solutions Architect for Selling Partner Agentic Primitives & Interfaces at Amazon.
