items.title: System 1 决策模型在Feed场景的应用
items.summary: 原创 欢迎关注的 2026-11-19 18:00 北京 决策模型不写文本、只输出概率，在 Feed 推荐中对低活用户和新内容更准；改用 Decoder 架构复用用户缓存后，打分计算量粗略估算降至约四分之一。 。 点击蓝字，关注我们 作者 | Signal 导读 introduction 推荐系统追求既快又准，这正对应《思考，快与慢》里的"快思考"System 1。本文介绍百度 Feed 团队怎样把"只输出概率、不写文本"的决策模型用于推荐打分。这类模型靠语言理解和世界知识判断兴趣，在低活用户和新内容上优势最明显：历史点击最少的一组用户，uAUC 比精排高 2.95%。落地的难点是同一个用户要给约 1800 条候选打分。文章对比了 Encoder、Decoder、双塔三条架构路线，并拆解了缓存复用、知识蒸馏、FP8 量化等降本方法。 全文 5016 字，预计阅读时间 6 分钟 System 1 是心理学家丹尼尔·卡尼曼在《思考，快与慢》中提出的双过程理论里的快速直觉思维模式，又称"快思考"。它恰好映射出我们对推荐系统的期待——既快又准。 TypeSafe AI 于 2026 年 9 月 15 日发布了首个 System One 模型 Jev，核心定位是高速结构化决策：放弃自由文本生成，只输出带类型的概率化结果。它真正的意义在于确立了一种新范式：模型不写文本，只输出概率。 System 1 与 System 2：区别在输出方式 传统大模型偏"慢思考"（System 2），自回归逐词写出一段文本，速度慢，还得二次解析；System 1 模型更接近人的直觉反应，一次前向就把最后的隐状态交给一个小决策头，直接读出带类型的概率，比如点击概率 0.37。 只给概率，带来三点好处： 省掉逐词解码。生成 N 个词要跑 N 次前向，决策模型只跑一次。 概率天然可用于校准。它能和线上其他分数一起排序、融合、过阈值，不必再从文字里抠答案。 自带世界知识。底座是预训练语言模型，这是传统 ID 类特征模型不具备的。 Laya、Kev 等复刻方案里的 pointer head（指针头）同理：通用语言模型要在几万个词里挑一个，指针头只在输入给定的几个选项（如"会点""不会点"）上打分再归一化，既快，也不会答非所问。 GEEK TALK 01 项目「System 1 决策模型」背景 自Jev发布之后，Feed 团队加大了对 System 1 决策模型在 Feed 场景应用的调研。先用官方版本的 laya-multilingual、Jev-API 在 MIND-small 公开数据集与内部场景数据集上做推荐排序打分，初始 AUC 约 0.539，基本等于随机水平；但经过简单微调后 AUC 迅速提升到 0.6 以上，足以证明决策模型能胜任 Feed 打分这一关键角色。随后在实验阶段尝试了多种用户特征组合，并结合若干内容判别力字段微调，快速筛选出一组高价值的上下文特征。首轮线下评估显示，该方案已超越线上粗排基线，在低活用户上更是优于精排 uAUC。 一条样本demo： { "state": { "user": { "recent_queries": [ "某热门行业的岗位待遇怎么样", "该行业适合新人的岗位有哪些", "某岗位最新招聘信息" ], "recent_consumption": [ { "title": "某热播剧集的剧情讨论……", "category": "影视-影视资讯" }, { "title": "某教育话题的热点解读……", "category": "教育-教育资讯" } ] }, "candidate": { "title": "某演员在新剧中的表演评价……", "summary_full": "内容 Agent 产出的候选文章摘要（此处省略）" } }, "questions": { "click": { "type": "bool", "instructions": "结合用户画像、近期阅读兴趣和上下文，该用户会点击这篇候选文章吗？", "criteria": { "true": "会点击", "false": "不会点击" } } } } Laya具备更强的世界知识和推理能力、可有效使用用户和内容理解的产出特征，在新内容/长尾内容/低活用户的预估、 用户和内容的兴趣匹配上存在优势 Case： 一位历史点击较少的低活用户，此前点击过某篇民生政策类内容；系统为其推荐了一篇相关的政策解读后用户点击，决策模型将该内容排进前 5%，而当前系统排序靠后。可见决策模型能基于用户基础属性与少量点击行为，更好地满足个性化需求。 一位对历史与国内时政感兴趣的低活用户，面对一条突发时政内容，决策模型将其排进前 5%，当前系统排序靠后。决策模型具备一定世界知识，在新发布/突发内容上更容易找到目标受众。 越"冷"的用户，收益越大 传统精排依赖大量 ID 类特征和历史统计，用户点击少、内容又新时，就没多少数据可用。决策模型靠语言理解和世界知识，凭少量行为也能推断兴趣，因此在低活用户、新内容和长尾内容上优势最明显。反过来，重度用户点击行为已经很充分，精排本就足够准，决策模型能带来的提升也趋近于零。 GEEK TALK 02 项目目标 为此，我们计划在 Feed 推荐链路层面对 Decision-Model 进行重构，并成立联合优化项目「System 1」，核心目标包括：用更大规模的用户样本探明离线评估的效能极限，同时对在线决策模型进行性能调优，以满足低成本推全的工程要求。 1. 将样本规模扩大至亿级，验证 System 1 决策模型在推荐场景下的 Scaling Law 表现 圈定千万级乃至亿级用户，通过天级任务产出数十亿训练样本，协同多机分布式训练资源，验证"模型/数据/算力越大、效果越好"的缩放规律在推荐场景下是否同样成立，并探明离线评估的效能极限。 2. 通过将决策模型升级为双塔结构，降低在线推理成本，支持高效的线上 A/B 测试与效果验证 提取决策模型的 Last Hidden State 作为向量输出，并将 Item 向量预先缓存至内部存储介质。结合 User 侧的实时预估能力，以低成本完成线上实验的快速验证。 3. 构建标准的 LLM Scoring 架构，通过推理成本优化实现合理成本范围内的全量上线 利用 Decoder 架构完全共享 User 侧 Prefill Cache，将推理成本压至最低，以支持全量部署所需的目标算力规模。 GEEK TALK 03 项目方案 核心难点：user 部分能不能只算一次 Feed 的难点不在模型准不准，而在于同一个用户要对约 1800 条候选打分时，user 部分能不能只算一次。三条架构路线的根本差别，就在于 user 部分能不能缓存、又能缓存到什么程度。 这又取决于注意力能"看"到哪里： Encoder（双向注意力）：每个 token 的表示都依赖左右两侧，后面新增一个 token，前面全部要重算，user 部分几乎无法提前缓存。 Decoder（因果注意力）：前面的 token 看不到后面，它们的 Key / Value 一旦算出就不再变，可以存下来复用，也就是 KV Cache / Prefill Cache。user 在前、候选在后时，user 的 prefill 只算一次，就能被约 1800 条候选共享。 ① 以Laya为代表的纯encoder架构 laya的单次预估延迟极低（tilelang & fp8 & 1k-token单条预估能跑进个位数毫秒内），但是laya-multiligual(mmbert-base模型)天生的双向encoder注意力结构导致在工程上无法提前预计算，而且Feed场景对对链路延迟要求极高 user 编码无法预计算：上下文 state 是 user-nid 信息对，而 mmBERT 是双向编码器，每个 token 的表示都同时依赖左右两侧上下文；一旦后面新增候选 token，前面 user 部分的表示就会随之变化，导致提前计算并缓存 user-state 的收益非常有限。 双向注意力推理算力消耗巨大：受双向注意力结构影响，单卡吞吐有限，在严格的延迟约束（p80速度在数十毫秒）下，处理单个用户一次约 1800 条候选的预估，需要占用相当可观的 GPU 资源。 如上图，线上要对同一个 user 预估约 1800 条候选时，当前架构只能硬算 user-state（约 1k token 上下文中 user 部分占比约 75%），而 mmBERT-base 的 22 层 Transformer 结构让单卡算力相当吃紧。下面是精排预估与 Laya 预估的算力对比。 双向编码器虽有潜力，但这套架构后续的策略迭代空间比较有限。 主要有两点原因： 1、token 数越多，延迟越高。目前对 laya 架构做 32k 上下文 token（约 100KB 的 UTF-8 文本）的测试，单条延迟已接近 1.5s。而策略迭代的方向恰恰是往上加上下文，这块延迟又已经压不动，继续扩展的余地就很小了。 2、蒸馏方面，我们借鉴 tiny-BERT 的多阶段蒸馏：在 teacher 指导下，参数减半的 student 效果损失很小，但小流量仍需不少算力，推全成本会成倍放大。 结合近一周的优化，联合团队综合运用了多项降本手段——FP8 量化（把权重/激活从 16 位压到 8 位，显存减半、张量核心更快）、libtorch（PyTorch 的 C++ 运行时，去掉 Python 调度开销）、tilelang（为特定形状定制高效 GPU 算子）与知识蒸馏——并在线上申请少量 GPU 做真实压测，验证了合适的 batch 与扇出配置可将 P90 耗时控制在 数十ms 以下。最终在满足线上小流量实验标准的前提下，Encoder 路线的小流量成本相比初始版本下降到约三成。 但这依然是一笔巨大的成本开销（评估推全成本约数万张GPU显卡）。 ② 以Qwen为代表的纯decoder架构 既然双向 encoder 的 cache 复用有限，而且同一用户多次 nid 预估的 user-state 基本不变，那么不妨转向 decoder 架构尝试。 如上图， 请求入口一收到用户请求，就向 Decoder 预估集群发送 user 信号，提前触发 user-state 的 prefill 计算。这段计算在全链路上可与「入口开始处理」→「预筛结束」完全并行，可用时间窗口约 数百ms，且 user 只算一次（user-id hash 到同一张卡，保证缓存命中）。 等到预筛结束，再发起约 1800 条候选的预估，此时直接复用已算好的 user-state，只并行计算各候选的增量部分。 粗略统计，encoder 架构换成 decoder 后，在不考虑参数量与网络结构差异的前提下，单个用户批量预估的 1000*1800 tokens 计算量可降低至 750*1+250*1800 tokens（降低至原来的25%）。 更大的空间还是在 decoder。 user-nid state 现在各占 75%:25%，未来的迭代只会让 user 部分明显变大；而在 Feed-decoder 架构下，前面架构图中多出来的 数百ms 正好能把 user-state 提前算好。 效果方面仍有优化空间，decoder 模型选择众多，实际上找到一个（甚至多个）decoder 超越当前 laya 的效果并不难。 所以，我们整个 10 月份的训练工作基本集中在 decoder 架构上；若重点看 uAUC，已经很接近精排了。 目前这套 Decoder 方案已能把小流量的成本控制得相当低，按比例推算推全成本在1万张GPU显卡内。 ③ 以startlux为代表的双塔架构 双塔与交叉编码器的取舍 交叉编码器把 user 与候选拼成一个序列整体编码，两边的每个词都能相互关注，交互充分，但每个 user×item 组合都要整体算一遍。双塔把它拆成独立的 user 塔和 item 塔：item 向量离线算好、小时级更新，线上每个请求只编码一次用户，最后做一步向量匹配。代价是 user 与 item 的细粒度交互会丢失，精度通常不及交叉编码器。它更适合用来低成本验证，再决定是否推全。 借鉴传统的双塔做法，把 startlux-gemma、startlux-decision 0.8B/2B/4B 的交叉编码器（cross-encoder：将 user 与候选拼成一个 prompt，读取 A/B 选项概率）拆成 user 塔和 item 塔，item 向量可以离线算好、小时级更新，线上每个请求只需编码一次用户。这样评估下来，小流量的单次上线成本可降到极低水平。 此外，在线上应用环节，user 预估不一定要实时完成，可视情况调整为次刷更新、小时级更新或天级更新；更新频率越低，成本越低。 三条路线一览 GEEK TALK 04 降本技术全景 推理和训练的成本，大体取决于两件事：算多少，以及每次算多贵。项目的降本手段也围绕这两点展开，可分为四类：复用缓存以减少重复计算、蒸馏裁剪以缩小模型、低精度与算子优化以压低单次开销、LoRA 与前缀打包以节省训练资源。 ① 知识蒸馏：让小模型学会大模型的"判断" 蒸馏的思路是用大模型（teacher）的输出分数来指导小模型（student），让层数更少的 student 也能逼近 teacher 的判断。我们借鉴 tiny-BERT 的多阶段蒸馏，把 mmBERT 的 22 层 encoder 压缩到 11 层。四组对比如下： 具体来看： Accuracy 区分度不够：四组都在 0.91 上下。点击样本占比低时，一律判"不点"也容易判对，所以真正拉开差距的是衡量排序能力的 AUC 和 uAUC。 只裁剪：AUC 0.51、uAUC 0.514，几乎等于随机。层数砍掉又没重新训练，判断力也就丢了。 通用蒸馏：让 student 模仿 teacher 的通用表示，能找回一部分（uAUC 0.569），但对"点不点击"这件具体任务学得不够。 任务蒸馏：直接用 teacher 在本任务上的打分来训练，uAUC 0.652 反超原模型的 0.649，单条耗时也从 20+ms 降到 10+ms。 ② 低精度与工程优化：让每次计算更便宜 FP8 量化：把权重和激活从 16 位浮点压到 8 位浮点，显存占用约减半，GPU 的张量核心处理 8 位数据也更快。 libtorch：PyTorch 的 C++ 运行时，去掉 Python 层的调度开销，适合延迟敏感的在线服务。 tilelang：用来写 GPU 算子的编程语言，能为特定形状定制高效算子。Laya 靠它 + fp8，把 1k token 的单条预估压进个位数毫秒。 batch 与扇出调优：在线申请少量 GPU 做真实压测，验证 batch=20、单次扇出约 90 次时 P90 耗时可控制在 数十ms 以下；在小流量实验标准下，Encoder 路线成本相比初始版本下降到约三成。 ③ LoRA 与冻结层：让训练装得下、跑得起 全量微调要更新所有参数，显存和耗时都很大。LoRA 的做法是冻结原权重 W，只训练一对小矩阵 A、B，让更新量 ΔW = B·A，其中 r 是"秩"（这里取 16），r 越小，要训练的参数越少。再叠加冻结底部若干层，只训练上层，进一步省显存。 可以看出：冻结一半层更省资源，代价是 uAUC 下降约 0.0064。 ④ 共享前缀打包：训练时也复用 user 部分 同一个用户会对应很多候选，样本里 user 前缀完全相同。共享前缀打包可以理解为：把共享同一 user 前缀的多条样本放进同一个序列里，前缀只算一次，每条候选只补自己那一段。这和线上"user prefill 只算一次"是同一个思想——训练端是打包，推理端是缓存。 GEEK TALK 05 项目成果 Encoder 模型（laya）优化 联合团队采用 libtorch、FP8、蒸馏等多种手段，小流量成本相比初始版本下降到约三成。 Decoder 模型（qwen 系）优化 联合团队通过复用 user-cache 等多种手段，进一步大幅降低小流量成本，相比Encoder模型下降到约三成。 双塔模型（startlux）进展 决策-双塔模型架构充分利用提前缓存的优势，继续降低实验成本。 END 推荐阅读 从代码生成到需求交付：DarkFactory 的工程实践 研发Loop的上下文优化与多Agent协作实践 AI 内容核查怎么做：智能内容 AI 核查系统实践 QCon上海2026：百度 items.title: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
items.summary: GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics. NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation. NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator. KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope. In this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment. Choose a GPU sharing approach MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs. Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing compute modes. NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing. These are not security guarantees. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute. Amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options: MIG, time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin, and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter. For guidance on choosing among them, see the GPU sharing guidance in the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide. Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) provides Kubernetes APIs for requesting and allocating devices. GPU sharing and isolation depend on the device driver’s implementation and enabled features. KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. This walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not DRA. GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services. Choose each GPU-memory request from measured peak usage plus overhead, then test latency under concurrent load. The demonstrated density improvement does not establish a throughput gain or a universal cost reduction. Solution overview The following diagram shows the validated single-GPU environment in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2). You use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), eksctl, Helm, and Packer to build and operate it. The Amazon EKS control plane runs Kubernetes version 1.36 in an AWS managed Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), separate from the customer VPC. It connects to EC2 workers in private subnets of the customer VPC. An m7i.large system node hosts the operator controllers and KAI Scheduler. KAI Scheduler places both Pods on a tainted g5.xlarge with one A10G containing 23,028 MiB of GPU memory. Each Pod has an 8 GiB GPU-memory limit and allocates 6 GiB of GPU memory. The GPU worker uses custom AL2023 with the NVIDIA R615 driver branch, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and containerd. It runs fractiond with Node Resource Interface (NRI) integration and MPS for sharing. The metricsd daemon exports per-Pod GPU-memory metrics. Figure 1: Validated example of two GPU-memory contracts on one A10G in Amazon EKS Implementation walkthrough The walkthrough uses the AWS Samples repository. Confirm the prerequisites and validated component versions, then complete Steps 1 through 10. Prerequisites Use an AWS account with permissions for Amazon EKS, AWS CloudFormation, Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and AWS Systems Manager for Amazon Machine Image (AMI) discovery. Confirm quota and capacity for g5.xlarge, the system node, and a temporary m5.xlarge image builder. Install AWS CLI v2, eksctl, kubectl, Helm, Packer, Git, jq, and curl. Use your normal AWS credential provider: a named profile, AWS IAM Identity Center, an assumed role, or access-key environment variables. Prefer temporary credentials. AWS_SESSION_TOKEN is required when using temporary access keys. The examples use us-east-2. Another Region must support the selected Amazon EKS version and instance types. Before choosing another GPU, check NVIDIA’s GPU Operator hardware list, the selected driver’s hardware support, and the GPU Fractioning Operator prerequisites. Hardware support alone does not establish fractioning compatibility. This walkthrough validates the G5/A10G configuration only. The AMI build targets x86_64. Check CUDA compatibility and memory headroom: The two 8 GiB contracts require room for both contracts and runtime overhead. Smaller devices need smaller contracts and adjusted probes. The walkthrough creates billable resources, including an Amazon EKS control plane, a NAT gateway, instances, volumes, and an AMI snapshot. Use a disposable environment and complete cleanup when validation finishes. Use the validated AL2023 stack At the time of validation, the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA image provided R580 and R595 driver branches. GPU Fractioning Operator v0.1.7 requires R615 or newer. R615 is short-lived and is not the GPU Operator default. This example builds a custom standard Amazon EKS 1.36 AL2023 image with AMI-owned driver and toolkit. It does not use an operator-managed driver container on another OS. The table records lab validation, not vendor support certification. Component Validated version Amazon EKS 1.36 GPU NVIDIA A10G, 23,028 MiB NVIDIA driver / Container Toolkit 615.71.10 / 1.20.1-1 containerd 2.3.5 with NRI GPU Operator / device plugin 26.7.1 / 0.20.1 KAI Scheduler / Fractioning Operator 0.18.5 / 0.1.7 We validated this walkthrough on October 22, 2026, using NVIDIA driver 615.71.10. On November 18, 2026, after updating the GPU node taint, we repeated every step except the Step 3 image build, using an image with the same driver. The results matched. The table lists the tested component versions, not a permanent support matrix. Recheck the Amazon EKS AMI documentation and NVIDIA prerequisites before changing any component. Step 1: Clone and configure Clone the repository, then create a local configuration file from the provided example and restrict its permissions: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-code-for-gpu-fractioning-on-eks.git cd sample-code-for-gpu-fractioning-on-eks cp walkthrough.env.example walkthrough.env chmod 600 walkthrough.env After cloning, use walkthrough.env for configuration and run.sh for each stage. Generated files and kubeconfig stay in the ignored .state directory. GPU_INSTANCE_TYPE selects the instance type. Changing it alone does not establish compatibility. Defaults and optional authentication settings in walkthrough.env AWS_REGION=us-east-2 CLUSTER_NAME=runai-fractioning-blog EKS_VERSION=1.36 GPU_INSTANCE_TYPE=g5.xlarge NVIDIA_DRIVER_VERSION=615.71.10 # Choose a profile or access-key variables, not both. # AWS_PROFILE=my-profile # AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=YOUR_ACCESS_KEY_ID # AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=YOUR_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY # AWS_SESSION_TOKEN=YOUR_SESSION_TOKEN Never commit credentials. The local configuration file is ignored by Git. Confirm the active identity before provisioning: ./run.sh check Run stages separately to inspect results, or use ./run.sh walkthrough to run through the memory-limit test. Cleanup is always a separate action. Step 2: Create the disposable cluster Run the following command to create the disposable Amazon EKS cluster and its system node: ./run.sh create-cluster The command provisions an Amazon EKS cluster running Kubernetes version 1.36, a dedicated VPC with one NAT gateway, OpenID Connect (OIDC) integration, and a private m7i.large managed node. Selected fields from config/eksctl-cluster.yaml.tpl iam: withOIDC: true vpc: nat: gateway: Single managedNodeGroups: - name: system-ondemand instanceType: m7i.large desiredCapacity: 1 privateNetworking: true Step 3: Build the custom AL2023 image Run the following command to build the custom AL2023 image with the R615 driver branch: ./run.sh build-ami The script discovers a public builder subnet and the recommended standard Amazon EKS AMI for Kubernetes 1.36 on AL2023. Packer installs the current patch release from the R615 driver branch and the toolkit, configures the NVIDIA runtime, checks package state, and creates an encrypted image. The Region-specific AMI ID is stored in .state/ami-id. NVIDIA_DRIVER_VERSION selects the R615 branch. It is not an exact patch pin. The workflow records the discovered driver version with the AMI ID and uses that version in AMI and node-group tags. Read .state/installed-driver-version for the version observed in your build. For production, pin exact packages and the base image in your own build and validate a supported driver-branch upgrade. You need this step only because the EKS-optimized AL2023 NVIDIA AMI did not include the R615 driver branch at the time of validation. Prefer an EKS-optimized NVIDIA AMI once the driver that it selects for your GPU and the remaining host prerequisites meet the GPU Fractioning Operator requirements. Check the driver versions in the Amazon EKS AMI releases on GitHub. The sample’s scripts currently require the R615 driver and metadata from the image build, so using a stock AMI also requires script changes. Relevant Packer settings from ami/eks-al2023-r615.pkr.hcl source "amazon-ebs" "eks_al2023_r615" { source_ami = var.source_ami_id region = var.aws_region encrypt_boot = true metadata_options { http_tokens = "required" } } SOURCE_AMI_ID and PACKER_SUBNET_ID are optional overrides for an approved base image or builder subnet. Rebuild and test images when the operating system or GPU stack changes. Step 4: Add the GPU worker Run the following command to add a GPU managed node group that uses the custom image: ./run.sh add-gpu-node By default, the managed node group uses the custom image and stays at one On-Demand g5.xlarge, the validated GPU worker. A GPU taint excludes ordinary workloads. The script disables eksctl’s NVIDIA device-plugin installation because GPU Operator manages that component. Selected fields from config/eksctl-gpu-nodegroup.yaml.tpl managedNodeGroups: - name: gpu-g5-r615-ondemand instanceType: g5.xlarge ami: <generated-ami-id> amiFamily: AmazonLinux2023 desiredCapacity: 1 minSize: 1 maxSize: 1 privateNetworking: true taints: - key: nvidia.com/gpu effect: NoSchedule Step 5: Install GPU Operator and inspect the host Run the following command to install GPU Operator and inspect the GPU worker’s host configuration: ./run.sh install-gpu-operator GPU Operator 26.7.1 supplies the device plugin and Kubernetes integrations. Its configuration preserves the image-owned driver and toolkit: driver: enabled: false toolkit: enabled: false The same command runs a temporary privileged inspection Pod on the GPU worker, prints the host configuration, and removes the Pod. The validated node reports: Observed host configuration GPU: NVIDIA A10G, 23028 MiB Driver: 615.71.10 NVIDIA Container Toolkit: 1.20.1-1 containerd: 2.3.5 cgroup filesystem: cgroup2fs NRI socket paths: /var/run/nri/nri.sock /run/nri/nri.sock On this AL2023 node, /var/run is a symbolic link to /run. Both paths identify the same socket. Limit privileged inspection to the disposable environment and confirm the Pod is removed. Step 6: Establish the whole-GPU baseline Run the following command to test whole-GPU scheduling before fractioning is installed: ./run.sh baseline Each baseline Pod requests and limits nvidia.com/gpu to 1. The test assumes one available physical GPU with sharing disabled: One Pod runs and the other remains Pending. This demonstrates the whole-device scheduling constraint before fractioning is installed. On multi-GPU nodes, adapt this baseline and verify that both fractional workloads use the same GPU. Measured baseline result NAME READY STATUS NODE whole-gpu-a 1/1 Running <gpu-node> whole-gpu-b 0/1 Pending <none> The script checks this state and removes both baseline Pods. Step 7: Install KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator Run the following command to install KAI Scheduler, which includes GPU Fractioning Operator: ./run.sh install-kai The pinned KAI Scheduler 0.18.5 chart includes GPU Fractioning Operator 0.1.7. The values turn on NvFractions and per-Pod metrics while retaining GPU-stack version checks. The optional nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode annotation selects compute mode. These workloads leave the default unchanged. Relevant fields from helm/kai-values.yaml global: gpuSharingMode: NvFractions nvFractions: set: true gpu-fractioning: metricsAgent: enabled: true skipGpuStackVersionChecks: false In the validation, FractiondReady, MpsdReady, and Ready are True. DriverUpgradeInProgress is False with reason NoDriverUpgrade, consistent with the AMI retaining driver ownership. Step 8: Run the positive sharing test Run the following command to deploy two Pods with 8 GiB GPU-memory contracts: ./run.sh share Each Pod requests and limits memory to 8 GiB and selects kai-scheduler. Neither requests a whole nvidia.com/gpu resource. The repository applies these scheduling fields and runs a CUDA probe that allocates 6 GiB: Essential fields from kubernetes/fraction-8gi-pods.yaml metadata: annotations: nvidia.com/container.gpu-workload.gpu-memory.request: 8Gi nvidia.com/container.gpu-workload.gpu-memory.limit: 8Gi spec: schedulerName: kai-scheduler runtimeClassName: nvidia Measured positive result NAME READY STATUS NODE fraction-8gi-a 1/1 Running <same-gpu-node> fraction-8gi-b 1/1 Running <same-gpu-node> The script verifies matching node names and GPU UUIDs. In the validation, both Pods see 8,192 MiB and report allocation_succeeded_mib=6144. Those checks establish placement on one physical GPU, the bounded device view, and successful allocations within each contract. Measured allocation output from each Pod NVIDIA_GPU_MEMORY_LIMIT=8192 requested_allocation_mib=6144 allocation_succeeded_mib=6144 Observe memory while both Pods remain active ./run.sh metrics The gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes metric attributes memory by Pod and GPU UUID. The observed 6,394 MiB (about 6.24 GiB) per Pod exceeds the probe’s 6,144 MiB allocation by 250 MiB. Metrics can include CUDA context and runtime overhead. This experiment does not measure that breakdown. Retain workload identity and request, limit, and usage values together when monitoring the shared device. Measured per-Pod metric series gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes{ gpu_uuid="<same-gpu-uuid>", namespace="runai-fractioning-test", pod="fraction-8gi-a"} 6.704594944e+09 gpu_fractioning_gpu_memory_used_bytes{ gpu_uuid="<same-gpu-uuid>", namespace="runai-fractioning-test", pod="fraction-8gi-b"} 6.704594944e+09 Step 9: Verify rejection above the limit Run the following command to test an allocation that exceeds the 8 GiB contract: ./run.sh limit This command removes the positive-test Pods and creates one Pod with an 8 GiB contract that attempts a 9 GiB allocation. The probe reports: Measured over-limit result NVIDIA_GPU_MEMORY_LIMIT=8192 requested_allocation_mib=9216 allocation_failed=out of memory Measured negative-test Pod status NAME READY STATUS NODE fraction-8gi-over-limit 0/1 Completed <gpu-node> Here, cudaMalloc returns an out-of-memory error, which the probe handles before exiting with code 0. Completed is expected, not OOMKilled. This demonstrates allocation rejection, not container termination or general fault isolation. Step 10: Clean up Capture the VPC ID before deleting the cluster. The independent checks that follow use the default cluster name and Region. Substitute your configured values if you changed them. Capture the VPC ID VPC_ID=$(aws eks describe-cluster \ --name runai-fractioning-blog --region us-east-2 \ --query cluster.resourcesVpcConfig.vpcId --output text) Remove the disposable environment ./run.sh cleanup Standard cleanup removes the test namespace, Helm releases, and disposable cluster while preserving the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot. Verify resource deletion aws eks describe-cluster \ --name runai-fractioning-blog --region us-east-2 aws cloudformation describe-stacks \ --stack-name eksctl-runai-fractioning-blog-cluster \ --region us-east-2 aws ec2 describe-vpcs --vpc-ids "$VPC_ID" --region us-east-2 Expect explicit resource-not-found responses for deleted resources. Authentication or permission errors do not establish deletion. Also inspect remaining node groups and cluster-tagged instances. If cleanup fails, inspect CloudFormation events and resolve owned dependencies before retrying. An absent Amazon EKS endpoint does not prove that its VPC is gone. Use ./run.sh cleanup-all only when the custom AMI and its Amazon EBS snapshot are no longer needed. If image deletion is refused, confirm the AMI ID and sample ownership tag. Do not bypass the safeguard. Production considerations Treat this as a behavior validation. Use trusted workloads and apply least-privilege IAM, namespace controls, approved images, and admission rules for fraction requests. Choose whole GPUs or MIG on supported hardware when stronger isolation is required. The pinned fractioning daemons use privileged containers, host PID access, and NRI/MPS host mounts. Restrict their deployment and configuration to trusted administrators. Allow headroom for CUDA contexts, caches, batching, and runtime overhead. Measure latency and throughput under concurrent load. Monitor allocation failures, MPS health, NRI connectivity, and GPU errors. Pin the base AMI, driver, toolkit, device plugin, operator, scheduler, and workload images as one tested combination. Rebuild images and test rollback before rollout. This walkthrough requires pre-provisioned GPU capacity. It does not configure or validate GPU-fraction-aware autoscaling. The fractional Pods select kai-scheduler, request no nvidia.com/gpu resource, and use a nodeSelector that targets a node group fixed at one node. Karpenter support for secondary schedulers is an open feature request (issue #742 on GitHub). The custom image cannot run on Amazon EKS Auto Mode-managed nodes, because Auto Mode selects and manages their AMI. A cluster can mix Auto Mode-managed nodes with managed node groups, but we did not validate this walkthrough in such a cluster. Teams that use Karpenter can reference the same custom AMI by ID in an EC2NodeClass. The autoscaling limit still applies. We did not validate this path. KAI Scheduler is a second scheduler. It handles queueing and placement for Pods that select it. If you already use Kueue, decide which component owns queueing for GPU workloads before you adopt KAI Scheduler. We recommend running the Amazon EKS node monitoring agent on GPU nodes. In a November 18, 2026 regression run, the agent ran on the custom R615 image with MPS sharing active and reported healthy GPU conditions throughout the sharing and limit tests. That run did not test fault detection. Because GPU Operator already runs a Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) host engine, configure the agent to use that host engine instead of its bundled one. Conclusion In this post, we showed how to configure GPU-memory fractioning on Amazon EKS with a custom AL2023 image, using G5/A10G as the validated example. The approach extends to compatible NVIDIA GPUs after checking prerequisites and validating the selected configuration. You established the whole-GPU baseline, ran two bounded workloads on the same GPU, inspected per-Pod memory usage, and verified rejection of an allocation above the limit. Fractioning can improve access to existing capacity when workload memory fits. Production adoption also requires isolation controls and performance testing. To repeat the experiment, clone the AWS Samples repository and compare your results with its validated evidence. Explore the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation and the Amazon EKS accelerated AMI guidance before adapting the example to your workloads. The content and opinions in this post are those of the third-party author and AWS is not responsible for the content or accuracy of this post. About the authors Muru Bhaskaran Muru Bhaskaran is a Sr. Specialist Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services. With more than 20 years of experience, he helps enterprises build secure, scalable AI training and inference infrastructure using accelerated computing and Kubernetes, with a focus on production readiness and price-performance. Robert Ferrer Robert Ferrer is a Specialist Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services. He focuses on large-scale model training and inference, GPU-accelerated infrastructure, distributed computing, and agentic AI. He works with customers to weigh architecture trade-offs across compute, networking, storage, orchestration, resilience, and cost, helping them move from experimentation to reliable production. Eliuth Triana Eliuth Triana is a developer relations manager at NVIDIA on the Amazon team. He connects Amazon and AWS product leaders, developers, and scientists with NVIDIA technologists and product leaders to accelerate Amazon model inference and training, ML/DL workloads, Amazon EC2 products, and AWS AI services. Eliuth is a passionate mountain biker, tennis player, skier, and poker player. Felipe Garcia Felipe Garcia is a Senior Solutions Architect for AI Cloud Services on NVIDIA’s Cloud Service Provider GTM team. He helps cloud providers build and scale GPU-accelerated AI infrastructure, with a focus on cloud-native architectures and moving AI workloads from experimentation to production.

items.title: 阿里巴巴两篇论文获 ATC 2026 最佳论文奖，并在港研讨 AI Native 系统的可靠性与效率
items.summary: 原创 阿里技术 2026-11-19 20:02 浙江 11 月 15 日，在 ATC 2026 期间，阿里巴巴于香港沙田万怡酒店举办 Alibaba Hong Kong Forum，主题为「面向下一代人工智能的全栈协同设计」（Full-Stack Co-Design for Next-Generation AI: Infrastructure, Systems, Models and Data）。设 AI Infra & AI Systems、Model & Data 两个并行 Session，高校学者与阿里巴巴技术专家分别介绍研究进展与当前面临的技术难题，30+ 位高校学者、50+ 位高校学生和阿里技术专家参与了本次技术交流。 11 月 16 日，大会公布最佳论文奖：本届 ATC 录用 135 篇论文，阿里巴巴入选 12 篇（文末附 12 篇论文解读链接🔗），并在 6 篇最佳论文中占 2 篇。 01 最佳论文：从生产系统里「长」出来的问题 本次阿里巴巴集团获评的两篇最佳论文分别为《Model-as-a-Service in the Wild: Characterizing Production LLM Inference Clusters at Scale》和《Lean: Saving OSS Network Cost by Application-Infrastructure Coordination》。 最佳论文《Model-as-a-Service in the Wild》获奖团队合影 平台技术团队的获奖论文《Model-as-a-Service in the Wild: Characterizing Production LLM Inference Clusters at Scale》，依托十万卡级大模型服务平台 xMaaS，研究连续六个月、覆盖约 30 万个应用与 7 万个模型变体的真实运行数据，从集群、应用与模型三个层面揭示显存预留与实际使用不匹配、冷模型长期占用资源等问题，为异构算力调度、精细化显存管理与弹性扩缩容提供生产依据，并同步开放脱敏数据。工作由平台技术团队与香港中文大学（深圳）余旻晨老师团队合作完成。 最佳论文《Lean》获奖团队合影 阿里云团队的获奖论文《Lean: Saving OSS Network Cost by Application-Infrastructure Coordination》聚焦对象存储 OSS 的网络成本，以应用与网络基础设施协同设计为思路，用 SRv6 实现轻量化边缘接入、灵活流量调度与业务流量物理隔离。系统已在生产环境持续运行四年，同等生产流量下将 OSS 网络总成本较原方案降低 55.6%。工作由阿里云与上海交通大学徐尔茨老师合作完成，徐尔茨同时担任本次系统 Room 主持人。两篇论文都以生产系统的真实约束为起点，再把结论放回生产验证。 02 两个研讨 Room：全栈协同设计为何成为共同议题 本次 Alibaba Hong Kong Forum 分设系统和模型两个 Room 进行研讨。主题设置上，系统方向讨论训推软硬协同与 Agent Infra 的可靠性，由上海交通大学徐尔茨主持；模型方向讨论 LLM 与多模态训练推理、Agentic RL、视频生成与数据评测，并要求模型侧反向定义系统所需的数据、实时性与安全边界，由香港科技大学王威主持。 2.1 系统 Room：从推理调度到 Agent 运行时的问题链 系统 Room 由来自阿里巴巴集团的谷朴开场，他表示，AI Infra 是一个非常巨大的机会，算力基建正以前所未有的速度扩张，很多天花板的突破需要从新的架构、新的方法，端到端、全栈地重新设计，才有机会把效率发挥到最大。 谷朴｜阿里巴巴集团｜系统 Room 开场 随后，四位来自阿里巴巴的技术专家依次展开 MaaS 资源调度与资源管理、推理引擎、Agentic OS，以及万亿参数与长序列模型的分布式训练。 推理服务：调度的前提已经改变 岩泉把大模型推理对基础设施的改变归到一句话，那就是：调度不再是把请求分给空闲机器，而要在有状态、强 SLO、负载还不可预测三个约束同时成立的前提下做决定。他给的两个例子最能说明这件事有多「新」——冷扩容实例因为没缓存预热要扛 100% 的计算，而热实例只扛 5%，弹性增益天然要打折；而模型与卡型的匹配决策周期，已经从搜推广时代的半年一年被压到了周级别。当 MaaS 推理、快训练、AIGC 训练和 Agent workflow 这些全都带状态的负载必须混在同一个集群里，资源调度就不再是单点优化问题，而是调度、网络和存储要一起重新设计的 co-design 问题。 喜德指出，真实 MaaS 流量下的多卡、多节点推理，计算、通信与显存成本相互牵制。团队已具备缓存感知路由、分层 KV 与 TP／PP／EP／DP 等方法，并在探索 EPLB、DP Balance、动态投机与 Kernel 优化。他提出的合作方向是联合成本模型与系统原型，在同负载、同硬件、同 SLO 条件下对照验证 Goodput、单位成本与资源开销。 训练系统：效率与正确性一起验证 雾汀结合生产案例，分享了万亿参数、百万 token 上下文训练面临的挑战。通过前置健康检查、分层 Checkpoint 和流水线预热，案例中的有效训练时间占比从约 90.5% 提升至 97%。 团队介绍了与高校合作的 VRouter、Tessera 和 Libra，分别应对 MoE 负载不均、通信开销和长序列训练扩展问题。Libra 在百万 token 上下文实验中，将数据并行扩展效率从 27.6% 提升至 70.3%。雾汀还以梯度求和为例，说明在低精度计算中，同一组数仅仅改变累加顺序，就可能得到不同的结果，进而影响模型参数更新。 Agent 运行时：系统软件的职责边界 伯瑜的问题位于系统软件层面。Agent 调用工具、修改环境并等待结果，任务进度分散在上下文、文件与远端服务之中，多个 Agent 还共享文件、工具与执行资源。开源系统软件 ANOLISA 已支撑阿里云 AgenticOS 对外服务，集成任务管理、安全治理、信息处理与恢复能力。他希望资源管理面向完整任务，协调跨轮次、跨 Agent 的状态，形成能够表达资源、权限与动作效果的公共系统接口。 学界观点：沿同一条链的不同切入点 六位学者沿着同一条链路发表观点：陈全与须成忠处理资源与调度，黄嘉逸与吴川处理训练与后训练，吴明瑜处理运行时正确性，潘恬落到网络底座。 陈全｜上海交通大学计算机学院先进计算研究所教授 陈全从 Agent 长会话切入：KV 与状态长期驻留显存，休眠会话持续占用资源，沙箱需兼顾秒级启动、高密度与强隔离。他将预填充与解码逻辑分离、物理混部，按 Transformer 层切分实现 SM 空分复用，优先保障解码阶段的每 token 时延，其余算力分配给预填充；沙箱镜像的只读页直接映射共享、写入私有，checkpoint 原位封存为新的只读来源；KV 卸载要求缓存池不打断 CUDA Graph、预取无损。 须成忠｜澳门大学讲座教授、科技学院院长 须成忠将分散在各卡的 HBM 视为统一 KV 池，主张将计算调度到数据所在位置。工具处理占据 Agent 时延的主要部分，CPU 的角色由辅助转为命令层，因此可选择性地将部分解码注意力卸载至 CPU，并在云边之间动态移动流水线边界。其中 Axon 采用阿里 Aone 的生产 trace 做回放评测，也是阿里入选 ATC 2026 的十二篇之一，构成当天学界与业务最直接的接口。 黄嘉逸｜香港科技大学（广州）功能枢纽微电子学域助理教授 黄嘉逸关注 MoE 的通信与负载。All-to-All 与专家计算存在强数据依赖，难以重叠；推理阶段热门专家的负载可达平均值的数倍。ScMoE（ICML 2025）以 shortcut 连接使 MoE 层不依赖上一层的中间表达，从而实现通信与计算的重叠。推理侧以扩展的本地专家选择配合 token drop，用闲置算力换取精度，或采用张量级与神经元级双稀疏，在精度与效率之间取得更优的折中。 吴川｜香港大学计算机科学系教授、IEEE Fellow 吴川的报告聚焦后训练框架。RL 的采样、训练、验证与奖励模块相互阻塞，长尾轨迹导致 GPU 空闲，失败经验也难以跨轮次复用。veRL／HybridFlow（EuroSys 2025）将算法写为单控制器、计算交由多控制器，先实现模块解耦；Laminar （EuroSys 2026）进一步做轨迹级异步采样与按完成量动态重打包，将生成与训练解耦；下一步是将新鲜、回放与过期数据混合纳入经验缓冲，走向以经验与验证驱动的 RSI。 吴明瑜｜上海交通大学计算机学院副研究员（IPADS） 吴明瑜讨论多个 Agent 同时修改一套运行中系统的情形。K8s 配置、共享文档等持续变化的状态会出现写偏斜，即各 Agent 单独执行均正确、并发执行后整体结果错误。经典并发控制将任务视为黑盒，冲突时整体阻塞或重新执行，但 Agent 的读集远大于实际使用的集合，任务按分钟与真实 token 计价，重新执行代价高昂。他以运行时记录的读写与输出构建细粒度因果图，冲突时通知 Agent 自行分析因果、仅修复受影响的步骤，并配合补偿与多版本读，最后配套 agent 工作流自动给工具绑定读写集与补偿动作。 潘恬指出，云网络的一些传统假设在 AI 负载下需要修正：拥塞瓶颈由网络部分转移至端侧接收，主机内PCIe 余量被压缩、PFC 背压向网络扩散；连接不再独立表示业务，RDMA 控制面使用 TCP建连、数据面使用 UDP传输，经过负载均衡器时需跨连接关联；访问服务地址到 Agent 运行时才确定，无法直接携带在数据包头；端点网络接入因 Sandbox 生命周期短而需要频繁配置更新。相应的探索包括事件驱动的最后一跳裁剪、支持 RDMA 穿越负载均衡、以 vNIC 预热池缩短网络准备时间。MCP Gateway 在注册时建立语义与词法双索引，在线融合检索候选工具，实现LLM context压缩和工具精确检索；这项工作也在阿里入选的十二篇之列。 系统侧的链条由此闭合。资源与调度、训练与后训练、运行时正确性、网络底座，共同要求是结论能在同负载、同硬件、同 SLO 下复现。 2.2 模型 Room：数据、评测与生成如何反向定义系统 模型 Room 由阿里巴巴集团的喜德进行开场。他说道，当天分享的都是商业化场景中面临的真实问题，希望和学界一起寻求更好的解法，把这些关键问题讨论清楚就是最大的收获。 喜德｜阿里巴巴集团｜模型 Room 开场 喜德介绍了四位阿里技术专家的分享方向：多模态生成场景下的训练与推理 Infra、面向真实业务的大模型评测、长程 Agent 的自我演化，以及支撑 Agent 运行的 Harness 工程。 生成模型 Infra：训练效率决定能力上限，部署效率决定成本 家忙认为，现有工程体系尚不足以承载参数量与数据量增长带来的效果收益。训练侧采用 packing 与动态并行、专家均衡与 FP8；后训练作业的多任务、多租户特性通过优先级、公平性与碎片整理进行调度；推理侧将量化、稀疏、蒸馏与 Cache 联合使用，并对有损优化做在线效果监控与自适应回退。他向学界提出的问题是预训练效率翻倍的机会点、视频生成与世界模型的每秒成本还需要哪些突破，以及如何高效判断有损优化是否满足效果需求。 评测与 Harness：结果可信性的建立 雄道介绍面向真实业务的大模型评测，出发点是基准本身未必可信：公开基准数量众多，被主流引用的高质量很少，开源评测集普遍存在错题与数据污染现象。团队先确立评测集健康度指数 BHI 作为基准选择准则；评测对象从单轮答题扩展到真实职业任务，并将模型与 Harness 放在一起评估——同一模型更换一套 Harness，分数即发生变化。判分采用动态评分细则逐维加权，同时对过程建模。他列出的未解决问题包括长程多轮的过程判分、真实任务如何数据化、出题到质控的全链路自动化，以及专家偏好如何放大为稳定标准并量化一致性。 懿川进一步介绍 Harness 工程的实践和 RSI 设计。随着模型的能力不断提升，对于模型能力的要求也从“让模型回答正确”转向“让系统可靠完成任务”。在 Harness 工程上拆分为规划、路由、工具接口、执行与验证几层，同时采用统一轨迹格式与适配层把 M×N 的模型—环境适配降为 M+N。通过将 Harness 进行设计优化，设计 api proxy 的方案记录 token 与 logprobs，并持续迭代 Harness 能力，进一步实现 Harness 能力内化到模型，从而实现 Harness 和模型的协同演进。 长程 Agent：让模型反过来优化系统 长程 Agent 把这条链路接回系统侧。垂瑟指出，状态依赖、误差累积与延迟反馈使单步正确不等于任务完成。他以 Engineering 任务作为长程 RL 环境，将编译检查、数值回归、性能测量与 EDA 验证转化为 dense reward，让模型通过中间反馈持续探索、诊断与修正。已完成的实验中，Qwen 在 Kernel 优化、推理系统适配与芯片设计中持续迭代数十小时，完成从算子提速、端到端性能优化到规格驱动的 RTL、验证与物理实现。被优化的对象，正是系统 Room 讨论的推理系统与芯片实现。 学界观点：数据、机制、算法与生成 本场的五位学者分别回答上游的问题：评测是否可信，数据从哪里来，信号是否可靠，学习算法能否持续，生成结果能否可控。 王历伟｜香港中文大学助理教授、LaVi Lab 负责人 王历伟的分享主题是《大语言模型的测评与进化》，与雄道形成学界与业务两侧的对照，工作沿“测评—进化”两条线展开。测评侧，他于 2023 年推出首批综合性中文大模型评测平台 CLEVA，覆盖 31 项任务、84 个数据集、37 万条测试样本与 9 个评测维度。值得一提的是，该平台已被斯坦福 HELM 收录，在其 2025 年综述中是唯一专注于中文评测的榜单。 针对基准污染，他提出 C²LEVA 以被动防御与主动防御相结合自动生成全新试题——爬虫与模拟器采集语料、入库后经预处理、污染检测与数据增广再释放为数据集，在中英文 22 项任务上测试了 15 个模型；并将动态评测扩展到视频，NeMoBench 在 13,486 段视频上自动生成 31,378 个时序定位问题。 进化侧，他提出基于反馈的测试时训练（FTTT）：由验证器判定答案对错，再用一个学习到的优化器依据失败尝试的梯度预测下一次权重更新，使模型不依赖一次性的静态训练，在推理阶段即可从反馈中持续改进。 骆昱宇｜香港科技大学（广州）助理教授、DIAL Lab 负责人 骆昱宇关注训练数据的来源与筛选。Agent 训练需要可交互、可验证、可复现的轨迹，以有限状态机合成网页环境，批量生成轨迹；数据选择不再额外执行一次推理，而是复用训练前向的副产物——loss、梯度、logits 与 attention——在样本与 token 两层筛选。推理侧将专家拆分为原子专家、以笛卡尔路由降低开销，目标是把执行瓶颈从访存受限转向计算受限。 邹荻凡｜香港大学助理教授 邹荻凡的报告系统性梳理了 LLM 可解释性的多个层次。理论层面，报告从 Transformer 的表达力、训练动力学与泛化出发，讨论上下文学习、思维链与推理能力的数学基础，并进一步揭示模型能力与网络深度及内部计算机制之间的关系。现象与物理驱动层面，报告强调通过可控数据干预、因果中介分析和机制观测，刻画模型真实决策依据，以及训练与规模变化对模型能力的影响。通用解释工具层面，报告以 circuits 与稀疏自编码器 SAE 为代表，覆盖机制定位、模型编辑、控制与扩散语言模型等应用，并指出目前常用的可解释工具 SAE 在 token 级容易停留在表层特征，chunk 级更有利于发现可靠语义特征。更进一步，报告还尝试从第一性原理出发，设计更自然可解释、更节能的模型架构。同时，报告阐述了可解释性研究对生产环境中性能的作用与机制，并强调其应反哺算法与数据设计，形成理解机制、验证效用、改进模型的闭环。 潘玲｜香港科技大学助理教授、智能决策实验室负责人 潘玲以“Keep RL learning at scale”为主线，回顾了强化学习从经典 RL、深度 RL 到基础模型RL的几次发展浪潮。在适应性上，她指出 RL 面临非平稳的学习环境，智能体会逐渐丧失学习可塑性；她提出以梯度幅值而非激活值度量神经元活性，周期性重置休眠神经元，并以动态拓扑生长调和稳定性与塑性的两难；提出在 SFT 到 RL 的交接处恢复模型塑性。在实用性上，她指出大模型可验证奖励的决策 MDP 结构比传统控制问题的 MDP 具备更清晰的结构，算法因而可以大幅简化：评估均匀随机策略、再根据其 Q 值贪心行动即接近最优，极简RL算法在多个模型规模与分布外任务上超过大模型RL算法；对图像与视频生成等不可验证奖励，则以多样性寻求抑制 reward hacking。最后，她展望了让 RL 在规模化中持续学习的路线：配合算法与系统协同设计，构建可靠的 RL 技术栈。 陈启峰｜香港科技大学副教授、CAiRE 主任 陈启峰的报告聚焦可控视频生成。可执行的世界已能给出相机、运动与持久状态的控制，但通用视频渲染器在事件时序、未见视角与回访时的外观一致性上仍不稳定。他的路线是 code-to-real：Builder 与 Reviewer 构建世界，Planner 与 Compiler 产出代理与状态轨迹，再以"生成—审核—修复"的有预算循环产出合格配对，最后冻结主干、每个世界一个 LoRA 适配器做递归蒸馏。其分工是程序保存世界状态，渲染器学习如何呈现。 2.3 开放问题与现场讨论 报告之外，为加强学界和业界的交流，本次 Alibaba Hong Kong Forum 设置了研讨环节。 系统 Room 从云端与本地 Agent 的系统支撑问起。阿里云技术专家认为两边并存，需要同一层面向 Agent 的系统抽象；云上更像沙箱，本地握着用户数据，操作须更谨慎。Agent 大部分时间在等待，难点是系统不了解任务状态，挂起与恢复要快到用户察觉不到。安全被反复提起：本地权限放开后环境可能被篡改，可信执行环境是一个思路。 模型 Room 两组讨论评测、数据与奖励的可信性。可解释性与数据组认为，判断“某个激活对应什么概念”仍靠假设与对比实验，没有理论保证；垂类与通用数据的投入与配比未定。视觉生成组先谈“训不动”：视频 token 极长，几十秒时长前后难一致；“高质量”标准互相冲突，审美难量化，多模态 RL 的 reward 难定义也易被 hack。与会者倾向从特定场景的小规模数据构建与验证开始合作。两组其实是同一问题：评测、数据与奖励都需要可信裁判。 03 Alibaba Hong Kong Night × AliStar Wonder Night晚宴 当晚，Alibaba Hong Kong Night × AliStar Wonder Night 晚宴圆满举办。晚宴进一步汇聚了 30+ 位高校学者、百余位学生，与阿里巴巴业务技术团队展开面对面交流，为高校师生与业务专家提供了开放、平等的对话平台。 现场特设的论文 Poster 展示区前，同学们与业务技术专家就具体的研究方向进行了深入探讨。在自由交流环节，与会师生不仅更直观地了解了阿里巴巴的前沿技术探索与产业落地中的真实难题，也让阿里业务团队听到了来自高校的研究思路与观察。期间，阿里星 HR 团队与青年学者们就课题方向及职业发展规划进行了深度沟通。 阿里巴巴希望通过此类交流，推动更多师生围绕产业问题开展研究，为后续科研合作、学生实习和人才交流建立长效联系。目前，“阿里星顶尖人才计划”持续面向全球开放招募，我们期待与更多顶尖大脑并肩同行，在真实的产业场景中，将研究落地为改变世界的力量。 04 展望 接下来，阿里巴巴会把更多生产一线的真实问题带进高校实验室，学界的新方法也会放到阿里的真实负载里检验，双方在 AI 系统和模型研究上能做成的事，会比今天更多。 现场花絮： *延伸阅读：阿里巴巴 12 篇论文入选全球系统顶会 ATC 2026（内附下载） 欢迎留言一起参与讨论~ 跳转微信打开

items.summary: EMNLP 2026 是国际计算语言学协会（Association for Computational Linguistics, ACL）举办的自然语言处理经验方法会议，是自然语言处理与计算语言学领域的国际顶级学术会议之一。 2026 年，美团技术团队共计 20 余篇论文被 EMNLP 2026 收录，我们从中精选了 12 篇主会论文（Long Paper）分享给大家。这些论文覆盖推理框架、策略优化、评估框架、强化学习、记忆框架、自适应训练框架、语义标签、数据合成框架、统计框架、奖励模型等技术领域和方向，希望能够对从事相关工作的同学以启发或者帮助。 1. A Listen-Think-Speak Framework for Efficient Streaming Voice Interaction via Semantic Triggering and Incremental Reasoning 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：实时语音智能体面临着两难困境：端到端模型往往缺乏深度推理能力，而级联流水线由于 ASR（语音识别）、LLM 推理和 TTS（语音合成）严格串行执行，导致延迟过高。现有的级联流式策略试图通过机械式分段（例如固定块大小、基于 VAD 的切分）或投机生成来降低这种延迟，但它们经常要么破坏语义单元的完整性，要么将计算资源浪费在必须回滚的预测上。 为了解决这些挑战，我们提出了 LTS-Agent，这是一个"听-想-说"（Listen-Think-Speak）框架，它显式地将流式场景下的"何时思考"与"如何增量推理"区分开来。LTS-Agent 引入了一个动态语义触发器（Dynamic Semantic Trigger），学习在语义饱和的前缀处被激活；以及一个双角色流式编排器（Dual-Role Stream Orchestrator），利用推理引擎的批处理能力来协调两个互补的角色：负责后台状态维护的"思考者（Thinker）"和负责前台投机求解的"说话者（Speaker）"。这种并行设计允许系统"边说边想"，在维护结构化推理状态的同时不阻塞即时响应。 此外，我们构建了一个"停顿与修复（Pause-and-Repair）"基准测试，在复杂的推理任务中注入迟疑和自我修正，以压力测试流式处理的鲁棒性。在 VERA、Spoken-MQA、BigBenchAudio 以及我们的基准测试上的实验表明，相比于串行级联基线和现有的流式策略，LTS-Agent 实现了更优的准确率-延迟-效率权衡。 2. Silence the Judge: Reinforcement Learning with Self-Verifier via Latent Geometric Clustering 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：群体相对策略优化（GRPO）显著增强了大语言模型的推理能力，但受限于稀疏的离散奖励信号和昂贵的外部验证器。为解决这些问题，我们提出 Latent-GRPO 框架，通过利用潜空间的几何特性来获取内在奖励，消除对外部验证的依赖。我们的实证分析揭示了一个重要的几何性质：正确推理轨迹的终端 token 表示在潜空间中展现出高的类内余弦相似度，形成紧密聚类，而错误轨迹则分散分布。 基于这一观察，我们引入迭代鲁棒质心估计（IRCE）算法。IRCE 通过球面投影消除幅度波动，并通过迭代软加权聚合估计"真值质心"，从而生成密集的连续奖励信号。在多种模型规模上的实验表明，Latent-GRPO 在推理性能上与外部验证器相当，同时显著降低了训练延迟和内存开销。本工作证明了高效、可扩展的无需训练的奖励建模可以直接在潜空间内实现，为内在奖励驱动的强化学习提供了新的范式。 3. One Instruction Is a Benchmark: End-to-End Instruction-Following Evaluation with FlexBench 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：大型语言模型在实际应用中日益依赖对用户提供指令的理解，这些指令往往篇幅较长、精确细致，且针对特定工作流程量身定制。在此类场景下，通用的排行榜综合表现往往难以有效反映模型忠实执行从业者拟部署的特定指令的能力。 为弥补这一空白，我们提出了 FlexBench/FlexEval——一个指令条件化的评估框架，能够根据用户提供的目标指令动态生成专门的测试套件。给定目标指令后，FlexBench 导出一组可验证的评估维度，并生成指令条件化的对话语料库。FlexEval 随后将维度级评判汇总为两个互补指标：COVERAGE（覆盖率），衡量工作流进度；ACHIEVEMENT（达成度），衡量条件正确性。我们在涵盖多种场景类别和工作流拓扑的九条多轮目标指令上，对九个当代 LLM 进行了评估，共涉及 3,888 段生成的对话。结果表明，模型排名和失败模式在不同目标指令间差异显著，凸显了超越固定综合基准、采用指令条件化评估的必要性。 4. SIRI: Self-Internalizing Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Skills for LLM Agent Training 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：智能体技能（Agent Skills）能够将成功经验压缩为可复用的策略知识，帮助智能体减少重复探索并完成长程交互任务。然而，现有方法通常依赖外部模型或独立模块生成技能，并在推理阶段持续检索和注入技能，不仅增加训练与部署复杂度，还会带来额外的上下文开销和推理延迟。一个关键问题是：智能体能否自主发现有效技能，并将其真正内化到模型参数中，从而在推理时不再依赖外部技能库？ 为此，本文提出 SIRI（Self-Internalizing Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Skills），一个面向技能自主发现、验证与内化的三阶段强化学习框架。SIRI 首先通过 GiGPO 预热策略，获得基础交互能力并积累无技能辅助的成功轨迹；随后由模型从自身成功轨迹中提炼候选技能，并通过成对的 Skill-Augmented 与 Skill-Free Rollout 验证技能效用；最后结合轨迹级技能增益与动作级优势，仅将真正有益的技能引导动作蒸馏至无技能策略中。训练完成后，模型无需检索或注入任何技能，仅使用原始任务提示即可完成推理。 在 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 上，SIRI 将 GiGPO 在 ALFWorld 上的任务成功率由 90.8% 提升至 93.0%，在 WebShop 上由 72.8% 提升至 81.3%，分别提高 2.2 和 8.5 个百分点，并整体优于提示学习、标准强化学习和记忆增强方法。进一步实验表明，模型自主挖掘的技能经过在线验证与内化后，可以达到与闭源大模型生成技能相当的效果。 5. SCOPE: Signal-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation Enhancement with Dual-Path Adaptive Weighting 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：在大语言模型的推理对齐中，在线策略蒸馏（On-Policy Distillation, OPD）通过引入教师模型的 token 级 KL 监督来缓解在线强化学习中结果级奖励的信用分配难题，但现有方法对所有策略采样轨迹无差别施加同等监督，忽略了信号质量的本质差异。 为此，我们提出 SCOPE（Signal-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation Enhancement）双路径自适应训练框架：以轨迹正确性为路由，将 rollout 分流至两条互补的监督路径——对错误轨迹，基于教师困惑度加权 KL 蒸馏，优先强化教师真正具备纠错能力的实例，同时抑制"自信犯错"的误导信号；对正确轨迹，基于学生困惑度加权 MLE，将强化重点集中在能力边界处低置信度样本上，避免对已掌握路径的过度强化。两条路径均采用组级归一化自适应校准权重分布，兼顾不同 prompt 间的难度差异。 在 MATH500、AIME24、AIME25、AMC23、Minerva、OlympiadBench 六个推理基准上，SCOPE 相较所有竞争基线取得 Avg@32 平均相对提升 11.42%、Pass@32 提升 7.30% 的一致性增益，验证了信号质量感知的自适应监督在 OPD 框架中的有效性。 6. TRUST-SQL: Tool-Integrated Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Text-to-SQL over Unknown Schemas 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：现有 Text-to-SQL 方法通常假设预载完整数据库结构（Schema），但在庞大且动态变化的企业库中易超出上下文窗口并引入噪声，结构缺失时模型又易虚构表或字段。 为使智能体在不预载结构下自主探明并核验信息以生成正确 SQL，本文提出面向未知结构的工具集成多轮强化学习框架 TRUST-SQL（Truthful Reasoning with Unknown Schema via Tools）。框架将任务建模为部分可观测马尔可夫决策过程，设计"探索—提议—生成—确认"（Explore–Propose–Generate–Confirm）四阶段协议，要求在 Propose 阶段显式确认已核验的表与字段，并支持据执行反馈回退修正；同时提出阶段感知群体相对策略优化（Phase-Aware GRPO），以 Propose 为界分别计算结构探索与完整轨迹的优势，结合 token 级掩码将结构奖励限定于对应阶段，缓解多轮信用分配难题。 在 BIRD-Dev、Spider-Test 及三个 Spider 鲁棒性基准上，不预载结构且贪心解码时，4B 和 8B 模型五项基准平均执行准确率较基础模型分别提升 30.6 和 16.6 个百分点；14B 模型在 BIRD-Dev 上达 68.1%（多数投票达 70.1%），无需预载全量结构即可在多数基准上达到或超越依赖结构预加载的强基线。 7. UniMem: Complementary Episodic-to-Parametric Memory for Boundary-Agnostic Task Streams 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：大语言模型智能体需要在长期交互中积累并复用任务经验，但真实部署中的任务往往持续变化且没有明确边界，单独依赖外部检索记忆或参数化记忆都会面临稳定性与可塑性的矛盾：前者能够快速吸收新信息，却难以内化重复出现的执行模式且增加检索开销；后者执行稳定高效，却依赖预定义任务边界和固定参数容量。 为此，本文受互补学习系统理论启发，提出统一记忆框架 UniMem，通过可学习的路由 Token 协调情景记忆与参数化记忆，并将任务识别与具体任务执行进行解耦。对于已知任务，模型激活对应的参数化记忆单元执行；对于新颖、稀疏或不确定的任务，则先存入情景缓冲区并通过检索增强方式处理。当缓冲区中出现重复且可靠的模式时，UniMem 无需任务标签即可自动发现潜在任务结构，并为其动态扩展新的路由 Token 和参数化记忆模块，实现从短期情景记忆到长期参数记忆的逐步巩固。 实验表明，UniMem 在多种长程流式任务和不同骨干模型上能够保持稳定的路由与任务执行性能，并在自主扩展记忆、控制参数增长的同时，整体优于外部记忆、参数高效微调和 Token 记忆等基线方法。 8. TagPR: Tag-Guided Process Supervision for Personalization Reasoning in Large Language Models 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：现有大模型虽然具备较强的通用推理能力，但在个性化任务中容易沿用模型自身的通用逻辑，忽略用户历史中体现的独特偏好；只依赖结果奖励的强化学习也无法约束推理过程，模型可能"答案正确、过程错误"。 为此，本文提出 TagPR，在个性化推理链中引入语义标签，把分析输入、检查用户样例、识别偏好模式、比较对象和形成结论等过程显式拆解为可监督的步骤。TagPR 首先自动构造高质量的带标签推理数据进行监督微调（SFT），再通过多阶段强化学习进行优化；其复合奖励同时结合标签级过程监督，以及带用户嵌入的个性化奖励模型（PRMU），从而让模型的推理过程更贴合用户特定逻辑。 论文在 LaMP、LongLaMP、PGraphRAG 及自建数据集上进行了实验，在 LaMP 全部任务上相对基础模型平均提升 32.65%，并表现出更准确、可解释且具迁移能力的个性化推理效果。 9. ToolForge: A Data Synthesis Pipeline for Multi-Hop, Multi-Turn, and Self-Reflective Tool-Use Data 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：面向工具使用的大模型训练，现有数据构建方法往往依赖大规模真实 API 调用，成本较高且难以覆盖多跳推理、多轮交互和错误反思等复杂场景。为此，本文提出 ToolForge，一套无需大规模在线工具执行的工具使用数据合成框架：以问答数据为种子，构建由 19 类基础虚拟工具及其自动扩展变体组成的可扩展工具空间，并通过单/多轮、单/多工具等交互范式，模拟正确检索、工具误选、参数误选及工具切换等场景，生成包含多跳证据整合与自我反思纠错过程的工具调用轨迹。为保障数据质量，ToolForge 进一步设计多层验证机制，结合规则校验与模型语义评估过滤结构或推理不一致的样本，并通过 MCTS 挖掘困难负例验证其可靠性。 实验表明，仅使用 4,250 条 ToolForge 合成数据微调 Qwen3-8B，即可在 5 个域外问答基准上相对 TIR 提升 21.6%，并在 BFCL、API-Bank 等工具调用基准上展现出良好的泛化能力。 10. RACE: Scalable Statistical Estimation of Functional Consistency in LLM Neurons 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：在机制可解释性领域，跨整个域发现稳定的神经元行为仍然是一项挑战。现有方法通常依赖实例级的点估计或计算成本高昂的过程，这些方法要么掩盖了群体水平的变异性，要么限制了可扩展的跨域分析。 我们提出 RACE（Residual Alignment for Consistency Estimation, 残差对齐一致性估计），这是一种前向传播统计框架，用于评估 Transformer 神经元跨域的功能一致性。扰动实验表明，与基于梯度的点估计相比，RACE 具有更优的域特异性。同时，词元分布层面的结果验证了所选神经元与目标域之间的关联。此外，其计算开销比基于梯度的方法低两个数量级。 11. Fast-Slow Thinking RM: Efficient Integration of Scalar and Generative Reward Models 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：在内容审核、客服评测等业务场景中，LLM-as-a-Judge 正逐渐成为一种重要的自动化判断范式。实际应用中，不同样本的判断难度差异很大：大量简单样本可以快速完成决策，而复杂、模糊或低置信度样本往往需要更充分的推理。如何让模型根据样本难度动态选择判断方式，在保证准确率的同时降低推理成本，是这类系统面临的重要问题。 针对这一问题，我们提出快慢思考奖励模型（Fast-Slow Thinking Reward Models, F/S-RM），一种受双加工理论启发的混合判断架构。F/S-RM 在单一模型中统一"快思考"与"慢思考"两种模式：面对较简单、判断较明确的样本时，模型通过首个 token 直接完成快速成对判断；面对更复杂或置信度不足的样本时，则自动激活基于思维链的慢思考进行进一步推理。模型通过双置信度激活机制动态决定是否进入慢思考，从而形成类似"快速判断—疑难升级"的自适应决策流程。 在混合推理模式下，F/S-RM 在多个奖励模型评测基准上取得 84.3 的平均得分，达到当前最优水平，同时将 token 消耗降低了 22.5%。值得一提的是，近期受到广泛关注的 Jev 快速决策模型，在概率与置信度利用方面与 F/S-RM 具有相似的设计思路；F/S-RM 在同一模型内进一步整合了首 token 快速判断与 CoT 慢思考。 12. FG²-GDN: Enhancing Long-Context Gated Delta Networks with Doubly Fine-Grained Control 论文类型：Main Conference，Long Paper 论文下载：PDF 论文简介：随着大语言模型应用向长文本理解和复杂交互场景拓展，如何兼顾长上下文建模能力与计算效率，成为模型架构设计的重要问题。线性注意力通过递归更新固定大小的记忆状态，为高效长上下文建模提供了新的路径。然而，现有 Kimi Delta Attention（KDA）虽然实现了逐通道的信息遗忘控制，记忆写入仍采用各通道共享的标量更新率，难以根据不同特征的需求灵活调整更新强度。 为此，我们提出双重细粒度门控 Delta 网络 FG²-GDN，将写入率从标量扩展为逐通道向量，使模型能够同时精细控制"保留多少旧信息"和"写入多少新信息"；进一步提出 FG²-GDN+，在逐通道写入的基础上分离键和值的缩放控制，增强记忆更新的灵活性。通过对称平方根缩放设计，该方法保留了 KDA 分块并行算法所需的更新结构，可直接复用其高效计算路径。实验在 340M 和 1.3B 两个模型规模上展开，覆盖语言建模、长上下文检索和真实长文本理解任务。 结果表明，在相同训练设置下，细粒度写入控制提升了语言建模的平均表现，进一步引入键值分离控制的 FG²-GDN+ 在 RULER 和 LongBench 上取得了优于 GDN、KDA 的整体结果，并在超出训练长度的上下文中保持了较好的检索能力。同时，该方法仅引入少量额外参数，预填充效率与 KDA 接近。该研究表明，在细粒度遗忘之外进一步细化写入控制，是提升线性注意力长上下文记忆能力的一条有效路径。

items.title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips
items.summary: At Exa, we are building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. We optimize the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. We use multi-tower semantic machine learning (ML) models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space, so users can express complex queries in natural language alongside traditional keyword search. The keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database. It must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. The unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything we do. At the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding the hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar isn’t a tuning detail. Any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. This post details how we optimized our embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware (AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2), and how an agentic development workflow drove the optimization. Inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline, but it must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving. Figure 1: A simplified view of the Exa stack Every structured web document we rank as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. This figure shows how raw web data moves from Crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of Parse, Moderate and filter, then Embed, with the result served from a vector database. Embedding documents at scale Our experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding our existing corpus. We selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. A migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate our hardware choices. Figure 2: The doubled inference load from the backfill The preceding figure shows two parallel pipelines sharing the crawl and parse stages, one embedding with the live model into the live index and one re-embedding priority documents with the new model into the new index, which is what doubles the load. This doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider our hardware and optimization choices. Optimization journey AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance (inf2.xlarge), with one chip and two NeuronCores. Our workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so we run Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving us container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. The same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Our initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model. From that baseline, it became a march to push throughput (docs/sec) as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. The following chart shows the throughput gains at each milestone. Figure 3: Throughput improvement across optimization milestones Starting from the naive compile, a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement. The first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. We also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. The downcast outputs met our correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference (see Agentic methodology), so the accuracy impact was within our acceptance threshold. NKI kernels The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. These pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and we used them to quickly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. A drop-in attention kernel gave us the next bump in performance. Memory layout optimization: A fused SwiGLU MLP kernel The next bottleneck was memory spill. Profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently showed large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Using a drop-in MLP kernel as a steppingstone to profile the shortcomings of the pre-built implementation, we wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls. We used the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops, and memory operations, and only dropped into the lower-level NKI ISA for specific tensor operations. Keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers, and easier to debug. FLOPS reduction At this point we hit a wall. Per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what we saw with both cores running simultaneously. That gap meant our theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above our realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores. Profiling and experimentation showed that our workload wasn’t yet saturating the Tensor Engine. The remaining headroom was ours to claim by making the computation leaner. The clearest path left was to reduce the overall FLOPS needed to produce our results by eliminating waste. We rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in our model to cut FLOPS spent on padding. This is where kernel customization really paid off. Generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they can’t take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. We wrung more performance out of attention by tailoring the implementation to the real shape of our model’s head architecture. We also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. That cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup. In total, our final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against our initial baseline. Agentic methodology Agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction. Using Flyte, an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. The workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. It then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware. The harness supports agents at different costs. Lightweight models handle tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters, and correctness checks prevent drift. Reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them. Matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Because many agents don’t know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped. The benefits of flexible compute So far, we have optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service. Exa schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Our scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts. Each hardware type we optimize for brings us closer to the global optimum. This is why our Inferentia2 work carried over directly to Trainium2. Shifting hardware profiles lets us free up nodes other teams need or absorb their unused reserved compute. For a long lived model, optimizing across hardware pays off enormously. Conclusion At the scale Exa operates, extracting maximum cost-performance from a flexible pool of hardware is what matters. Adding Neuron hardware to that pool and optimizing it with NKI has proven to be a major source of long-term cost savings. About the authors Summer Devlin Summer is a data infrastructure engineer at Exa Labs, who focuses on solving messy data problems at web scale. Jim Burtoft Jim is a Senior Trainium Solutions Architect at AWS and works directly with companies and educational institutions as well as the team at Hugging Face to make it easier to use models on Trainium. Jim is a CISSP, leader of the Neuron Data Science Technical Field Community, and works with the open source community to enable broader use of Neuron and Trainium. Jim holds a bachelor’s degree in mathematics from Carnegie Mellon University and a master’s degree in economics from the University of Virginia. Pinak Panigrahi Pinak works on performance optimization of AI models on AWS Trainium at Annapurna Labs, Amazon. Venu Geddam Venu is a Senior Technical Account Manager with AWS Enterprise Support, where he partners with strategic customers to run resilient, high-scale workloads on AWS. His work spans EC2 capacity and storage-optimized compute, cost and operational optimization, and the infrastructure behind modern AI/ML platforms — including GPU and Graviton fleets, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and Amazon Bedrock. Venu helps engineering teams turn ambitious technical goals into production-ready, operationally sound architectures.

items.title: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock
items.summary: Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the model infrastructure. It integrates with AWS access controls and monitoring, and processes prompts, code, and model responses within AWS. As coding agents move into production, changes in models and usage can affect latency, capacity, and cost. Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics in Amazon CloudWatch help teams investigate latency increases, throttling, and changes in token consumption. Evaluations, or evals, complement these operational metrics by assessing the quality of an agent’s work on a fixed set of representative tasks. In this post, we show how Airbnb evaluates models for coding agents and monitors their use on Amazon Bedrock. We explain how cost per task guides model selection and how production data helps us revisit those choices as usage changes. We also describe the runtime signals used to investigate latency, throttling, and spend. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers and engineering-adjacent people use AirChat, our internal tool for running coding agents, every week. The agents send their model requests through our large language model (LLM) gateway, which runs on Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock processes Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses within AWS. Eight new models came out in about five weeks. By mid-October, about two thirds of the requests our engineers sent through coding agents went to those new models. Each release can change output tokens, cost, latency and capacity at once, and the benchmark charts published with a launch don’t show how a model handles our engineers’ work. So we run two systems side by side. Before a rollout, we run evals on our own tasks to measure each model’s score and cost per task. Cost per task is the list-price cost of all the tokens an agent uses to finish one task. After a rollout, observability shows us what changed in production. When production usage doesn’t match the eval results, we find out why. Solution overview You can diagnose most production problems with a few signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch: Latency: InvocationLatency, TimeToFirstToken, OutputTokenCount, and output tokens per second (OTPS), which you derive. Throttling: InvocationThrottles, plus the tokens each request reserves against your quota, which you publish yourself. Bedrock also publishes EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage, which measures your estimated tokens per minute (TPM) quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across all inference APIs (Converse, InvokeModel, ConverseStream, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream). You can use this metric to set proactive alarms before reaching your quota limit, track your quota consumption across your models, and request further quota increases before usage is rate limited. Cost: InputTokenCount (uncached input), CacheReadInputTokenCount, CacheWriteInputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount, each priced at its own rate. Cache reads cost less than uncached input, and cache writes can cost more depending on the model. A lower cache hit rate can increase cost per request. On top of these metrics, we add cost per task. Our evals measure a score and a cost per task for every model and every reasoning effort we allow. Reasoning effort is a setting that controls how much a model reasons before it responds. We use the results to choose each default, which is the model and effort that our coding tools use unless an engineer picks another, and each effort ceiling, which is the highest effort we allow for a model. Architecture Engineers run AirChat on their AirDev workspaces, which are personal development machines in the cloud. They can also hand a task to AirChat Remote, which runs cloud agents in separate cloud workspaces while the engineer does something else. Both paths go through our LLM gateway to Amazon Bedrock. Figure 1 shows how AirChat and AirChat Remote reach Amazon Bedrock through our gateway. It also shows how evals and production monitoring guide model defaults and effort ceilings. Figure 1: Coding agents and cloud agents call Amazon Bedrock through our LLM gateway. Our usage records and CloudWatch metrics show real use, and we use eval results to set defaults and effort ceilings The gateway records the model, client, team, and user for each request. We use these records only in aggregate, for cost and capacity planning. CloudWatch supplies token counts, latency, errors, and throttles. We compare those production signals with our eval scores and cost per task to decide when defaults or effort ceilings need to change. Prerequisites On the AWS side, you need: Access to the models in Amazon Bedrock you plan to run and evaluate. For model availability by AWS Region, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Streaming calls through ConverseStream or InvokeModelWithResponseStream. Bedrock publishes TimeToFirstToken only for the streaming APIs. Model invocation logging, turned on in every AWS Region you call. It’s off by default. The logs can hold full prompts and responses along with the caller’s identity, so restrict who can read them and set a retention period. Tagged IAM roles for your callers, with cost allocation tags activated. Activate them before you start collecting, because activation doesn’t backfill earlier costs. You also need three things of your own: A set of tasks from your own engineering work. Give each one a starting repository state, the prompt an engineer would write and a grader you trust. A grader is the program or model that scores the agent’s work. We build our tasks from real code changes, the review comments on those changes and the decisions that the original ticket didn’t spell out. Step 2 shows one. A gateway or proxy in front of Bedrock that records the model, the client, the team, the user and the token counts for each request. A table of public list prices for every model you run, with a date on each entry, so you can price eval tokens and production tokens on the same basis. Before rollout, define what the agents can access and which actions need human review. Run code in isolated workspaces and test generated changes before merging. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can help filter harmful content and sensitive information in prompts and responses. For responses based on supplied reference material, contextual grounding checks can flag unsupported claims. Test these controls on your own tasks and include their latency and cost in your measurements. Walkthrough Start by measuring what a complete task costs. Then use those results to choose model defaults, check production behavior, manage capacity, and attribute spend. Step 1: What does one finished task cost you? A coding agent takes many requests to finish one task, and on each request the model re-reads the context so far. So we price the whole task. Bedrock reports four kinds of tokens for each request: uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output. In an eval run we price all four for every request and add up the requests in the task. Every cost in this post uses the public list prices dated for that run. We record the average cost next to the score for every model, reasoning effort and agent client we test, and the average includes low-scoring attempts. Reasoning effort changes both score and cost. On one model we tested, moving from low to high effort raised the score by 0.8 points. Cost per task was 2.5 times as high. We use these results to set effort ceilings, which the gateway enforces. Step 2: How fast can you evaluate a new model? On the afternoon a new model came out, a single request to our agents started an eval campaign, which runs the new model through all our task suites. A suite is a fixed set of tasks of one type, and we have seven. Agents spread hundreds of tasks across the suites and several cloud workspaces, and each result appeared as soon as a grader scored it. First results arrived within hours. By the next morning, every suite had a score and a cost per task, and we had what we needed for a deployment decision for the entire org. That speed depends on tasks that are already written down. Each task is a folder that holds everything one run needs. Here is a trimmed task from our machine learning work: honest-holdout-bakeoff/ instruction.md what the agent is told task.toml time limit, CPUs and memory environment/ Dockerfile for the sandbox tests/test.sh runs the grader and writes the reward tests/grader.py the checks solution/ a reference solution that must pass the grader instruction.md (excerpt): We have two candidate models for a prediction task, and we need to know which one to ship. ... Then answer the question we actually have to decide: is either candidate worth rolling out over the system already in production? The grader recomputes the right answer from frozen data on every run, and the agent earns a reward of 1 only if every check passes. To test one model at every effort, list each effort as its own agent in a job config: job_name: model-a-effort-sweep n_attempts: 1 # one attempt per task at each effort datasets: - path: tasks/ml # each task brings its own grader agents: - name: model-a-low model_name: vendor/model-a kwargs: {reasoning_effort: low} - name: model-a-medium model_name: vendor/model-a kwargs: {reasoning_effort: medium} - name: model-a-high model_name: vendor/model-a kwargs: {reasoning_effort: high} Both examples use the formats of Harbor, an open-source framework for running agent evals in sandboxes. It’s one option if you’re starting out. Running the evals can be optimized. Writing the rubric, the scoring guide that a grader follows, is the hardest part. Our long tasks run over several rounds, with a simulated reviewer pushing back between rounds. A model grader scores each run on eight weighted dimensions. Each dimension gets a score from 0 to 3. Correctness of delivery 25 Judgment 10 Verification quality 15 Evidence and reporting 10 Autonomy 15 Readability 10 Design and workload fit 10 Operational discipline 5 Ceiling: if the reviewer had to rescue the agent repeatedly (autonomy 0 or 0.5), the total is capped at 25 of 100. Because of ceilings like this one, an agent that needed rescuing can’t score well on polish alone. Step 3: What do you watch after a rollout? When latency rises, chart three signals before you open a support case: TimeToFirstToken for the wait before generation starts, OutputTokenCount for response length, and OTPS for generation speed. Bedrock has no native OTPS metric. You derive it with metric math, as the Amazon Bedrock User Guide describes: OTPS = OutputTokenCount / (InvocationLatency - TimeToFirstToken) * 1000 In the example from our session, latency rose 40 percent while time to first token and OTPS stayed flat. Someone had changed the system prompt to ask for more thorough answers, and output tokens per request rose 50 percent. The model generated at the same speed and wrote longer responses. Treat prompt changes and model upgrades as deploys, and mark them on your dashboard. Each week we put the CloudWatch runtime metrics next to the usage records from our gateway for each model. For cost and capacity planning, we also look at usage in aggregate: cost per request and the average number of requests per user each week. A new model can move both. After every rollout, we compare them with what we expected from the eval’s cost per task. Step 4: The evals looked good. What did production show? One model, which we call model A, looked good in our evals. On our coding tasks, it scored more than three points above our previous best model. Cost per task was about the same, and the same grader scored every model. We rolled it out, capped effort at high, and asked people to use low or medium for most work. A few weeks after launch, we priced model A’s production usage at list price and looked at it in aggregate. Average weekly spend per user was several times higher on model A than on the model before it. Each model A request cost about three times as much, and the average model A user sent about three times as many requests. Output tokens made up only a tenth of a request’s cost. Most of the cost went to cached context, which the model re-read on every request. Model A could work on its own for a long time, so people started long, self-directed sessions with it. The eval measured the model on a task. Production measured how people chose to work with it. Later, a newer model scored higher than model A on the same tasks and grader, at about a sixth of its cost per task. We moved model A’s users to it with a configuration change. We then checked the change in aggregate on the same user group, the heavy users of model A. In their first full week on the newer model, the group sent about the same number of requests to their main model, and the group’s spend on that model fell to about a seventh. Step 5: Why you get throttled, and where traffic goes next On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, Bedrock checks your tokens-per-minute quota when a request arrives, before the model writes anything. It reserves your uncached input tokens and your cache writes, plus max_tokens, the most output the request is allowed. It adjusts that reservation as the model generates and returns the unused part when the request settles. Cache reads never count against the quota, so a request can be cheap against your quota and expensive on your bill. Output tokens settle at a burndown rate that is 1:1 on most models and several times that on some current models, so check your model’s rate. A dashboard of billed tokens can show room while requests are being throttled. In our session’s example, the quota was 1 million tokens per minute and traffic was 300 requests per minute. The dashboard showed about 30 percent of quota. After applying a 5:1 output-token burndown rate, completed requests consumed about 77 percent. Admission uses a different calculation. Each request initially reserved 600 uncached input tokens plus a max_tokens of 4,096, for a total of 4,696 tokens. Responses were about 800 tokens at p99. Lowering max_tokens to 1,024 cut the initial reservation to 1,624 tokens, about 65 percent smaller. The limit was still above p99. For unchanged input and output, final quota consumption stays the same. The smaller reservation leaves more room to admit requests. Monitor stopReason to catch truncated responses. Use backoff and jitter, and cap retries. Demand can also outrun the headroom you have on any one model. You want to know where work can go before you need it, and our evals answer that. The answer can be a model from another model family. For every major model we use, we keep at least one equivalent that performs as well on our evals and that we can load-balance to. Without those evals, choosing where the work goes would be guesswork. If headroom on a model stays tight, we can rebalance by changing a default in our configuration. First check that the equivalent model has capacity for the extra load and that your quota covers it. Keep enough traffic on it to hold your access, too: after a model enters its Legacy period, existing customers can lose access after 15 days of inactivity. A Legacy model works until end-of-life, and after that Bedrock removes it from every Region, requests to it fail, and Bedrock doesn’t move your traffic automatically. Alarm when LegacyModelInvocations rises above zero. Step 6: Whose spend is it? Bedrock runtime metrics are dimensioned by ModelId, so you can see which model served a request but not which team sent it. Bedrock publishes these metrics both with and without the ModelId dimension, and a request that fails before Bedrock resolves the model appears only in the series without it, so filtering by ModelId undercounts errors. Bedrock offers three ways to attribute spend: Which team or user? Bedrock records the caller’s IAM identity on every request. Tag your roles, or pass session tags, to see cost by tag in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0). Which application? Application inference profiles are model-specific, so create one tagged profile per application and model, and call the matching profile’s ARN. Which feature or prompt? Pass key-value pairs in requestMetadata on Converse. Bedrock writes them to the model invocation logs and leaves them off the bill. To price them, multiply the token counts in the logs by the published rates. Neither classic CUR nor CUR 2.0 carries a per-request ID, so reconcile the two by comparing totals by model, usage type and time period. Behind a gateway, Bedrock sees the gateway’s role, so have the gateway assume a role for each user with its own RoleSessionName or session tags. Cache those credentials for the session, because assuming a role on every request can exceed your AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) rate quotas. Requests keep succeeding when attribution breaks, so set an alarm for when Bedrock fails to deliver invocation logs. Our usage records let us attribute usage by model, client, team and user, which we use only in aggregate for cost and capacity planning. We compute cost per task from the same four token counts, so we can compare token mix and cost between our evals and production. Results We can go from a model release to a deployment decision overnight. After one rollout, average weekly spend per user on model A was several times that on the previous model. We moved its heavy users to a newer model. In their first full week, the group’s spend on its main model fell to about a seventh, with roughly the same number of requests. For every major model we use, our evals identify an equivalent we can rebalance to. Clean up After testing, stop the eval jobs and agent processes you started. If you enabled model invocation logging only for this walkthrough, disable it in each Region using DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration. After callers no longer use them, delete the application inference profiles you created using DeleteInferenceProfile. Remove IAM roles, policies, and resource tags created only for this walkthrough. Deactivate cost allocation tags used only for these tests. Delete test CloudWatch log groups and S3 log objects you no longer need. Conclusion We run four checks every time a model ships: Release day: run the new model on your own tasks at every effort, and record a score and a cost per task together. Before rollout: choose the default and cap effort from those numbers. Block any effort that costs more and scores less than a lower effort. First weeks: compare cost per request and average requests per user with the eval’s cost per task, pricing both from the same four token counts. Before you need it: know which models score the same on your evals, from any model family, and check their capacity and your quota before you rebalance. We chose Amazon Bedrock for access to multiple model families through one API. It lets us use our existing AWS access controls and logging while AWS manages the model infrastructure. We use evals to choose models for our work and observability to know when those choices need another look. To go further, see these pages in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide: Monitor runtime metrics in CloudWatch Diagnose latency with output tokens per second How tokens are counted Prompt caching Track usage and costs Monitor model invocations with logs Model lifecycle About the authors Alan Yao Alan is a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Airbnb, where he leads model evaluation for AI-assisted engineering. He builds the evals that measure each model’s score and cost per task. Airbnb uses them to choose the coding models and reasoning efforts its engineers get by default. Rashim Gupta Rashim is a Senior Manager Product Management on the Amazon Bedrock team. His team builds service features such as Web Search, Observability, Spend Control, and Governance. Jayadev Vadakkanmarveettil Jayadev is a Principal Product Manager on the Amazon Bedrock team. He works on projects that help drive growth and owns product experience for quotas and capacity management. Sang Kong Sang is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS. He helps strategic customers deploy scalable, resilient, cost optimized solutions. Based in Northern California, he enjoys taking long hikes with his family and creating ambient musical soundscapes.
