items.title: Introducing CodeRabbit Verify: Agentic application testing and AI quality assurance
items.summary: AI coding agents are helping developers take on more features and fixes, but someone still has to find out whether the application actually works after those changes. Think about the last agent-generated PR your team worked on. Did a developer have to deploy the infrastructure and get the app running, click through the workflows those changes touched, and send bugs back to the coding agent? The volume of code coming from coding agents makes manually testing every change impractical. You either slow down releases while QA works through the backlog, or ship changes you haven’t properly tested and hope they work. You can only release software as fast as you can trust it, so dev and QA teams need to rethink how they test agentic code to ship faster without sacrificing quality. Today, we’re announcing that [CodeRabbit Verify is in public beta](https://www.coderabbit.ai/verify). CodeRabbit now tests your running application, checks behavior changed by a PR or across your whole codebase, and catches functional bugs or broken workflows before they reach your customers. When a test uncovers a bug, you can send the finding to CodeRabbit Agent for a fix or hand it to your preferred coding agent. [Watch the CodeRabbit Verify demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cLMXOAn9xEs 'CodeRabbit Verify demo') Verify tests a coupon change through three scenarios. Two report bugs involving the simulated charge; the invalid-coupon and removal scenario passes. This is a demo application, with no real payments. CodeRabbit Verify checks whether your application behaves as intended when someone uses it, if new changes break existing workflows, and what your unit tests missed. That first pass means your QA team doesn’t have to work through every agent-generated change by hand to find out which user journey hits a dead end or bug. ## Test changes in each PR CodeRabbit Verify builds test scenarios based on the commits in a PR, relevant source code, user-provided tests and documentation. When CodeRabbit has reviewed the latest commit, that review context can also inform the testing plan. Expected results come from the intended behavior, documentation and existing test expectations, so a new implementation doesn’t get to define its own correctness. You can inspect and refine the scenarios before running them. For example, let’s say you are testing whether a coupon works during checkout in an e-commerce application. You apply a coupon named SAVE20 to a $100 order, and it should reduce the order total to $80. CodeRabbit Verify follows the checkout flow and finds that the confirmation displays the correct $80 total, but the application still records a $100 simulated charge. The customer can apply the coupon and complete checkout, yet the amount recorded as charged is wrong. Testing only whether the coupon was accepted or the confirmation appeared would miss that bug. CodeRabbit Verify posts test results directly in the PR. Here, all three scenarios pass, each with a run summary and links to evidence and recordings. As new commits arrive, Verify can update the PR’s user scenario plan and rerun checks that need fresh validation. Earlier results stay associated with the commit they tested. When a scenario finds a bug or a blocker, you can send the observed behavior and evidence to CodeRabbit Agent for an automatic fix or hand them to your preferred coding agent, instead of reconstructing the issue from another report. ## Generate user journeys for regression testing Engineering teams also need to know that existing functionality keeps working as agents change the codebase. A new feature can break checkout, account creation or another workflow your customers depend on, even when the PR wasn’t intended to change it. Regression testing needs to keep pace with those changes without making your team write and maintain every test by hand. CodeRabbit Verify inspects your repository and proposes user journeys in plain English. Each journey describes who the user is, what they want to accomplish, the steps they take and the outcomes that must hold true. Your team can discuss the proposals with the agent, revise them and approve them when satisfied. You don’t have to start by writing the entire regression test plan yourself. The journey library brings reusable application workflows and their latest results together, with controls to edit journeys with an agent and run them again. Approved journeys become a reusable regression testing library. You can run selected journeys on demand, group them with tags or schedule them against a branch and test environment. As developers and agents change the application, Verify exercises those workflows to catch previously working behavior that has broken. That gives your team repeatable regression coverage across the application, including functionality beyond what the latest PR appears to touch. For scheduled runs, you can enable automatic issue creation in a connected Jira or Linear tracker for new bugs and testing blockers. A later run that verifies a fix can close the finding and update its linked issue. ## See which tests failed and fix the failures You can watch Verify work through scenarios and user journey in a live browser view, then use the retained recordings, screenshots and logs to investigate a failure. TYou see what it did and what happened at the point where the workflow failed, instead of starting from a vague report that something is broken. In the coupon example, the saved screenshot shows the $80 order total alongside the $100 simulated charge. The scenario includes the expected behavior and the observations behind its result, giving a developer or coding agent a concrete starting point for the repair. The saved order-confirmation screenshot exposes an $80 order total and a $100 simulated charge. Developers can inspect the recording and execution details or use Fix with Coding Agent to start the repair handoff. Verify confirms the journey’s goals and assertions are met before marking it as passed. If the application couldn’t start or a required check couldn’t be completed, it reports the limitation separately from an application bug, so your team knows what still needs checking. Fix with CodeRabbit Agent carries the finding, tested revision, environment and supporting evidence into the repair workflow. Developers can add guidance and review the task before handing it over. You can also export the findings and reproduction context for your preferred coding agent, including copying the handoff as Markdown that can be opened anywhere. Verify sends selected failed scenarios and their supporting evidence to CodeRabbit Agent for a fix. Developers can add guidance or export the handoff to their preferred coding agent. ## Automatically deploy infra to test your application Your team shouldn’t have to spend an afternoon setting up a test environment before running QA tests. CodeRabbit Agent inspects the project’s requirements, prepares a sandbox for Verify, installs dependencies, configures supporting services or emulators, starts the app, and checks that it’s ready. All testing takes place in CodeRabbit’s sandbox, away from your production environment. A prepared environment for Verify. Shared settings and variables are on the left; the repository's machine size, setup method, and saved setup and startup scripts are on the right. Once the application is ready, CodeRabbit saves reusable setup and startup instructions and a snapshot of the prepared environment. Later test runs reuse that preparation, so developers get test results instead of repeatedly setting up infrastructure. ## Try CodeRabbit Verify in beta If you want to ship software at agentic speed, testing can’t depend on someone manually checking every change. CodeRabbit Verify tests your running application, checks critical user journeys and helps you get functional bugs fixed with CodeRabbit Agent. Your team can move changes through QA with less manual work, so faster coding translates into faster shipping without sacrificing quality. During the public beta, Verify PR test runs, full-repo journey runs, and fixes with CodeRabbit Agent are all free. Start with a PR you want to test and comment `@coderabbitai verify`. If the repository isn’t configured yet, follow the setup link in CodeRabbit’s reply to prepare its test environment. You can also generate user journeys from your codebase and run them on demand or on a schedule to check that existing functionality continues to work as your application changes. For details, check out the [CodeRabbit Verify documentation](https://docs.coderabbit.ai/verify). Let us know what you find and how Verify changes application testing in your agentic SDLC. items.title: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard
items.summary: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case. Today we are launching the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard, a new way to compare JumpStart models side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model. What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard? The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information: Quality scores on three public benchmarks (BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro) that AWS runs itself, using the same evaluation setup for every model so the numbers are comparable. Performance and cost metrics that AWS measures by sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint using each JumpStart deployment configuration, so you see how fast a model responds and what it costs to run. Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers 70+ models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time. The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model. Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio Key concepts This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves. Quality benchmarks A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs: Benchmark What it measures, in plain terms BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) A set of challenging tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as logical deduction, tracking objects, and multi-step arithmetic. GPQA Diamond Graduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer by searching the web. A good signal of deep reasoning. MMLU-Pro Broad knowledge and reasoning across many subjects, such as science, law, and engineering, using harder multiple-choice questions. Higher is better for all three. The leaderboard shows each benchmark separately rather than blending them into one number. That keeps the results transparent: You can weigh the benchmarks that matter for your application and check each score against the public definition of the benchmark. Use case profiles and optimization goals Speed and cost depend on your workload and on how the model is deployed. Two menus above the leaderboard control which performance and cost numbers you see: Use case profile. Select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu. The default is Max Context. The profile changes only the performance and cost metrics. Quality benchmark scores are the same for every profile. Optimization goal. For each profile, a model can have several deployment configurations, and the leaderboard shows metrics for one at a time. Choose which one with the Optimized for menu. The default is Balanced. Each optimization goal picks a different configuration: Optimization goal Configuration shown Balanced The configuration with the lowest estimated cost per token. Because cost per token depends on both instance price and throughput, this balances what you pay per hour against how fast the instance generates tokens. Cost optimized The configuration with the lowest hourly instance price. Latency can be higher and throughput lower than with other goals. Latency optimized The configuration with the lowest time to first token. Throughput optimized The configuration with the highest throughput. These configurations can use speculative decoding. Performance metrics Metric What it tells you Time to first token (TTFT) How long a user waits before the model starts responding. Lower is better, and it matters most for chat. Throughput per request (tokens/s) How many tokens the model generates per second. Higher is better, and it matters for batch and high-volume workloads. Instance cost ($/hr) The estimated cost per hour given a specified instance type. A note on cost: Estimated cost reflects SageMaker instance cost only, based on the on-demand hourly rate for the configuration’s default instance type. It does not include data transfer, storage, inference component costs, or discounts such as Reserved Instances or AWS Savings Plans. Your actual bill will vary. Use the AWS Pricing Calculator for billing estimates. How we benchmark Published benchmark scores often come from different teams using different prompts, settings, and hardware, which makes them hard to compare. We took a different approach: One method for every model. AWS runs each benchmark with the same evaluation harness and settings across all models on the leaderboard. Measured on SageMaker. Performance and cost come from sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint deployed with each JumpStart deployment configuration, the same configurations you can launch. For full details, including prompts, generation settings, and how configurations are measured, see JumpStart model leaderboard benchmarks. Walkthrough: Finding a model The following steps show how to go from browsing to a deployed model. You need access to SageMaker Studio and permission to deploy JumpStart models. Step 1: Open the leaderboard In SageMaker Studio, open the Models page, then select the Leaderboard view. The leaderboard keeps the same search bar and filters as the other views, and it has its own URL. You can bookmark it or share a direct link with your team. The following screenshot shows the Models page with the Leaderboard view selected. Figure 2: JumpStart base models page with the Leaderboard view selected Step 2: Narrow the list with filters Use the same search and filters you already use elsewhere in JumpStart to keep only the models that fit your requirements. Common filters include license, provider, and input and output modality. Start with hard requirements, for example a license that allows commercial use, before you look at scores. The following screenshot shows the leaderboard filtered by input modality, output modality, and license. Figure 3: Leaderboard with filters applied Step 3: Choose a use case profile and optimization goal Above the leaderboard, select the profile closest to your workload from the View benchmarks for your use case menu (default: Max Context). Then choose a goal from the Optimized for menu (default: Balanced). For a chatbot your customers interact with, Latency optimized is a sensible start. For overnight document processing, Throughput optimized or Cost optimized may fit better. The performance and cost columns update, and quality scores stay the same. The following screenshots show the View benchmarks for your use case and Optimized for menus above the leaderboard. Figure 4: View benchmarks for your use case menu Figure 5: Optimized for menu Step 4: Read the heatmap and customize columns Each column has a blue heatmap, so the top-performing models stand out at a glance: the deeper the blue, the stronger the result in that column. Sort any benchmark column to rank models by the metric you care about most. Use the column settings (gear icon) to hide metrics you don’t need, and scroll horizontally to see more. The model name columns stay frozen as you scroll, and a fade at the edge shows when more columns are available. The following screenshot shows the heatmap and the column settings menu. Figure 6: Heatmap and column settings Step 5: Deploy or customize the model Choose a model to open it. From there, you have options to deploy the model or, for models that support serverless customization, to customize it. If you deploy, choose the same use case and optimization goal you compared on the leaderboard. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on, and a different configuration can change quality, latency, throughput, and cost. The following screenshot shows a model page with the Deploy and Customize options. Figure 7: Model page with the Deploy and Customize options Example: Picking a model for a chat assistant Suppose you are building an internal help-desk assistant. Employees ask questions and expect fast, accurate answers that follow a set response format. You need a commercially licensed model and want to keep costs predictable. After filtering by license and choosing a chat-like use case profile with Latency optimized, your shortlist might look like this: Model BBH MMLU-Pro TTFT (s) Throughput (tokens/s) Instance cost ($/hr) Model A (large) 95.9 87.2 2.33 37 $37.66 Model B (medium) 94.2 84.9 0.98 44 $5.75 Model C (small) 77.4 66.1 0.27 61 $2.61 Reading the table, Model A has the highest knowledge score but also the highest cost and the slowest first response. Model B scores almost as well, holds up on multi-step reasoning, and runs on a smaller, cheaper instance. For a help desk, where reasoning through a question and responding quickly matter more than the last few points of general knowledge, Model B is the better starting point. A bigger model is not always the better choice, and the leaderboard makes that trade-off visible in seconds. From there, you would deploy Model B, test it with real questions from your help desk, and keep Model C in mind as a lower-cost option if quality holds up. Tips and things to know Use the leaderboard to build a shortlist, not to make the final call. Benchmarks measure general ability. Always evaluate your top two or three models on your own data and prompts before going to production. Filter first, then rank. Requirements like license and input or output modality rule models in or out. Scores only help you order what is left. Compare models within a benchmark. Each benchmark has its own difficulty, so a score on one benchmark isn’t directly comparable with a score on another. Account for model type. Reasoning and non-reasoning models are evaluated with different generation parameters, and GPQA Diamond scores for reasoning models are averaged over 10 passes. Comparisons between the two types are approximate. Check the deployment configuration. Each metric applies to the configuration it was measured on. Compare models on the configuration you plan to deploy. Treat close scores as ties. Small differences can fall within normal run-to-run variation and don’t mean one model is meaningfully better. Look for clear gaps. Coverage is growing. Not every JumpStart model has benchmark scores yet, and launch benchmarks focus on LLMs. A model without a score is not a weak model. It simply has not been benchmarked yet. What’s next We’re continuing to expand the leaderboard. Areas we’re exploring include: Private hub support, so organizations that use curated JumpStart private hubs can see a leaderboard for their approved models. More task leaderboards beyond LLM text generation, such as object detection, text embeddings, and image understanding. More models and benchmarks as new models are added to JumpStart. Conclusion The SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard brings quality, speed, and cost together in one place, measured consistently on SageMaker. Instead of comparing numbers from different sources, you can filter to the models that fit your requirements, compare them on the configuration you plan to run, and deploy with a few clicks. To get started, open the Models page in SageMaker Studio and select the Leaderboard view. To learn more, see the following resources: JumpStart model leaderboard benchmarks. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. SageMaker JumpStart documentation. Use-case based deployments on SageMaker JumpStart. Customize a model with SageMaker serverless customization. Open the leaderboard, shortlist two or three models for your workload, and deploy them to test with your own prompts before you choose one for production. About the authors Dan Ferguson Dan is a Solutions Architect at AWS, based in New York, USA. As a machine learning services expert, Dan works to support customers on their journey to integrating ML workflows efficiently, effectively, and sustainably. Naidile Murali Naidile is a Product Manager at AWS based in Bellevue, WA. She focuses on enhancing the AI/ML developer experience on SageMaker Studio, JumpStart, and IDE capacity management. Prior to AWS, she worked as a software engineer at HSBC. Naidile holds an MBA from Georgetown University. Joseph Zhang Joseph is a software engineer at AWS. He started his AWS career at EC2 before transitioning to SageMaker and now works on developing GenAI-related features. Outside of work he enjoys both playing and watching sports (go Warriors!), spending time with family, and making coffee. Rachel Park Rachel is a software engineer on the SageMaker JumpStart team at AWS, based in New York. She is passionate about how people interact with technology and about building better customer experiences. Rachel holds a M.Eng. from MIT, where she studied computation and cognition. Mike James Mike is a Software Development Manager at AWS, where he leads the engineering teams for SageMaker JumpStart and the developer experience in SageMaker Studio and Console. His focus is making it easy for customers to adopt the newest models, hardware, and software innovations from across the industry.

items.title: Introducing workload recovery and expanded infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
items.summary: Large training jobs can fail even when every node looks healthy. A GPU with a subtle fault can pass its stress tests and still return wrong values. When a job stalls on an NCCL timeout, it keeps its GPUs, and Slurm still shows it as running. If a device plugin crashes on one node, the job fails with an error that never mentions the plugin. Teams usually find these problems only after the loss diverges or the job fails, and by then the compute is spent. Each of these failures lowers goodput, the share of your cluster’s time that goes to useful training. Today, we’re introducing workload recovery and infrastructure checks on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod that catch these failures sooner and raise the goodput of your training workloads. SageMaker HyperPod already handles nodes that report hardware faults. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors, deep health checks test nodes during provisioning, and automatic node recovery reboots or replaces faulty hardware. These features look at one node’s hardware at a time. They can’t tell whether the GPUs train correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the Kubernetes components a job depends on are working. In this post, we walk through the three new capabilities that catch these failures. For each one, we show how to set it up and what it reports when it finds a problem: MultiNodeTrainingValidation is a new deep health check for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When HyperPod provisions an instance, or when you run the check on demand, it trains a small model on the instance and then across instances of the same type. The instance fails if the loss becomes NaN or infinite, or training doesn’t finish in time. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the Kubernetes layer of an EKS cluster for problems such as crash-looping device plugins, missing DaemonSets, and tainted nodes. When a job fails, it reports the pods and nodes involved as Kubernetes events and Amazon CloudWatch logs. Hung job detection finds Slurm jobs that have stopped making progress. An agent on each node watches the job’s output and GPU activity, or log patterns that you define. It writes an event to CloudWatch and can cancel the job so that Slurm requeues it. Why node health alone isn’t enough The existing HyperPod resiliency features check a single node at a time. The health monitoring agent (HMA) watches each node for GPU errors such as Xid and NVLink faults, Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) errors, and kernel errors. The InstanceStress deep health check runs DCGM level 4 diagnostics and tests each instance’s GPUs, GPU memory, NVLink, and EFA devices. The InstanceConnectivity check runs NCCL tests across GPU instances, or NCCOM tests on AWS Trainium. Together, these confirm that each node’s hardware works. They don’t show whether the GPUs compute correctly, whether a job is still making progress, or whether the cluster’s Kubernetes components are healthy. Three kinds of failure get past them: Numerical faults – A GPU can pass every hardware test and still compute wrong results. The first sign is often NaN or infinite loss in a production run. Meta attributed 6 of the 419 unexpected interruptions in its 54-day Llama 3 405B pre-training run to silent data corruption (The Llama 3 Herd of Models). Hung jobs – An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can stop a job without ending it. The job keeps its GPUs and their memory, and Slurm reports it as running until someone checks the loss curve or the log. Cluster-level failures – Some failures happen in Kubernetes, not in a node’s hardware. A device plugin crash-loops, a required DaemonSet never starts on a new node, or ranks on different nodes fall out of step in an NCCL collective. HMA checks each node on its own, so it doesn’t see these problems. When the job fails, the error often doesn’t say which pod or node caused it. Solution overview Each capability covers a different point in a training run. MultiNodeTrainingValidation runs when instances are provisioned, or on demand, and confirms that their GPUs train correctly. Hung job detection runs alongside each Slurm job and catches a job that has stopped making progress. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches the cluster continuously and, when a job fails, reports the pods and nodes that were involved. The following table summarizes the three. Capability What it catches When it runs Available on MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time, on GPUs that pass hardware checks When instances are created or updated, or on demand EKS clusters, on supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instances HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent Node condition changes, pod and DaemonSet failures, and failed training jobs, with the pods and nodes involved. NCCL communication state for jobs that opt in Continuously EKS clusters Hung job detection Jobs that stop making progress but don’t exit While each job runs Slurm clusters Hung job detection is new for Slurm clusters. On EKS clusters, HyperPod already detects hung jobs that run through the HyperPod training operator, and Ray Train jobs get hang detection by default. We describe both options in the hung job detection section. Each capability targets a different source of lost goodput. Scheduling goodput is the share of time that all the resources a job needs are available. Runtime goodput is the share of that time in which the job makes forward progress. Program goodput is the share of the hardware’s peak performance that the job gets. The following table shows the effect of each capability. Capability Scheduling goodput Runtime goodput Program goodput MultiNodeTrainingValidation Instances that fail the training test are labeled and, with automatic node recovery, replaced, so jobs don’t start on hardware that produces invalid output Fewer production runs lost to NaN or infinite loss from a faulty GPU Flags instances whose training doesn’t finish within the time limit HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent Reports nodes that lose GPUs or EFA devices, missing device plugins, and taints, so you can restore capacity sooner Names the pods and nodes behind a failed job, so you find the cause and restart sooner No direct effect Hung job detection No direct effect Flags a hung job in minutes instead of hours, and can cancel it so Slurm requeues it No direct effect Consider a pre-training job running on 32 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (256 NVIDIA H100 GPUs). If the job hangs at 1:00 AM and no one notices until 9:00 AM, it wastes 256 instance-hours or 2,048 GPU-hours. At the SageMaker HyperPod on-demand price of approximately $66 per instance-hour in US East (N. Virginia), the hang costs about $16,900. With a 15-minute hung job detection rule, HyperPod cancels the stalled job and Slurm requeues it. The hang costs about $530 instead, saving approximately $16,400. Validate training correctness with the MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check The MultiNodeTrainingValidation deep health check trains a fixed, known-good workload, first on each instance and then across instances. It catches GPUs that pass InstanceStress and InstanceConnectivity but produce NaN or infinite loss once they train together. If an instance fails, HyperPod labels it as failed and, with automatic node recovery turned on, reboots or replaces it. When the check runs during provisioning, this happens before your jobs can use the instance. How it works MultiNodeTrainingValidation adds two tests to the deep health check run: Tiny Megatron test: A short Megatron-LM training run on all GPUs of each instance. Megatron test: The same workload across instances of the same type, communicating over EFA. Either test fails an instance if the training loss becomes NaN or infinite, or if training doesn’t finish within the time limit. The workload is fixed, so a failure points to the hardware rather than to a model or code change. The following table shows how it fits with the other deep health checks. Check What it runs What it catches InstanceStress GPU and NVLink count, DCGM level 4 diagnostics, and EFA latency and bandwidth tests (Neuron tests on Trainium) Hardware that’s missing, failing, or unstable InstanceConnectivity NCCL tests across GPU instances (NCCOM on Trainium) Slow or broken communication between instances MultiNodeTrainingValidation Tiny Megatron test on each instance, Megatron test across instances GPUs that run but train incorrectly: NaN or infinite loss, or training that doesn’t finish in time Prerequisites You need the following: An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS. An instance group of a supported EFA-enabled NVIDIA GPU instance type, such as ml.p5.48xlarge. The Megatron test runs across instances of the same type. Turn on MultiNodeTrainingValidation for an instance group HyperPod runs deep health checks when it creates or updates instances. To include MultiNodeTrainingValidation, add it to OnStartDeepHealthChecks in the instance group configuration that you pass to create-cluster or update-cluster. We turned on all three checks: { "InstanceGroupName": "<instance-group>", "InstanceType": "ml.p5.48xlarge", "InstanceCount": 2, "LifeCycleConfig": { "SourceS3Uri": "s3://<bucket>/<prefix>", "OnCreate": "on_create.sh" }, "ExecutionRole": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<hyperpod-execution-role>", "OnStartDeepHealthChecks": [ "InstanceStress", "InstanceConnectivity", "MultiNodeTrainingValidation" ] } To confirm the setting, run the following command: aws sagemaker describe-cluster \ --cluster-name <cluster-name> \ --query "InstanceGroups[?InstanceGroupName=='<instance-group>'].OnStartDeepHealthChecks" The output lists the three checks: [ [ "InstanceStress", "InstanceConnectivity", "MultiNodeTrainingValidation" ] ] Run MultiNodeTrainingValidation on demand You can also check instances that are already in the cluster, for example before a long pre-training run. Use the StartClusterHealthCheck API: aws sagemaker start-cluster-health-check \ --cluster-name <cluster-name> \ --deep-health-check-configurations \ '[{"InstanceGroupName": "<instance-group>", "DeepHealthChecks": ["MultiNodeTrainingValidation"]}]' To check specific instances instead of the whole group, add "InstanceIds": [...] to the configuration. Check the results HyperPod writes one line per test to the DeepHealthCheckResults/<id> log stream in your cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>. Here’s the stream from our run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. TINY_MEGATRON and MEGATRON are the two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests: 2026-11-11T10:58:33Z Deep health check configuration validation passed 2026-11-11T11:01:41Z 2 out of 2 nodes succeeded HARDWARE_CHECK test. Instance IDs: [i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002] 2026-11-11T12:16:07Z 2 out of 2 nodes succeeded DCGM test. Instance IDs: [i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002] 2026-11-11T12:17:14Z 2 out of 2 nodes succeeded EFA test. Instance IDs: [i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002] 2026-11-11T12:21:16Z 2 out of 2 nodes succeeded TINY_MEGATRON test. Instance IDs: [i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002] 2026-11-11T12:22:25Z 0 nodes failed NCCL test at batch size 2. Instance IDs: [] 2026-11-11T12:22:29Z 2 out of 2 nodes succeeded NCCL test. Instance IDs: [i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002] 2026-11-11T12:26:31Z 0 nodes failed MEGATRON test at batch size 2. Instance IDs: [] 2026-11-11T12:26:31Z 2 out of 2 nodes succeeded MEGATRON test. Instance IDs: [i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002] When the run finishes, each instance carries the result as a node label: kubectl get nodes \ -l sagemaker.amazonaws.com/instance-group-name=<instance-group> \ -L sagemaker.amazonaws.com/deep-health-check-status NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION DEEP-HEALTH-CHECK-STATUS hyperpod-i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001 Ready <none> 120m v1.34.2-eks-ecaa3a6 Passed hyperpod-i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002 Ready <none> 120m v1.34.2-eks-ecaa3a6 Passed For the training details, read /var/log/aws/clusters/sagemaker-deep-health-check.log on the instance, for example through an AWS Systems Manager session. On the instance that ran rank 0, the log ends with a summary of the Megatron test: CONVERGENCE TEST PASSED Completed 300 training iterations in 161.5s Training forward steps: 300 Evaluation forward steps: 20 Total forward steps: 320 Final training loss: 3.6213 Initial training loss: 11.5671 Loss reduction: 7.9458 Training iterations per second: 1.86 The other instance’s log has a line for every iteration, with the loss and a running count of NaN iterations: iteration 300/ 300 | consumed samples: 9600 | elapsed time per iteration (ms): 509.5 | learning rate: 1.000E-04 | global batch size: 32 | lm loss: 3.397480E+00 | loss scale: 1.0 | grad norm: 1.386 | number of skipped iterations: 0 | number of nan iterations: 0 | In our run, the loss fell from 11.57 to 3.62 over 300 iterations, with no NaN or skipped iterations, at about 507 milliseconds per iteration on 16 H100 GPUs. How long MultiNodeTrainingValidation takes On our two-node cluster, the full deep health check took 1 hour 28 minutes after the instances finished their lifecycle scripts. DCGM level 4 diagnostics took most of that. The two MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests added about 8 minutes. Instances can’t take workloads until the checks finish, so plan for this additional time when you add capacity. Test Check Time since previous result HARDWARE_CHECK InstanceStress 3 min DCGM (level 4) InstanceStress 74 min EFA InstanceStress 1 min TINY_MEGATRON MultiNodeTrainingValidation 4 min NCCL InstanceConnectivity 1 min MEGATRON (2 instances) MultiNodeTrainingValidation 4 min Keep in mind that MultiNodeTrainingValidation tests the hardware with a fixed reference workload. A pass means the instances trained that workload correctly. It doesn’t guarantee that your own job will converge. We recommend running it on new capacity, on replacement instances, and before long pre-training runs. Catch cluster-level failures with the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent HMA watches the hardware on each node, but many failures that stop a training job happen in Kubernetes. A device plugin can crash-loop until its node stops offering GPUs to the scheduler, or a taint can evict a job’s pods. The job error rarely names the pod or node involved, so engineers piece together what happened from kubectl output, per-rank logs, and timestamps. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent watches these resources from one place in the cluster. When something breaks, it tells you what changed and which nodes, pods, and jobs are affected. It reports through Kubernetes events and structured CloudWatch logs. The agent only reports. It doesn’t reboot nodes or restart jobs, because the cause might be in the workload. HMA and HyperPod node recovery still handle hardware faults, and the HyperPod training operator still handles job restarts. How the agent works The agent runs as a single pod per cluster in the aws-hyperpod namespace and prefers CPU nodes, so it doesn’t use GPU capacity. It watches the following: Nodes: The agent reports these changes: Condition changes such as NotReady or memory, disk, or PID pressure. Fewer allocatable GPUs or EFA devices. Lost NVIDIA capability labels. Added, changed, or removed taints. Missing HyperPod labels. Critical infrastructure pods: DaemonSet pods in kube-system, aws-hyperpod, and kubeflow, plus the training operator’s controller. The agent reports crash loops, restarts, container errors, and pods that stay not ready. DaemonSets: Required DaemonSets that are missing or have no available pods, rollouts that stall, and pods running on nodes that no longer allow them. Training jobs: HyperPodPyTorchJob, Kubeflow PyTorchJob (v1), and Kubeflow TrainJob (v2). When a job fails, the agent records the failure reason with the job’s pods and nodes. NCCL communication: For jobs that opt in, the state of the job’s NCCL communicators, read from NCCL’s built-in reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem. The agent reports what it finds in two places: Kubernetes events on the affected node, pod, DaemonSet, or job. A Warning event marks a problem and a Normal event marks its recovery. You read them with kubectl get events and kubectl describe. Structured JSON logs in the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, which keep the history after Kubernetes events expire. The following table lists the events you’re most likely to see. Event reason Raised when TrainingJobFailed A HyperPodPyTorchJob or Kubeflow job fails. The message includes the failure reason from the job’s operator. CriticalPodCrashLoop, CriticalPodRestarted A device plugin, HMA, or another critical pod crash-loops or restarts. NecessaryDaemonSetMissing A DaemonSet you declared as required is missing or has no available pods. NodeResourceDegraded A node’s allocatable GPUs or EFA devices drop or disappear. NodeConditionDegraded A node becomes NotReady or reports memory, disk, or PID pressure. NodeTaintAdded, NoExecuteTaintApplied A node is tainted. For a NoExecute taint, the log lists the pods and jobs that might be evicted. DaemonSetMisscheduled DaemonSet pods are running on nodes that no longer allow them. NodeRecovered, PodRecovered, DaemonSetRecovered A problem reported earlier has cleared. For the full list of events, see the documentation. Prerequisites You need the following: A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon EKS. For an existing cluster, kubectl and Helm access to the cluster, and the HyperPod Helm chart from the sagemaker-hyperpod-cli repository. NCCL 2.24 or later in the training container, if you want to monitor NCCL communication. Install and verify the agent If your cluster already uses the HyperPod Helm chart, apply the agent’s custom resource definition (CRD) first, because Helm doesn’t install CRDs during an upgrade. Then upgrade the release with the agent turned on: git clone https://github.com/aws/sagemaker-hyperpod-cli.git cd sagemaker-hyperpod-cli/helm_chart helm dependencies update HyperPodHelmChart kubectl apply \ -f HyperPodHelmChart/charts/hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor/crds/ helm upgrade dependencies HyperPodHelmChart \ --namespace kube-system \ --reset-then-reuse-values \ --set hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor.enabled=true \ --set hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor.region=<region> The upgrade also moves the other HyperPod components in the chart, such as HMA and the device plugins, to the chart’s current versions. To see what will change first, run the same command with --dry-run=server. Check that the agent is running and that its health report exists: kubectl get deployment \ -n aws-hyperpod \ hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitoring-agent kubectl get hyperpodkrmaconfigs default -o yaml The health report lists the HyperPod components that the agent tracks, such as HMA, and when their status last changed: status: components: - name: DaemonSet/aws-hyperpod/health-monitoring-agent since: "2026-11-10T16:47:57Z" status: Healthy instances: [] lastReportTime: "2026-11-10T17:19:36Z" By default, HMA is the only required DaemonSet. If your cluster uses the device plugins from the HyperPod Helm chart, add them so that the agent reports a missing plugin. Also add the namespaces where your training jobs run, so that it can link pod failures to their jobs. Each list replaces its default, so keep the default entries. Save the following as krma-values.yaml: hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitor: monitoring: monitoredNamespaces: - aws-hyperpod - kube-system - default - kubeflow - ml-team-a necessaryDaemonsets: - name: health-monitoring-agent namespace: aws-hyperpod - name: dependencies-nvidia-device-plugin namespace: kube-system - name: dependencies-aws-efa-k8s-device-plugin namespace: kube-system Then apply it: helm upgrade dependencies HyperPodHelmChart \ --namespace kube-system \ --reset-then-reuse-values \ -f krma-values.yaml See what the agent reports To see how the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent handles an infrastructure failure, we deployed a small DaemonSet into aws-hyperpod, pinned it to one node, and made it exit a few seconds after starting. It behaves like a crash-looping device plugin without touching the real one. Within seconds, the agent raised events on the pod and the DaemonSet: kubectl get events -A \ --field-selector source=hyperpod-kubernetes-resource-monitoring-agent NAMESPACE TYPE REASON OBJECT MESSAGE aws-hyperpod Warning CriticalPodRestarted pod/demo-plugin-4wsqw Critical infrastructure pod container crash restarted (count: 2) aws-hyperpod Warning CriticalPodCrashLoop pod/demo-plugin-4wsqw Critical infrastructure pod container crash in CrashLoopBackOff aws-hyperpod Warning DaemonSetMisscheduled daemonset/demo-plugin DaemonSet has 1 misscheduled pods Next, we ran a two-node HyperPodPyTorchJob and made one rank exit during training. The agent raised a TrainingJobFailed event on the job: NAMESPACE TYPE REASON OBJECT MESSAGE ml-team-a Warning TrainingJobFailed hyperpodpytorchjob/llama-pretrain Training job HyperPod PyTorchJob failed: Fault detected on training pod llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-nh5gb: A training worker process has crashed: Local Rank 0 exited ... It also wrote the failure to CloudWatch with the pods and nodes involved, so you don’t need to look them up from the job’s pod list: {"level":"warn","msg":"=== Job Failure Detected ===","component":"HyperpodPyTorchJob", "job":"llama-pretrain","namespace":"ml-team-a","type":"HyperPod PyTorchJob", "reason":"Fault detected on training pod llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-nh5gb: A training worker process has crashed ..."} {"level":"warn","msg":"Affected Pods","component":"HyperpodPyTorchJob", "pods":["llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-nh5gb","llama-pretrain-pod-7dc7c-f9dmg"]} {"level":"warn","msg":"Affected Nodes","component":"HyperpodPyTorchJob", "nodes":["hyperpod-i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001","hyperpod-i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60002"]} The agent writes these logs to the cluster log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>, in streams named SageMakerClusterMonitoringAgent/<instance-group>/<instance-id>. It starts a new stream when it moves to another node, so filter by the stream prefix. For sample queries, see the documentation. Monitor NCCL communication for a job NCCL 2.24 and later include the reliability, availability, and serviceability (RAS) subsystem, a small listener in each NCCL process that reports the state of the job’s communicators. For jobs that opt in, the agent reads this report from every pod every 30 seconds. By default, NCCL binds the RAS listener to localhost inside the pod, where the agent can’t reach it. To opt a job in, you bind the listener to the pod IP instead. That makes port 28028 reachable on the pod network, which NVIDIA’s documentation notes has security implications. Before you turn it on, apply a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that allows TCP port 28028 only from the agent’s pod and still allows traffic between the job’s own pods. The agent’s documentation includes an example policy. Then set NCCL_RAS_ADDR in the training container: apiVersion: sagemaker.amazonaws.com/v1 kind: HyperPodPyTorchJob ... containers: - name: pytorch env: - name: POD_IP valueFrom: fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.podIP} - name: NCCL_RAS_ADDR # set only after the NetworkPolicy is in place value: "$(POD_IP):28028" To confirm the setting, turn on NCCL debug logging with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO and NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,RAS. Each rank then logs the address RAS listens on: [default3]:llama-pretrain-workers-6c7f5bb445-gxnsf:129:203 [3] NCCL INFO RAS client listening socket at 10.0.1.11<28028> If the address is ::1 or 127.0.0.1, NCCL_RAS_ADDR isn’t set and the agent can’t reach the listener. For each monitored job, the agent combines the per-pod results into a job-level state. The job is healthy when every pod returns a valid report, degraded when only some do, and unhealthy when none do. Unhealthy usually means the training processes have stopped. The agent logs a summary after each polling cycle. In a run on two ml.p5.48xlarge instances, every cycle reported both training pods healthy, 30 seconds apart: {"level":"info","timestamp":"2026-11-12T07:14:27.163Z","msg":"NCCL RAS monitoring cycle completed","component":"nccl-ras-informer-llama-pretrain","duration":4.00535305,"total_endpoints":2,"healthy":2,"failed":0,"overall_status":"healthy"} The agent also writes each RAS report to CloudWatch, so you can spot communicator problems while the job is still running. In our test, we made one rank of a two-node job stop calling all_reduce. The report from the next polling cycle showed the communicator out of step and named the rank, GPU, process, and node that had fallen behind: Group Comms Nodes Ranks Ranks Ranks Status Errors # in group per comm per node per comm in group 0 1 2 1 2 2 RUNNING MISMATCH #0-0 (2958ae23ccc57a88) MISMATCH Communicator ranks have different AllReduce operation counts Rank 0 has launched up to operation 3078 -- GPU 0 managed by process 473 on node 10.0.1.11 Rank 1 has launched up to operation 3077 -- GPU 0 managed by process 474 on node 10.0.2.22 Rank 1 is one operation behind rank 0, so start with rank 1’s GPU on node 10.0.2.22. Detect and recover hung jobs on HyperPod Slurm clusters A training job can hang without exiting. An NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock can leave the job holding its GPUs while Slurm still shows it as running. It stays that way until someone notices that the loss or the log has stopped changing. Teams that run Slurm often build their own watchdog scripts and alarms to catch these jobs, and then need to maintain them. Today, we’re launching hung job detection for SageMaker HyperPod Slurm clusters. It finds these jobs, writes an event to CloudWatch, and can cancel a hung job so that Slurm puts it back in the queue. You turn it on for each job with an environment variable that points to a small rules file. It needs no changes to your training scripts or containers, and it works with PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, and custom scripts. How hung job detection works Hung job detection runs as an agent on every node and is off by default. The agent watches only jobs that set the HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES environment variable to the path of a rules file. The rules file decides how the agent detects a hang: Default detection watches the job’s standard output and GPU activity. It declares a hang when the output stops for an extended period while the GPUs sit idle but still hold memory. That’s what a rendezvous hang looks like, when one node fails and the others wait at a barrier. It also declares a hang when the output stops for a longer period, whatever the GPUs are doing. In our test, the first case fired 15 minutes after the job’s last output. Custom rules watch your log for regular expressions that you choose. A progress rule declares a hang when a line such as your training step message doesn’t appear within its timeout. An error rule declares a hang as soon as a line such as an NCCL error appears. Custom rules replace default detection for that job. Default detection Custom rules Turn on with {“enabled”: true} One or more enabled log_pattern rules Declares a hang when Output stops while GPUs are idle but hold memory, or output stops for a longer period A progress pattern doesn’t appear within its timeout, or an error pattern appears Misses Jobs that keep their GPUs busy without making progress, such as a job stuck in a loop Hangs your patterns don’t describe. If a pattern keeps matching, no hang is declared, even with idle GPUs When the agent declares a hang, it writes a HANG_DETECTED event to CloudWatch. If the rules file sets the action to cancel, the agent also cancels the job and Slurm requeues it. With the default action, notify, the agent writes the event and leaves the job running. Hung job detection is separate from auto-resume, which restarts jobs that exit after a hardware failure. Auto-resume handles jobs that crash and hung job detection handles jobs that keep running without making progress. On HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, HyperPod already detects hung jobs in two cases. The HyperPod training operator checks the logs of each HyperPodPyTorchJob against rules in the job specification and restarts the job when it hangs. The same rules can also restart a job whose throughput drops or whose loss spikes. You don’t need Ray for this. For Ray Train jobs, HyperPod hung job detection for Ray watches every worker by default, with no changes to your code. Prerequisites You need the following: A SageMaker HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Slurm. A HyperPod Slurm AMI released on or after November 10, 2026, which includes hung job detection. Clusters created on or after that date already have it. To check an existing cluster without updating it, run srun --help on a cluster node. If the output lists --no-hang-detection, the cluster supports hung job detection. If it doesn’t, update the cluster software first. The update replaces each instance’s root volume, so back up anything stored there before you update. A rules file that every compute node in the job can read at the same path. The agent reads the file from that path on each node. Shared storage such as Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) is a straightforward option. To keep rules files in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), copy them to the same path on every node, for example in your lifecycle script. If you plan to use a directory such as /opt/slurm, first confirm that it’s shared across nodes rather than local to each one. Turn on hung job detection Create a rules file on shared storage. The smallest valid file turns on default detection: echo '{"enabled": true}' > /fsx/my-project/rules.json chmod 600 /fsx/my-project/rules.json The agent uses whatever rules file a job points to and doesn’t check who owns it. Anyone who can edit the file, or replace it in its directory, can change detection for every job that uses it, including making the agent cancel those jobs. The chmod 600 in the example keeps a personal rules file private to its owner. For a file that a team shares, use chmod 644 so the team can read it and only its maintainer can edit it. In both cases, make the parent directory writable only by its owner so nobody can swap the file. Then point the job at the rules file when you submit it: #!/bin/bash #SBATCH --job-name=llama-pretrain #SBATCH --nodes=4 #SBATCH --export=ALL,HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES=/fsx/my-project/rules.json srun python train.py To use one rules file for many jobs, you can also set HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES in a shell profile or a site-wide profile script. When a monitored job starts, the first lines of its output show that the agent registered it: [Auto Resume] Info: [hang_detection] Exported stdout path for job 1: /fsx/my-project/llama-pretrain-1.out [Auto Resume] Info: [hang_detection] Registered job step: job=1 step=0 node=ip-10-1-40-47 These lines also appear when the rules file is invalid, so check CloudWatch for a CONFIG_ERROR event too, as described in the next section. Add custom rules to track training progress Default detection can’t catch a job that keeps its GPUs busy without making progress, so we recommend at least one rule that watches for your training steps or epochs. The following rules file cancels the job if no epoch finishes for 45 minutes, or as soon as an NCCL error appears: { "enabled": true, "rules": [ { "name": "epoch_progress", "type": "log_pattern", "enabled": true, "log_pattern": "Epoch \\d+/\\d+ complete", "start_timeout_minutes": 30, "timeout_minutes": 45, "stop_pattern": "Training complete" }, { "name": "nccl_error", "type": "log_pattern", "enabled": true, "log_pattern": "NCCL error", "fault_on_match": true } ], "action_policy": { "action": "cancel" } } The fields work as follows: Set enabled to true on each rule. Rules are off by default. start_timeout_minutes is how long the job can run before the pattern first appears. Set it longer than the time your job needs to load the model, compile, and restore a checkpoint. timeout_minutes is how long the pattern can stay absent after that. Set it longer than the biggest normal gap, including checkpoint saves and evaluation. stop_pattern turns the rule off when it matches, so work after training ends isn’t flagged. fault_on_match marks an error pattern. One match means the job is hung. By default, the agent reads the job’s Slurm output file. To watch a different file, set monitoring.log_file. To cut false positives, set metric_evaluation_data_points on a rule so that several 10-second checks in a row must fail before the agent declares a hang. A rules file can have up to 20 rules and be up to 1 MB. Start with "action": "notify" while you tune timeouts and patterns, and switch to cancel once the events match real hangs. View hung job detection events in CloudWatch HyperPod writes detection events from the controller node to the cluster’s CloudWatch log group, /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id>, in the stream SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents/<controller-instance-group>/<controller-instance-id>. Events for every job land in this stream, whichever node the job ran on. To find the events for one job, filter by its job ID: aws logs filter-log-events \ --log-group-name /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id> \ --log-stream-name-prefix SageMakerHangJobDetectionEvents/ \ --filter-pattern '{ $.job_id = "12345" }' We tested each detection method on a HyperPod Slurm cluster with two ml.p5.48xlarge instances. The first test job allocated GPU memory and then stopped producing output. Default detection flagged it 15 minutes after its last output: { "time": "2026-11-12T16:49:36.39710952Z", "level": "INFO", "msg": "HANG_DETECTED", "event_type": "HANG_DETECTED", "job_id": "1", "step_id": "0", "node": "ip-10-1-40-47", "evidence": "stdout stale for 15 min and GPU idle with memory allocated", "layer": "signal_evaluator", "detected_at": "2026-11-12T16:49:36.378940227Z", "job_action": "notify", "config_source": "per_job_env_var" } The layer field shows which method fired: signal_evaluator for default detection, or pattern_evaluator for a custom rule. In a second test, a progress rule with a 2-minute timeout fired 2 minutes after the job’s last step. In a third, an error rule fired about one second after the job printed an NCCL error line. Because that rules file used cancel, the agent also wrote a HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event with the action Slurm took (we’ve left out the time, level, and msg fields): {"event_type":"HANG_DETECTED","job_id":"3","step_id":"0","node":"ip-10-1-40-47","evidence":"rule \"nccl_error\": fault pattern matched immediately","layer":"pattern_evaluator","detected_at":"2026-11-12T16:34:41.870908329Z","job_action":"cancel","config_source":"per_job_env_var"} {"event_type":"HANG_ACTION_TAKEN","job_id":"3","action":"requeue","node":"ip-10-1-40-47","instance_id":"i-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001"} Slurm put the job back in the queue, and the requeued run started about 2.5 minutes later. sacct shows both runs: $ sacct --duplicates -X -j 3 --format=JobID,State,Restarts,Start,End JobID State Restarts Start End ----------- --------- ------- ------------------- ------------------- 3 REQUEUED 0 2026-11-12T16:34:25 2026-11-12T16:34:41 3 COMPLETED 1 2026-11-12T16:37:10 2026-11-12T16:37:26 Slurm requeues a job up to the cluster’s MaxBatchRequeue limit, which was 5 on our cluster. A job submitted with #SBATCH --no-requeue reported "action": "cancel" instead and stayed canceled. With notify, there’s no HANG_ACTION_TAKEN event. The agent follows HANG_DETECTED with a record that says Hang notification sent, no automatic action taken. If a rules file is missing or invalid, the agent doesn’t monitor the job and writes a CONFIG_ERROR event instead. Here’s the event for a rules file with a JSON syntax error: {"event_type":"CONFIG_ERROR","job_id":"5","node":"ip-10-1-40-47","config_path":"/fsx/my-project/rules.json","error":"config file found but failed to load: load failed: invalid JSON in config file /fsx/my-project/rules.json: unexpected end of JSON input","message":"Hang detection rules file is invalid and will not be applied. Please fix the rules file and resubmit your job."} The job ran to completion without monitoring, and nothing appeared in sbatch, squeue, or the job’s output. Test a new rules file with a short job and check for this event before you use it for production jobs. With notify, the job keeps running until someone acts on the event. To get an alert, create a CloudWatch metric filter for HANG_DETECTED events and an alarm that notifies an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic: aws logs put-metric-filter \ --log-group-name /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/<cluster-name>/<cluster-id> \ --filter-name hung-jobs \ --filter-pattern '{ $.event_type = "HANG_DETECTED" }' \ --metric-transformations \ metricName=HungJobsDetected,metricNamespace=HyperPod/HungJobs,metricValue=1 Turn off hung job detection To turn off detection for a job that would otherwise inherit HYPERPOD_HANG_RULES, add --no-hang-detection to srun, or to sbatch to cover every step in the job. To turn it off for every job that uses a rules file, set "enabled": false in the file. Running jobs keep their current settings, and the change applies to jobs you submit afterward. srun --no-hang-detection python train.py Conclusion Node health is essential to reliable distributed training, but it does not provide a complete picture of workload health. MultiNodeTrainingValidation detects instances that pass hardware diagnostics but produce invalid training results. The HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent connects Kubernetes infrastructure failures to the jobs, pods, and nodes involved. Hung job detection identifies Slurm jobs that remain active after they stop making progress and can return them to the queue automatically. Together, these capabilities help you detect failures earlier, shorten investigations, and raise goodput by reducing the GPU time spent on workloads that can’t make useful progress. Use MultiNodeTrainingValidation when adding or revalidating capacity, run the HyperPod Kubernetes Resource Monitoring Agent continuously on supported Amazon EKS clusters, and begin hung job detection in notify mode before you switch to automatic cancellation. To get started, see the SageMaker HyperPod resiliency documentation for Amazon EKS and the hung job detection documentation for Slurm. To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod product page. The authors would like to thank Hengyu Lou, Vishal Shahane, Ziyao Huang, and Haard Mehta for their contributions to this post and features. He works on resilience related features. Kethan Gaddam Kethan is a Software Development Engineer at AWS working on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. Kethan focuses on cluster resiliency for large-scale distributed training on both Slurm and Amazon EKS, helping customers detect and recover from failures with minimal downtime. 从工具提效到统一经营智能体：快手电商用 AI 重塑商家经营流程
items.summary: 快手技术 2026-11-18 19:11 北京 快手电商如何将分散的 AI 工具整合为统一经营智能体，串联商家经营流程，让 AI 从单点提效走向任务协同。 摘要： 平台能力越来越多，商家经营为何仍然复杂 当店铺流量突然下滑，商家需要先判断问题出在哪里，再决定使用哪些工具、采取什么动作。平台提供了越来越多能力，但把这些能力组织成一套经营方案，仍然依赖商家的经验。本文结合快手电商的实践，分享商家端 AI 如何从单点工具、统一问答入口，逐步走向能够拆解目标、组织执行的经营智能体，以及这一过程中的技术选择与落地难题。 经营难题：工具能完成任务，商家仍需组织流程 平台能力越来越多，商家经营为什么没有变得更简单 店铺日常经营涉及商品、内容、营销、客服、履约、售后和资金等场景，平台能力却通常按照产品和职能组织。商家面对的是一个经营问题，使用的却可能是分散在不同入口的工具。如何选择工具、衔接动作并判断效果，仍需要商家投入时间和经验，也带来试错成本。 每次电商大促启动前，运营团队都需要回答一连串具体问题：预算怎样分配，消费券发给谁，门槛和面额怎样设置，什么时候放量，效果不及预期时又该调整哪里？ 我们的目标：让商家更容易完成经营任务 过去，我们通过完善平台功能和政策引导帮助商家开展经营。但调研反馈表明，功能增加并未消除使用门槛，商家仍然面临“不知道怎么做、不知道如何用”的问题。 随着大模型能力提升，智能客服、智能数据分析等场景逐步具备应用条件。从2024年末开始，我们重新梳理商家经营链路，探索如何让 AI 更好地承接具体工作，帮助商家更简单、有效地开展经营。 一、三阶段演进：从完成单点任务到承接经营目标 2024～2025年：AI单点能力布阵 AI结合商家经营工具全面改造 从2024年末开始，快手电商围绕短视频创作、客服接待、商品运营、店铺装修等环节升级经营工具，推出智能客服（快语）、AI成片（灵机）等产品，帮助商家减少重复性工作。这一阶段重点解决具体任务的执行效率。 2025年：全经营链路AI经营助手 7 × 24 小时在线的专业答疑帮手 2025年，我们整合已有 AI 工具，构建覆盖商家经营链路的统一助手，并联合入驻、物流、数据、资金、店铺等方向团队建设专业子 Agent。商家可以通过一个入口提出问题，由系统选择相应的专业能力处理，获得 7 × 24 小时在线支持。 2026年：迈向“数字员工” & “托管经营”阶段 从被动响应到AI托管自主经营 2026 年，我们把经营诊断、任务拆解和托管执行串了起来，用同一套 AI 能力支撑商家自主经营和平台全托管运营，商家侧，构建商家统一AI经营阵地，以一个“AI店长”协同多个“数字员工”的形式，让 AI 从提供建议走向承接经营任务，平台侧，推出全托管运营「灵顺」，把平台运营策略变成商家具体经营动作，提升经营效果 二、落地实践：工具、助手与经营智能体如何协同 2.1 单点工具：优先解决高频、重复的经营任务 商家端 AI 的建设由多个团队围绕不同经营场景推进，此处，从商家经营链路出发，整体介绍客服、内容和直播三个方向的建设成果。其中，智能客服由商家中心团队主导建设，本文将进一步展开其关键技术与实现。；内容和直播部分重点介绍兄弟团队已经建设的产品能力及应用结果 我们优先选择 AI 能稳定承接、且占用较多经营投入的日常工作，主要包括客服接待、内容生产和店铺运营。不同类型、不同规模商家的成本结构并不相同，以下从常见经营任务展开。 以下场景用于说明商家的常见经营投入，不代表所有商家具有相同的成本结构。 店铺的客服人力投入：客服接待是店铺的日常工作，咨询量和人力需求会随店铺规模与大促周期变化，尤其在双11等活动期间，集中咨询会给接待能力带来压力。 店铺的素材设计投入：这里面包括了商品的图片、店铺的装修、短视频的创作等等，过往这些事情想要做好并不简单，包括了设计、拍摄以及最后的加工合成 店铺的日常经营投入：这里面主要指的是店铺日常的运营，包括活动的报名、分销达人的合作方案以及投流推广的设置等等，这部分对专业度的要求非常的高，是一个典型的以经验驱动的较高门槛岗位 AI客服：从自动回复到可验证的问题解决 客服咨询量会随店铺规模和大促周期波动，其中又有大量高频、重复且具有标准处理路径的问题，因此成为 AI 较早试点的场景之一。 整体技术架构 核心技术 核心技术1：意图识别与规划编排，把模糊表达转换为可执行任务 消费者进线表达的可能只是“这个怎么退”“为什么还没到”，也可能只发送订单/商品卡片，甚至是一段语音，系统会结合当前会话、历史记忆、浏览商品、近期待处理订单、入口渠道和商家配置补齐上下文，再完成多模态解析、意图识别、Query 改写和风险判断，最终交由专业 Agent进行处理，当意图或对象无法可靠判断时自动携带完整上下文转交人工 核心技术2：专业Agent突破，提升售前、售后问题解决能力 在规划 Agent 完成意图识别、上下文补齐、风险判断和任务分发之后，最终承接问题解决的是按业务职责拆分出来的专业 Agent。我们没有把所有咨询都交给一个通用大模型链路处理，而是按照电商客服的业务分工，把专业能力拆成售前商品 Agent、售后处置 Agent等，从会话占比和业务价值看，售前商品咨询和售后处置是最核心的两类场景，因此我们主要以售前商品 Agent 和售后处置 Agent 为例，说明专业 Agent 建设中两类典型突破方向：一类是用知识库补齐大模型知识盲区，另一类是用 SOP 收敛大模型不确定性。 售前 Agent：全网商品知识中枢的构建 售后 Agent：用 SOP 收敛大模型不确定性 核心技术3：统一评测体系的构建，让每次自动判断可验证 早期智能客服主要关注覆盖率、接待量和转人工率。这些指标能够反映使用情况，却不能单独证明用户问题得到解决。进入 V3.0 后，评估重点转向真实解决，从回答正确、引导清晰、回复质量和方案可执行性四个维度综合判断，并通过记录、归类会话问题，支持常态化标注、评测与训练。 业务结果 AI内容：从生成工具走向稳定内容供给 图片和短视频是商家持续经营所需的内容。传统生产涉及策划、设计、拍摄、剪辑和审核，多角色协作成本较高，也难以快速跟上商品与活动变化。因此，我们分别围绕素材加工和短视频生产引入 AI 能力。 素材侧，「可译」提供扩图、高清修复、抠图、裁剪和模特上身等能力，帮助商家加工商品素材。短视频侧，「灵机」覆盖商品成片、直播切片和视频优化，让已有商品与直播素材可以继续用于短视频生产。两类产品解决的都是具体生产任务，商家可以在原有经营流程中使用。 这一阶段已形成 10+ 项 AI 内容能力，相关产品的使用商家数增长 49% 核心结果 AI直播：让直播方法与直播供给同时规模化 直播涉及多个经营环节，需要系统性的辅助能力。主播需要在直播前、中、后完成10+环节的工作，部分中小主播难以完整执行这些环节，因此我们围绕直播全链路提供辅助能力，降低准备与运营门槛。 电商慧播把直播全流程的工作拆成选品、台本、计划、讲解卡、智能回复和直播诊断等环节，帮助真人主播准备和调整直播。女娲数字人直播提供直播脚本、数字人形象与音色、直播间装修、互动库、组件挂载和定时开播等能力，支撑缺少主播的商家持续供给直播内容。 目前相关产品集成20+ 项 AI 直播能力，覆盖 10 万+ 商家与主播；女娲侧沉淀了900+ 数字人主播、150+ 地区音色和 200+ 装修模板 核心结果 2.2 全经营链路AI经营助手：从产品矩阵走向统一经营助手 产品介绍 随着单点 AI 产品增多，我们发现商家仍然需要知道应该在什么时候使用哪项能力。客服、内容和直播能力分别有效，并不意味着它们已经形成一套经营服务，2025 年，我们开始把不同业务方向的知识、数据和专业能力接入统一经营助手。商家不再需要先理解平台的产品结构，只需要直接表达问题。系统负责识别真实意图、补齐商家上下文，再选择知识库、经营数据或领域 Agent 进行处理。 页面入口-智能小二 Multi-Agent经营能力协同 架构介绍 经营助手采用 Multi-Agent 架构，由网关层、Agent 运行层和底层基建三层构成，支撑不同领域专业能力通过统一入口提供服务。 成果 到 2025 年第四季度，经营助手已经串联 20+ 经营场景，商家自助解决率超过 70%，月均服务商家超过 10 万。自然语言由此开始成为商家使用平台能力的新入口 从回答问题到推进任务：统一入口之后还缺什么 单点工具解决了具体任务，统一助手降低了寻找能力的门槛，但商家仍需要把建议变成行动：系统给出原因和建议之后，接下来做什么、如何组织执行，仍需要商家决定。这成为下一阶段的重点。 2026年初，我们进一步探索 Agent 的工具调用、记忆和长任务能力，让 AI 能够持续推进一段经营任务，而不只处理一次请求。升级方向是整合已有 AI 工具，将“商家是谁”“经营问题在哪里”“下一步该怎么优化”串起来，形成面向具体商家的商家统一经营智能体 2.3 商家经营智能体：从拆解目标到自动执行 产品形态：一个虚拟店长，协同多个数字员工 在产品形态上，面向商家，呈现为一个统一的虚拟店长；在虚拟店长背后，不同数字员工分别承担数据分析、商品优化、内容生产和经营执行等任务。商家不再需要理解系统内部如何分工，只需要提出目标、确认关键决策并查看执行结果 经营智能体-入口 经营智能体-能力 核心技术 1.B端统一经营大脑：为商家制定下一步专属成长计划 经营大脑核心是将商家增长目标拆解到 GMV、流量获取、转化效率、运营健康、服务保障等不同经营层级，再针对不同分型和成长阶段的商家给出差异化行动建议，最终输出给商家的就是当前优先处理哪个问题、为什么要处理、可以由哪个数字员工承接 商家经营画像：识别商家的商品特征和经营生命周期，从不同维度刻画商家的经营潜力、经营习惯。 AI经营策略：基于商家的经营画像，参考同类标杆商家的经营策略知识库，进行个性化经营策略规划，拆解经营目标、制定行动方案。 AI经营执行：基于AI制定的经营策略，进行自动化的经营执行。 AI优化策略：跟踪经营动作的执行效果，沉淀至商家的个性化经营记忆，并对之前的经营策略进行调整，持续优化。 2.可编排的AI工作流：把多个动作串起来，解决高频重复问题 很多时候不是单个工具不好用，而是动作太多、链路太长。商家真正要完成的，往往是一整条链路：发现问题，分析原因，选出对象，生成方案，执行动作，再看结果，因此我们把商家在B端常态化的经营场景按工作流拆解并组织，把不同数字员工的 Skill 通过流程进行组织，形成可编排、可托管、可自动化执行的经营任务链路，这样把原来需要商家跨多个页面、多个工具、多个角色才能完成的复杂经营动作，组织成一条可执行链路 3.多租户 Agent Runtime：共享计算，隔离商家状态与权限 为了支撑数字员工业务，我们整体构建了一套面向B端的分布式 Agent OS。将 Agent 改造成云端统一调度、分布式无状态运行的服务，把商家上下文和任务状态从实例中抽离，并统一提供 Agent、Skill、Memory、任务串行化、权限风控、运行观测和成本治理能力。 同一套集群可以服务大量商家，计算节点可以替换，经营任务仍能沿着已有状态继续执行，同时在安全方面，整体从数据安全、应用安全、内容安全、网络安全多个角度设计满足 AI 应用安全环境要求的统一安全防护网，提供可靠的身份认证、全链路可审计、网络访问限制、执行环境隔离等能力 业务结果 三、踩过的坑 3.1 坑一：复杂经营任务，不是一次规划就能解决的 项目初期，我们希望模型一次生成完整计划，再依次调用工具完成经营任务，但计划容易在执行中途失效。比如当排好一次计划后，对应的商品、时令乃至商家本身经营状态的变化，都影响了计划的延续，因此，我们将确定的步骤交给工作流，在关键节点重新读取状态，需要重新判断时再由 Agent 调整下一步3.2 坑二、B端SKILL集成的复杂度挑战 想要代替商家做托管执行，其背后最关键的就是将业务接口标准并SKILL化，商家经营链路里涉及到的能力盘点下来累计有200+个，而这些接口最初为页面操作设计，参数语义、幂等方式、权限模型和错误码并不统一，因此在开放给 Agent 之前，需要先补齐这些契约，让工具调用具有明确、可校验的边界 3.3 坑三：原型验证通过，不代表能直接承载生产任务 OpenClaw帮助我们验证了 Agent、工具调用和长任务运行方式，但面向个人场景的强状态架构难以直接承载商家侧生产任务。我们初始在入驻场景小规模跑通的架构，当复用到商家完整经营链路的时候，发现需要为每个商家独立申请机器，这就意味着我们要去申请数十万台的机器，这根本不现实，因此我们重构多租户 Runtime，把状态从实例中抽离，把计算变成可以弹性调度和替换的 Worker，再统一建设权限、审计、恢复和成本控制 四、下一步：在授权边界内逐步扩大托管范围 当前系统能发现问题、给出建议、生成方案，但关键动作还需要商家频繁确认和手动推进。下一阶段，我们希望在授权和风控边界清晰的前提下，逐步走向有限托管执行，让系统可以 7 x 24 小时自动完成经营问题识别、优化方案生成、执行落地和结果反馈。 这并不意味着系统替商家做所有决定。高风险动作需要商家确认，低风险、高频、重复的动作则逐步交给系统自动推进；执行后，再将数据变化、执行记录和下一步建议反馈给商家。 五、团队介绍 快手电商商家和运营赋能中心技术团队，面向商家、达人与平台运营，覆盖全链路经营场景。团队定位为连接经营目标与系统能力的经营技术团队，聚焦商家经营与平台运营的智能化升级，由此降低经营成本、提升运营效率，驱动业务增长。技术体系以智能经营闭环为业务主线，贯通经营场域的洞察、决策、执行与复盘归因；数字员工，即面向平台运营的 AI 运营智能体，是规模化运营载体。AI、数据智能与B端平台构成技术底座，并以 AI 原生研发方式支撑从业务判断到产品验证的迭代。 【活动推荐】 跳转微信打开

items.title: 动线Agent：AI驱动的全链路用户转化引导
items.summary: 原创 淘特用户技术团队 2026-11-18 16:37 浙江 本文介绍了淘特App推出的动线Agent——一套由大模型（LLM）驱动的全链路用户转化引导系统。针对近90%到端用户未完成转化的痛点，该系统围绕用户旅程（ 进端/在端/离端 ）部署了三个差异化智能体。三者均取得显著业务增益，整体峰值增量GMV占比超大盘5%，且通过技术手段将token成本降低60%以上。未来将推动三端从数据回流走向共享决策状态，构建统一的用户智能体。 摘要 在注意力经济时代，短视频足够好刷，游戏和内容 App 也在持续争夺用户时间。如果用户打开了一个购物 App，本身就是一次昂贵且高价值的行为。一般电商App 的访购率约为百分之十几，这意味着近百分八九十的到端用户并没有完成转化。从入端到成交，用户并不会沿着一条直线前进，而是会经历浏览、比较、犹豫、放弃与回归，如何在这个过程中完成对用户的转化引导？ 本文提出 动线 Agent —— 一套面向淘特场景、由 LLM 驱动的全链路用户引导系统。它围绕用户「进端 → 在端 → 离端」三个核心时机，部署三个差异化的智能体，构建三种互补的决策模式： TensorLiftAgent（精细化模式）于进端时机，通过多维用户特征张量分解，生成网格人群和差异化的权益策略，后台天级寻优、入端毫秒命中，结合AB 实验持续汰换策略做大SOTA桶； PeiAgent（快决策模式）于在端时机，端云协同实时计算用户的个性化购物热情指数（PEI, Purchase Enthusiasm Index），当判断用户的指数衰减达到某个阈值，立即触发基于行为序列与意图的AI推理的权益干预； DeepFlowAgent（慢思考模式）于离端未购时机，异步执行长链 CoT 深度归因推理，生成个性化权益与营销话术并多渠道召回。 效果上，三个模式均上线并达到一定规模效果：进端增益 ROI 提升三成左右；在端与离端的增量 ROI 均超过目标十个百分点以上。同时在token规模上，消耗峰值达到数百亿token/日的规模，通过技术手段也将token成本降低了超一半以上。目前三种模式只做到了数据层面的回流，还没有形成用户视角的联动，这也是下一阶段重点工作。 用 AI 重新做一遍用户动线 这一部分回答两个问题：1）用户动线agent是什么？ 2）动线agent的三种模式为什么？ ▐动线agent是什么？ 真实的用户购物过程往往不是“进入—浏览—下单”的直线，而更像： 打开 APP → 搜索商品 → 比较几款 → ... → 返回搜索 → 再看商详 → ... → 犹豫 → 暂时离开 → 跨APP对比→... → 可能再次回来。 在这个过程中，用户的意图也在变化：反复查看某件商品，可能意味着需求明确但价格尚未达到预期；频繁换搜索词，可能是在细化需求，也可能是一直没有找到合适的商品；加购后离开，既可能是等待优惠，也可能只是被其他事情打断。因此，问题不只是“有没有发优惠券”，而是：平台是否理解了用户当下需要什么，是否在合适的时刻采取了合适的动作？ 用户动线agent是一套面向电商用户全动线、由 LLM 驱动并受确定性规则约束的智能经营系统，在不同时间尺度上完成用户理解、策略生成、权益干预、效果验证与持续优化。 ▐三种时机，三种决策模式 如果目标都是促进转化，为什么不使用一个 Agent 处理所有场景？ 原因在于，不同决策的时效、粒度和信息条件差异很大。入端策略需要覆盖较大规模人群，不能让每次打开 APP 都等待复杂推理；在端决策需要及时捕捉状态变化；离端后则可以利用更完整的行为轨迹，进行更充分的分析。 用户时机 对应 Agent 首要问题 决策粒度 计算方式 时间预算 入端 TensorLiftAgent 这类用户适合什么目标与权益策略？ 人群网格 后台生成与验证，在线读取策略 在线命中小于 50ms 在端 PeiAgent 购物热情是否衰减，现在是否需要干预？ 当前用户、当前会话 端侧感知，云端生成干预策略 百毫秒级感知秒级干预 离端未购 DeepFlowAgent 为什么没买，是否值得召回，怎样召回？ 单用户及其行为序列 云端异步、多阶段推理 秒级到分钟级异步推理 三类 Agent 的差异，不只是部署位置不同，而是分别对应三种问题形态： 进端是组合优化问题：需要从复杂人群和策略空间中寻找更优组合。 在端是时机判断问题：需要在极短时间里判断用户热情是否衰减，并做轻量干预。 离端是深度理解问题：可以利用更完整的行为上下文，进行多步意图推理和策略生成。 ▐动线Agent 整体架构 以上是由TensorLiftAgent/PeiAgent/DeepFlowAgent共同组成的动线agent体系，以下就围绕进端/在端/离端三个问题展开： 进端：TensorLiftAgent 如何实现精细化经营？ 在端：PeiAgent 如何抓住转瞬即逝的干预窗口？ 离端：DeepFlowAgent 如何完成一次深度归因？ 进端：TensorLiftAgent 如何实现精细化经营？ ▐核心思路：张量分解与区隔度寻优 在后台定时策略运行，不直接面向用户。 将传统「人群粗放运营」升级为基于多维用户特征张量分解的精细化策略生成， 通过Agent不断从各个维度切分人群、生成策略、AB验证、回收效果，构建自优化的持续循环。 用户进端时仅做策略命中——实时匹配预先生成好的策略，保证毫秒级响应。 ▐基于LLM的多层Loop寻优方案 每天调度器拉起一条流水线：规划先看昨天的成绩和历史记忆，决定今天往什么方向执行；张量下钻把人群切成网格；定价给每个网格出价；回测当考官判卷，不过关就打回重做（② 中层循环）；每个环节的产物还要先过质检，不合格原地重做（① 内层循环）；校验通过才投放上线，第二天回收诊断拿真实 AB 数据批改，结论喂给次日的规划（③ 外层循环）。所有过程与经验都沉淀在 Memory Engine 里跨天复用——整个系统就形成了一台「找答案、判卷、复盘」的寻优机器。 ▐四桶实验策略设计 线上实验则提供四类不同角色： 空桶：保留自然成交基准，用来观察干预带来的增量。 运营桶：承接既有人工或业务策略，提供业务比较基准。 探索桶：在受控流量中验证新候选，用于不断探索潜在最优方案。 SOTA桶：承接已验证的较优方案，作为后续挑战的对象。 为什么对照 SOTA 而不是对照空桶与空桶对照只能回答做了比不做好吗，与 SOTA 对照才能回答新策略比当前最好的策略更好吗——只有后者能保证 SOTA 桶单调变优。空桶的价值在数仓口径（绝对增量与增量 ROI），运营桶的价值在不劣于人工这条底线。 ▐定价决策链 定价环节每天要做的是在 SOTA 桶现有价格的基础上，为桶内每一个人群网格重新求一个更优的确定价，产出一份整桶提案，再交给回测与线上实验去验证。 可以概括成一句话：以现价为起点、整桶只攻一个短板方向、只有目标匹配的网格才承接调价、承接格锁定历史更优点、最后在成本上限内腾挪预算。经过这样每天一轮的重新求解，SOTA 桶的价格被持续、单调地推向更优。 ▐帕累托寻优 基于以上的实验方案设计，通过不断地的loop策略调整，整体的策略呈现出如下图的寻优轨迹。 在「访购率提升 × AB 增量 ROI」这个二维平面上，各桶的表现如下： 帕累托前沿由 SOTA 桶（高 ROI 端）与探索桶（高提升端）共同构成 中控桶被探索桶支配，在本期指定人群及指标口径下，中控桶处于观测到的帕累托前沿内侧 这个结论对业务侧的意义比单个指标大：用几何方式证明了AI 寻优机制整体上已经超越了人工中控，而且前沿的两端分别由"守住效率"和"探索提升"两种角色构成——这恰好就是四桶实验体系设计意图。 在端：PeiAgent 如何抓住转瞬即逝的干预窗口？ ▐实时购物热情指数 用户在 App 内的购物意愿会不断变化：一次有效搜索可能让意愿上升，连续无点击、频繁换词、商详秒退和回退首页，则可能意味着用户正在失去耐心。我们定义了 PEI（Purchase Enthusiasm Index，购物热情指数），用于实时描述用户购物意愿的变化，而不是只判断用户“有意图”或“没意图”。 PEI 随用户行为变化，并在重度衰减时触发干预，类似一支“购物体温计”，例如： 搜索、点击商品、深度浏览和加购会提高热情； 无点击浏览、频繁换词、商详浅出和回退会拉低热情； 系统持续记录当前值、历史峰值和衰减轨迹； 当 PEI 跌破个性化阈值时，触发一次干预决策。 ▐端云协同：为什么算分必须在端上 PEI 的实现是一个端云协同模式： 在端内构建一个PEI（Purchase Enthusiasm Index，购物热情指数）的实时计算体系， 像体温计一样持续感知用户的购物意愿。如果热情出现明显衰减，会触发Agent的推理和干预，在用户离开前完成转化。 层 职责 为什么放这里 App 端 PEI 实时计算 + 决定是否需要干预 行为事件在端上产生，端上算分免去网络往返，才能压进 < 200ms 的约束；同时避免把全量行为流水实时上抛 服务端 用户意图推理 + 生成干预策略 需要聚合画像、历史记录、权益库存、成本约束，只有服务端有全量上下文 ▐LLM快速推理权益干预 在 PEI 场景中，大模型不能只根据“用户快流失了”就给出大额红包，策略必须同时满足： 服务端采用明确的决策顺序： 这种拆分把语义理解交给 LLM，把金额计算和红线检查交给代码，避免模型因为强意图而跨越预算或费比边界。这些结果验证了一个重要判断：干预效果不仅取决于发什么，更取决于是否在用户热情真正衰减的时刻发。 离端：DeepFlowAgent 如何完成一次深度归因？ ▐离端其实是信息量最大的一刻 直觉上，用户关掉 App 就意味着这一轮引导失败了，只能等下次。但换个角度看，用户的完整行为序列信息在他离端的那一刻是最完整的。而"没有时间限制"并能从非结构化的日志数据中提出有效的信息，恰恰又是 LLM 最擅长的场景。 ▐一个朴素猜想的验证 这个的起点是基于一个很朴素的猜想：基于用户的原始行为日志，LLM 能推导出什么？ 以上基于用户的原始IPV行为日志，LLM可以结合世界知识以及当前时间地点以及气候推导出很多额外的信息（将气候和用户需求联系起来）。于是从这个猜想开始，想构建一种能力：基于用户行为序列做意图深度推理，并构建针对性的转化策略。 ▐慢思考，三轮Chain架构 当用户没有购买就离开APP时，触发Agent的深度思考模式。 不受实时性约束，可以调用更复杂的推理链（Chain-of-Thought），深度分析用户未购原因， 并生成个性化的权益策略和营销话术，通过Push等方式推送给用户实现召回。 实现上是一套三轮 Chain 架构： Chain 1 召回判断 —— 该不该召回？置信度多少？犹豫原因是什么？ Chain 2 选品定价 —— 钩哪个商品？发多大红包？门槛多少？成本比是否可接受？ Chain 3 文案生成 —— Push 标题怎么写？正文怎么写？什么时机发？走哪个渠道？ 为什么拆三轮，因为这三件事的失败代价、评测口径和优化手段完全不同： 召回判断错了 → 打扰用户，代价是退订率和品牌感受，评测看准确率/召回率 选品定价错了 → 花冤枉钱，代价是真金白银的损失，评测看成本比和增量 ROI 文案生成错了 → 点击率低，代价是转化效率，评测看 CTR 和主观质量分 混在一次调用里，任何一环出问题都会污染整个输出，而且没法归因到底是哪一环错了。拆开之后每一轮可以独立评测、独立迭代、独立灰度。慢思考的另一个好处是不受实时性约束，因此可以调用更复杂的推理链，也可以用多轮换取质量。 ▐一个真实的推理归因 以下是一个真实的推理输出： { "confidenceScore": 92, "hesitationReason": "price", "needRecall": true, "pushTitle": "🎣 您看的加重渔网，立减6元！", "pushContent": "进口三层沉网捕大鱼，原价47元，专属红包再省6元！湛江老乡专享", "searchKeyword": "加重渔网", "redPacketThreshold": 4700, "recommendedRedPacketAmount": 600, "redPacketCostRatio": 0.128, "userIntent": "用户为55岁男性农林牧渔从业者，多次浏览垂钓用渔网（价格47-52元）和低价小说（18-39元），结合其职业和地域（湛江沿海），对渔具需求明确且真实，小说浏览可能为兴趣延伸。核心意图是购买实用渔网用于捕鱼作业。", "recallReason": "用户多次深度浏览高相关性渔具商品，职业与商品强匹配，且最后行为聚焦在渔网上，价格敏感但购买力中等（buyLevelCode=7），通过精准红包可有效降低决策门槛促成转化" } 可以看这几处： "湛江老乡专享" —— 地域信息被用成了情感钩子。这不是模板里配的字段，是模型自己决定要这么说的。 "进口三层沉网捕大鱼"—— 这是渔具行业的专业卖点话术。模型知道捕鱼用的沉网和观赏渔网不是一回事，知道"三层沉网"对这个用户意味着什么。 "原价47元，专属红包再省6元" —— 47 元正是用户反复浏览的那个价格带的下沿。门槛 4700 分贴着到手价定，面额 600 分对应 12.8% 的成本比，全落在合规区间内。 "小说浏览可能为兴趣延伸" —— 它没有被那几条低价小说的浏览记录带偏，正确判断出主线意图是渔具、小说只是干扰项。 传统规则系统能写出"您关注的商品降价了"，但很难写出"湛江老乡专享"和"三层沉网"——因为它不知道湛江靠海、不知道沉网是干什么的、也不知道这两件事和买渔网有什么关系。 下一步：走向统一的用户智能体 动线 Agent 的价值，在于尝试建立一种新的用户经营方式：平台能够沿着用户完整旅程持续感知状态，在不同时间尺度上做出合适决策，并通过真实业务结果不断修正自己。用户进端时，系统已经为他准备了更精细的策略；用户在端内犹豫时，系统能够感知热情变化并及时提供帮助；用户未购离开后，系统还能理解他为什么放弃，并给出一个更有针对性的回来理由。 但三种模式分别落地，只是全链路经营的起点。用户不会感知自己正在被哪个 Agent 服务，他只会感知平台有没有理解自己、给出的权益是否一致、提醒是否过于频繁。 因此下一步协同需要从共享数据走向共享决策状态：已经发放和使用过什么权益，当前还有哪些动作在执行，用户是否完成购买，预算与频控还剩多少。新的决策应基于这些状态，而不是每个模式都从零开始判断。接下来的重点需要补齐一些基础能力，例如统一用户经营状态，建立全链路实验视角，让个性化与自优化服从证据等。 最终，动线 Agent 希望形成的能力可以归结为一句话：看得见用户的状态变化，算得清干预的真实增量，能在有效窗口内行动，也能根据结果修正甚至撤销自己的判断。 团队介绍 本文作者山泽，来自淘天集团 - 淘特用户技术团队，主要负责淘特C端链路&淘宝行业的研发工作，包含搜索推荐、用户运营、导购、交易等C端基础服务及B端招商供给业务。在这里我们致力于探索人工智能与大数据技术在核心电商业务的落地与实践。 ¤ 拓展阅读 ¤
